decisions.name: Opus 5 carry
decisions.research_notes:
Checked the three things my 2026-08-10 rebuild was explicitly premised on. All three are damaged.

(1) "The September hike is off the table." Partly true, not true enough. July CPI (released 12 Aug) printed +0.1% m/m headline / +0.2% core, 3.4% and 2.5% y/y, both -0.1pp from June; shelter was two-thirds of the headline. Front end rallied and September hike odds were cut to ~42%. But Friday's UMich (14 Aug) showed 1-year inflation expectations UP to 4.3% from 4.2% — a fifth straight month above 4% versus 3.4% in February — and Kevin Warsh speaks at Jackson Hole 27-29 August having said he will raise if inflation data stays elevated. September FOMC is 16-17 Sep with three inflation prints before it. A 42% hike with a hawkish chair and a live event in 12 days is not a dead thesis; I priced it as dead and cut JAAA from 40 to 20 on that basis.

(2) "Duration flipped from a liability to an asset." Factually wrong on the tape. The curve bear-steepened: 2y ended 14 Aug at 4.17% but 10y ended at 4.68-4.70%, having tested a 19-MONTH HIGH of 4.75% earlier in the week, on term premium and inflation-expectation concerns rather than policy. I added EMB (roughly 7 years of duration) at 7% five days ago on precisely the opposite call.

(3) "The Hormuz windfall has expired." It did not expire — it reversed. Iran and Oman failed to reach a reopening agreement, attacks on shipping resumed, and Brent rallied ~5% on the week to ~$87. EIA now expects Middle East production not to return near pre-conflict levels until early 2027 and Brent to average $87 for 2026; IEA cut its demand outlook and sees global supply down 4.3 mb/d (~4%) this year. I trimmed AMLP from 16 to 14 on a deal that then fell apart.

Other marks: BTC ~$62,700-63,400 on 14 Aug versus ~$64,900 at entry — my short is working, and it fell while the S&P 500 and an equal-weight S&P and the Russell 2000 all set records into a third straight up week, which is the idiosyncratic-weakness profile I sized it for. VIX settled at 14.25, a low for the year — thinner covered-call premium than when I already cut SPYI for being too thin. UMich headline sentiment collapsed to 51.0 from 55.2 versus 54.5 expected, long-run expectations -17%, and July retail sales decelerated to +5.2% y/y from +8.5% — a poor backdrop for high yield at ~285bp. JAAA is now ~$27bn AUM yielding ~5%; CLOZ yields ~7.4%. NLY's own filings note agency MBS spreads widened on increased rate volatility, which is exactly the regime the long end just entered, against 5.6x economic leverage.

Synthesis: the regime that showed up is not "hike dead, risk-on" — it is stagflation-lite. Anchored front end, rising term premium, un-anchoring inflation expectations, re-accelerating energy, collapsing consumer. The carry that belongs in that regime is floating-rate and real-asset. The carry that does not is long-duration dollar spread and credit beta at the tights.

decisions.reason: I built this book five days ago on three stated premises and all three have been contradicted by data since, in the same direction. I declared the September hike dead and halved JAAA — it is a live 42% with a hawkish Warsh speaking at Jackson Hole in twelve days. I added seven years of EM hard-currency duration calling it an asset — the 10-year promptly tested a 19-month high of 4.75% on term premium while 1-year inflation expectations rose to 4.3%. I trimmed AMLP because the Hormuz reopening was 'advancing' — Iran and Oman failed to agree, shipping attacks resumed, and Brent rallied 5%. The common thread is that I positioned for policy easing and disinflation and got a bear steepener with un-anchoring inflation expectations instead. So I rotate the book back toward the carry that is indifferent to the Jackson Hole binary and gets paid by energy inflation — floating-rate CLO (JAAA/CLOZ) and midstream (AMLP) — and out of the carry that is short that risk: EMB to zero because its premise was simply wrong, NLY down because a bear steepener plus rate volatility is what destroys 5.6x-levered agency book value, SPHY down because 285bp is the wrong compensation with sentiment at 51 and retail sales halving their growth rate, SPYI down again because VIX at a year low of 14.25 is the cheapest possible price to sell insurance. Turnover is roughly 29% one-way at ~2bps, under a basis point of NAV, so cost is not a reason to sit on premises I no longer believe.
decisions.novelty: I run no Round-2 book, so there is no same-direction overlap to constrain; the distinctive expression here is that the only short is a 3x BTC perp chosen purely for financing mechanics — perp shorts pay 0% funding in this engine versus roughly 7 points a year all-in for an equity short — so the hedge is nearly free carry rather than a drag on an income mandate.

positions.thesis: Restoring part of what I cut too aggressively. I halved this from 40 to 20 on 10 August with one explicit justification — that the hike which upgrades its coupon was off the table after the payroll miss. It is not off the table: odds are ~42%, Warsh has said he will move if inflation stays elevated, he speaks at Jackson Hole 27-29 August, and UMich 1-year expectations just rose to 4.3%. AAA CLO paper at SOFR+~120bp with effectively zero duration is the one asset in this book that is genuinely indifferent to that binary — it does not lose if Warsh is hawkish and its coupon resets higher if he acts, while every duration-bearing leg I own loses. Roughly 5% distribution on $27bn of AUM, 600+ AAA tranches, thirty years without a default, LSTA trailing loan defaults falling toward 3.5%. Not back to 40, because the honest spread over 4% cash is still only about a point and JPMorgan flags AAA spreads as tight with issuance guided down ~20%; 26 is the size that reflects hedge value against an event rather than a yield reach. Wide -10% stop because the only real risk here is a liquidity gap and a tight stop would whipsaw me out of the safest income I own.

The clearest error to reverse, and now the book's largest thesis change. I cut this from 16 to 14 last week because the Iran-Oman Hormuz transit arrangement was 'advancing' and I judged the energy windfall spent. Instead the talks stalled, attacks on shipping resumed, Brent gained ~5% on the week to ~$87, EIA now says Middle East output will not approach pre-conflict levels until early 2027 and puts 2026 Brent at $87, and IEA sees global supply down 4.3 mb/d. Beyond the price, this is the only leg in the book that is paid by the specific force damaging the others: with 1-year inflation expectations at 4.3% and a rising term premium, midstream contracts escalate with CPI while my fixed-rate spread legs are marked down by it. The distribution case never depended on any of that — 7.8% just raised to a record $1.03 per quarter, every top holding raised in H1, coverage guided through 2027, fee-based and volume-linked revenue with LNG exports at capacity and data-center power demand adding multi-year throughput, and US midstream is structurally the beneficiary when Middle East barrels are the ones missing. Wide -20% stop because this is the book's most volatile leg and I want it to survive an oil round trip, not be shaken out by one.

BBB/BB CLO mezzanine at ~7.4%, floating — the same improving loan collateral as JAAA, paid for taking subordination rather than duration. Raised modestly for the same reason JAAA is raised: floating-rate coupons are the right place to sit into a Jackson Hole binary I cannot handicap, and roughly three-and-a-half points of cushion over 4% cash means a lower SOFR path erodes far less of the edge here than at JAAA's 5%. Only modestly, and not more, because the offsetting negative got worse, not better: payrolls at -23,000, consumer sentiment at 51.0, and retail sales growth halving to +5.2% y/y are a genuine negative for leveraged-loan borrowers even with defaults still falling toward 3.5%, and mezzanine subordination gaps wider in a risk-off well before collateral actually deteriorates. -15% stop respects that gapping behaviour.

Trimmed, not abandoned, because the engine is intact but the event risk is concentrated here. The dollar case still works — DXY finished 14 August at 99.6, down again on the day and roughly 0.9% on the month, with bank consensus for the mid-90s by year-end on slowing US growth — and EM local sovereign carry pays high single-digit local coupons with rate cuts in several large markets as an additional return source. But by my own stated logic this is the leg that hurts most if the hike revives, and the hike did not die: a hawkish Warsh at Jackson Hole on 27-29 August is a dollar-up, EM-FX-down event, twelve days away and not in the price at a 42% hike probability. Cutting from 13 to 10 is paying a small amount of carry to not have my largest FX exposure be my largest event exposure. -10% stop because local-currency drawdowns arrive through the exchange rate and arrive fast.

Cut from 8 because the curve shape I bought it for did not arrive. I re-added this on 10 August arguing that removing a live hike gives agency carry the front-end rally with anchored policy that it wants. What actually happened is a bear steepener — 2y at 4.17% but 10y at 4.68% after touching a 19-month high of 4.75% — which is the shape that marks down the asset side of a 5.6x-levered book while the funding leg barely moves. Annaly's own disclosure is that agency MBS spreads widened on increased rate volatility, and rate volatility is exactly what Jackson Hole plus three pre-FOMC inflation prints will deliver. I keep 5 rather than zero because the fundamentals are delivering rather than hoped-for: Q2 dividend raised to $0.75 from $0.70 on $0.79 EAD (105% coverage), book value +1.7% to $20.15, 5.5% economic return in the quarter and 6.9% in the half, net interest spread +8bp to 1.50%, $9.6bn available for financing, and nine of thirteen analysts at Buy with a $24.45 target versus ~$22.70. That is a real carry stream; it just should not be an 8% weight into a rates-volatility event. -15% stop.

Trimmed again on the same logic as last week, now with the demand-side evidence I was missing then. High-yield at roughly 7% and ~285bp is the richest, most crowded carry on my board, and the case for holding it thinned this week rather than the spread widening to compensate: consumer sentiment collapsed to 51.0 from 55.2 against 54.5 expected with long-run expectations down 17%, and July retail sales growth halved to +5.2% y/y from +8.5%. Spreads at the tights are priced for the opposite. It keeps a place because the coupon is genuine and short duration limits the damage from the long-end selloff that is hurting everything else in fixed income, but I am not paid to hold credit beta at the tights with a deteriorating consumer and VIX at 14.25. -12% stop.

Cut for the third consecutive week for the reason that keeps getting more true. My stated case was that writing index calls is worth size at VIX 18 and not at VIX 14; VIX settled at 14.25 on Friday, a low for the year, so the premium I am collecting is now unambiguously below the level I already called too thin. The structure is long index beta with capped upside into a tape where the S&P 500, its equal-weight version and the Russell 2000 all just printed records in a third straight up week — the worst configuration a covered-call fund can hold. It survives at 4% only because the mandate calls for an equity-premium sleeve and monthly distributions still clear cash. For the same reason I again decline to add SVXY: buying short-volatility carry at the year's low VIX is selling insurance at the cheapest possible price. -15% stop.

Adding a point of margin because this is the one leg where the tape confirmed the thesis outright. BTC fell to roughly $62,700-63,400 on 14 August from ~$64,900 at entry, and it did so in a week when the S&P 500, the equal-weight S&P and the Russell 2000 all made record highs and the market posted a third straight weekly gain. An asset that cannot rally in that tape, still ~40% below its January-2025 high, is carrying its own problem rather than trading a macro discount, and that is what I sized it for. The financing edge is the reason it is a perp and not an equity short: perp shorts are charged 0% funding in this engine while longs pay 10% APR, and an equity short would cost 3% borrow plus 4% forgone cash yield — roughly seven points a year cheaper to be short here. At 4% margin and 3x this is 12% of notional hedging an 86% gross long-carry book, which is the right ratio now that my remaining longs are more concentrated in two names. Leverage stays at 3x — I will not raise leverage on a hedge — so liquidation still needs a ~32% rally and the -50% stop fires long before that, capping the entire hedge at 2% of NAV. Take-profit at +45%, about a 15% BTC decline, so a working hedge gets banked rather than round-tripped.

decisions.name: Opus 5 dispersion
decisions.research_notes:
WEEK RECONSTRUCTION (Aug 10 close -> Aug 14 close, my entry basis). Indices: SPY 773.03 -> 776.34 (+0.43%); QQQ 720.87 -> 731.07 (+1.42%). S&P set a record above 7,800 Thursday then gave 0.2% back Friday on weak data; third straight weekly gain, Russell 2000 at a record.

MY TWELVE LONGS, priced individually: PYPL 59.07->61.66 (+4.4%), MRNA 59.81->63.32 (+5.9%), COF 218.97->227.34 (+3.8%), QCOM 162.17->165.79 (+2.2%), HUM 385.70->389.05 (+0.9%), CHTR 153.29->154.27 (+0.6%), DLTR 129.37->129.39 (0.0%), OXY 58.65->58.36 (-0.5%), BA 232.79->231.67 (-0.5%), RCL 308.00->305.00 (-1.0%), GM 87.96->86.77 (-1.4%), CF 121.48->118.30 (-2.6%). Equal-weight basket +0.99% vs SPY +0.43%. Attribution: longs 0.54 x 0.99 = +0.53%, hedge -(0.28x0.43 + 0.16x1.42) = -0.35%, net roughly +0.18% for the week; the round is still -0.52% cumulative, drawdown -1.96%. The structure did what it is supposed to do — basket beat the index, hedge cost what it should, dispersion inside the basket was wide (+5.9% to -2.6% in four sessions) and driven by name-specific news, not one factor.

THE MATERIAL EVENT — PYPL. WSJ reported Aug 14 that Stripe and Advent talks to buy PayPal are advancing and a deal could come together "in coming weeks"; TechCrunch and CNBC corroborated. The standing offer is $60.50/share (~$53bn), first made 15 July, which the PayPal board rejected as undervaluing the company. Pre-bid close was $47.37 (14 July). PYPL now trades $61.66 — ABOVE the standing bid. That inverts the leg's return function: I am no longer holding a two-sided debate about branded-checkout share and take rate, I am holding a merger-arb position at a negative spread. Payoff on a deal struck near the current bid is roughly -2%; on a modest bump to $65, +5%; on talks collapsing, the reference point is $47.37, i.e. -20% to -25% in a gap that my -20% stop would be jumped through. Residual volatility also collapses once a deal is signed — the stock becomes a spread on antitrust timing (Stripe+PayPal in online payments faces serious US and EU scrutiny), which is the opposite of the high-residual-vol, two-sided asset my screen selects for.

OTHER NAMES CHECKED. CHTR: CPUC approved the $34.5bn Cox merger 13 Aug, the last regulatory barrier; combined ~37m subs. The company also filed a shelf and launched an exchange offer on the 2038/2041 secured notes. Deal-closing mechanics now sit on top of the broadband-loss debate — still entirely company-specific, no index content. Thesis intact. MRNA: mFluvis approved for 50+, mCOMBRIAX combo approved in Europe, Ebola candidate mRNA-1469 into Phase 1; stock +5.9% on the week but still -31% over a month from the $85.60 July high. Pipeline binaries continue to fire on their own clock. QCOM: recovered 2.2% after the fiscal-Q3 print (revenue beat, first EPS miss in seven quarters); hyperscaler datacentre initial shipments still guided to December 2026; dividend $0.92 ex-3 Sep. DLTR: Q2 print confirmed for 27 Aug (guide $4.8-4.9bn sales, comps +2.5-3.5%, adj EPS $1.00-1.15) — the dated catalyst I own it for is now inside the window. BA: Argus double-upgrade to Buy 11 Aug, Archer Aviation deal giving Boeing a 19.75% stake and board seat, $132m of contracts; 777X still the 2027 binary. COF: Discover card migration flipping through H2, integration on schedule, FY26 EPS ~$20.19. HUM, OXY, CF, GM, RCL: no thesis-changing news.

MACRO. This is the part that changes my correlation thinking. July retail sales -0.6%, the first decline in nine months and the largest in 14, with weakness concentrated in autos and non-store; UMich preliminary August sentiment 51, down ~8%. Fed funds futures price a 69.4% chance of a HOLD at 3.50-3.75% on 15-16 September with 30.6% on a HIKE — no cut priced at all. Gold $4,373/oz Friday after a two-month high, up ~$1,019 y/y. The consumer is the single visible common factor in my basket right now: COF, RCL, GM, DLTR and PYPL are five of twelve legs that would move together in a consumer-led downturn. That is a mutual-correlation problem the screen exists to prevent.

REPLACEMENT CANDIDATE. Newmont (NEM, $117.76): gold miner, measured beta ~0.4, near-zero correlation to any of the other eleven, and the only large-cap return stream that is structurally long the exact scenario (sticky inflation with a hiking Fed and a softening consumer) that would hurt the rest of my basket. Q2 on 23 July: record $2.2bn free cash flow, $2.9bn operating cash flow, adj EPS $2.10 on $6.12bn (both slightly short of consensus), $1.8-1.9bn returned, 100m+ shares repurchased cumulatively, FY26 guidance reaffirmed at ~5.3moz attributable and ~$8.5bn FCF. The bear case is live and company-specific: production declining y/y on the Nevada Gold Mines and Pueblo Viejo transitions, AISC rising to ~$1,680/oz on royalties and lower by-product credits, and the stock is +24% in a month so it is extended. Consensus PT ~$131. I considered FCX instead and rejected it — copper carries growth beta, which defeats the point.

decisions.reason: Two things, one forced and one overdue. (1) PYPL stopped being a dispersion asset this week. WSJ reported Friday that Stripe/Advent talks are advancing toward a deal in coming weeks, and the stock closed $61.66 against a standing $60.50 bid the board already rejected. I now own a merger spread at a negative basis, not a debate about branded checkout: the payoff is roughly -2% if a deal signs near the bid, about +5% on a bump, and -20% to -25% back toward the $47.37 pre-bid price if talks break, in a gap my -20% stop would be jumped straight through. My screen selects for high residual volatility that is two-sided; a signed deal collapses that volatility into an antitrust-timing spread with capped upside. Being paid +4.4% since entry and ~30% above the pre-bid price to exit an asymmetry I was never mandated to hold is the easy half of this decision. (2) I am putting the hedge back to the mandate's own arithmetic — 51% long, 28% SPY + 19% QQQ. Last week I ran 54/44 on the argument that the basket's realised beta is far below one and 47% over-hedges it. That argument rested on a single week's observation, against a 28/19 split calibrated to minimise residual volatility across five half-year windows, and it left a +10-point net-long notional tilt and roughly +0.10 of net index beta that my mandate does not authorise. On fundamental betas the basket at 51% carries ~0.49 against a 47% hedge worth ~0.50 — net beta essentially zero, which is the operative constraint. The turnover to get there is about 15% of NAV at ~2bps, so cost is not a reason to keep an unauthorised tilt. Replacing PYPL with NEM also fixes a correlation problem the week exposed: July retail sales fell 0.6% and sentiment dropped to 51, and five of my twelve legs were consumer-spending assets that would move as one in a consumer-led downturn. A gold miner with ~0.4 beta and near-zero correlation to the other eleven is the correction the screen would make itself.
decisions.novelty: This book is the only one I run — it is a single equal-weighted twelve-name residual-volatility basket carried fully index-hedged to zero net beta, and it shares no leg, no sizing rule and no directional expression with any other book, since every position is held for its idiosyncratic clock rather than for a view on where the market goes.

positions.thesis: Managed care and still the purest single-name scatter in the screen: ~52% vol, ~99% idiosyncratic, measured beta 0.35, driven by MA rate notices, star ratings and utilisation trend with no index analogue. Q2 adjusted EPS $7.61 on revenue +26%, and the sell side has been converging my way since late July (Morgan Stanley to Equal Weight 4 Aug, Piper to Overweight 30 July, Barclays PT $407). The 2027 exit from plans covering ~600k members and the recovery from the 3.61 average 2026 star rating toward the 3% pretax margin target run on a dated, company-specific clock that the index cannot price.

Consumer finance, and the highest-idiosyncratic-volatility large cap in its sector. The volatility is calendar-driven rather than macro: Discover card migration flipping through the second half of 2026, back book by Q1 2027, $2.5bn of synergies by 2027. Q2 adjusted EPS $5.81 against $4.85 consensus with credit costs down sharply sequentially. The July retail-sales miss is the live bear case on the credit side, which is exactly the two-sidedness the mandate wants, and integration milestones have no index analogue.

Discount retail: ~46% vol, ~96% idiosyncratic, driven by comp-store prints and banner restructuring, with a trade-down profile that runs against the cyclicals elsewhere in the basket rather than with them. The Section 301 forced-labour tariffs were finalised 23 July so the import-cost shock was in the price before I entered. The Q2 print is now dated to 27 August against a guide of $4.8-4.9bn sales, comps +2.5-3.5% and adjusted EPS $1.00-1.15, and a consumer trading down after a 0.6% retail-sales decline is a tailwind here where it is a headwind for the discretionary legs.

Nitrogen fertiliser: the return function is the natural gas feedstock spread and crop economics, with essentially no equity-index loading. The 5 August print lifted the mid-cycle EBITDA target to $2.9bn, guided nitrogen tightness through 2030, raised the dividend 20% and showed gas cost down 11% y/y. It gave back 2.6% this week as the weakest leg in the basket, which is precisely the point of holding it: with a single AI factor still dominating cross-asset correlation, a name that trades on gas and grain is the cleanest correlation diversifier available.

Cruise: ~54% vol with a large booking-curve-driven company-specific component sitting on top of a cyclical beta the index short already absorbs. Q2 adjusted EPS $4.21 vs $3.98, FY guide raised to $17.73-17.87, record booking activity and accelerated buybacks, against fuel, airfare and softness in Mediterranean and West-Mexico itineraries. With sentiment at 51 the consumer bear case has real teeth here, which is the two-sided idiosyncratic debate I want; tighter 18% stop because it carries the highest beta in the basket.

The one semiconductor long I keep, because its ~63% vol is 76% idiosyncratic and driven by licensing and customer concentration rather than the AI capex cycle. Fiscal Q3 beat on revenue and posted the first EPS miss in seven quarters, and Apple modem revenue is guided to fall faster than previously flagged from fiscal Q4 as Apple's in-house share rises. I hold it because customer concentration resolving on its own clock is the residual, offset by the 1 September price increases, initial hyperscaler datacentre shipments due December 2026 and the $5bn FY27 / $15bn FY29 targets. Sized at the basket weight, not on conviction.

Energy, the basket's macro-offset leg: crude-driven returns are the classic low-correlation block and measured beta is near zero. The 5 August print was a blowout — adjusted EPS $2.40 vs $1.87 on revenue $8.33bn vs $7.18bn, realised crude $96.78, production above the top of guidance, Midstream pre-tax $961m above guide and $1.9bn of debt retired in one quarter against the $10bn target. Held for orthogonality to the other eleven rather than for a crude view, with the deleveraging clock as a company-specific catalyst in its own right.

Biotech: ~72% vol, ~90% idiosyncratic, pipeline binaries being the archetypal dispersion asset, and the best leg in the basket this week at +5.9%. mFluvis is approved for adults 50+ as the first US mRNA influenza vaccine, mCOMBRIAX cleared in Europe, and mRNA-1469 has entered Phase 1 for Ebola — three separate platform-specific events in ten days with no index content whatsoever. Still 31% below the $85.60 July high, so the two-sided debate between the 2026-27 flu launch and cash guided to $4.7-5.2bn at year end is genuinely live. No take-profit: the binary I bought it for has resolved and it is now an ordinary scatter asset. Wide 22% stop because burn is the bear case.

Aerospace. 777X certification is arguably the largest purely company-specific binary in US large cap — over 55% of certification flight testing complete, a fifth test aircraft added, first delivery promised for 2027 and already slipped once, with no index analogue and zero AI-factor loading. The operating base is turning: record $715bn backlog, 171 Q2 deliveries and +$631m free cash flow after four quarters of burn. The debate stayed usefully two-sided this week with Argus double-upgrading to Buy on 11 August against RBC's more conservative certification assumptions, and the Archer stake adds an option with its own clock.

Cable and communications, the highest residual volatility available at this market cap and none of it with any index or AI-factor content — the stock has halved over a year inside a $111.55-$285.82 range. The debate is entirely company-specific and got sharper this week: broadband erosion at 172k lost subs in Q2 against 406k mobile line adds to 12.5m, and the CPUC cleared the $34.5bn Cox merger on 13 August, removing the last regulatory barrier to a deal that adds ~6m customers. The concurrent shelf filing and 2038/2041 secured-note exchange put balance-sheet execution on the clock too. Wide 22% stop because the tape here is violent in both directions.

Autos, and the leg I most want for correlation reasons. The return function is tariffs, pricing and input costs rather than anything the index trades on: $2.5-3.5bn of gross tariff cost and $1.5-2bn of commodity and DRAM cost against a $500m refund after the Supreme Court struck the IEEPA tariffs, with adjusted EPS guidance raised to $12-14. The DRAM line is the point — GM's cost base is directly hurt by the same memory squeeze lifting the AI complex, making this one of the few large caps with a negative loading on the factor currently dominating cross-asset correlation. July retail sales showed the weakness concentrated in autos, which is the bear case doing its job on a name I hold for scatter, not direction.

New, replacing PYPL: gold mining, measured beta ~0.4 and near-zero correlation to any of the other eleven legs — the best score in the whole screen on the mandate's second criterion, which is what I need after this week left five of twelve legs levered to the same consumer. It is also the only large cap here that is structurally long the specific state of the world that would hurt the rest of the basket: gold at $4,373/oz with futures pricing a 30.6% chance of a September hike and zero chance of a cut. Deliberately two-sided at entry — record $2.2bn Q2 free cash flow, $1.9bn returned, 100m+ shares bought back and FY26 reaffirmed at ~$8.5bn FCF, against attributable production falling to ~5.3moz on the Nevada Gold Mines and Pueblo Viejo transitions, AISC rising to ~$1,680/oz, a slight revenue and EPS miss, and a stock already +24% in a month into Friday's profit-taking. Ordinary 20% stop.

Primary hedge, restored to the mandate's stated size. A long book that is managed care, consumer finance, discount retail, nitrogen, cruise, mobile semis, energy, biotech, aerospace, cable, autos and gold carries broad-market beta rather than Nasdaq beta, so the broad index is the residual-vol-minimising instrument against it. At 28% SPY plus 19% QQQ the hedge is worth ~0.50 of beta against ~0.49 from the 51% basket on fundamental betas — net index beta straddling zero, which is the mandate's operative constraint and the thing my 44% version last week failed. No take-profit: a hedge that closes itself into a 7% index drawdown would leave the book 51% net long at the exact moment it is doing its job.

Secondary hedge, returned to the mandate's 28:19 split from the 28:16 I ran for a week. That split was calibrated to minimise residual volatility across five half-year windows; my reduction to 16% was calibrated to one week of observed basket beta, which is not enough evidence to override it, and it is exactly the kind of tape-driven re-cutting that cost me on 30 July when I ran 21% as a bet on mega-cap concentration unwinding. QQQ outran SPY again this week (+1.42% vs +0.43%), which is a reason to carry the mandated Nasdaq hedge rather than a reason to guess at it. Take-profit removed for the same reason as SPY: the hedge must survive the drawdown it exists to absorb.

decisions.name: Opus 5 event driven
decisions.research_notes:
WEEK 08-10 to 08-14 TAPE. Index: S&P closed 7,785 Friday, -0.2% on the day off Thursday's record 7,798.99 (first close above 7,800), third straight weekly gain; Nasdaq 26,729; Russell 2000 set a fresh record. Soft data turned: July retail sales fell the most in over a year and the preliminary August U. Michigan sentiment print came in at 51 vs 55 expected. This is a melt-up tape with weakening consumer data underneath it — relevant only to the SPY hedge, not to the event legs.

WINDOW ACCOUNTING (the thing that actually drives this week). My two capitulation legs from the 07-17 gaps reached the end of their measured 20-session horizon on 08-14 and both paid: ISRG went $378.81 (08-07) to $394.51 (08-14), NFLX went $74.14 to $78.16, on top of the recoveries already banked. TSLA (07-23 gap) runs to ~08-20; LMT/RTX/TMO (07-23) to ~08-20; SLB/THC (07-24) to ~08-21. So next week's meeting is the wholesale roll, and this week's job is to retire what has expired.

TEAM POST-GAP PATH: $149.07 (gap close 08-07) → 151.87 (my 08-10 fill) → 154.08 → 155.24 → 165.98 → 162.22. Up 6.8% from my fill with no reversal and a contained post-gap range; the drift is running and the window does not close until ~09-04. This is now the only leg with meaningful window left.

NEW-SIGNAL SCREEN — three candidates checked against my filters, all rejected, and I want the rejections on the record:
(1) SMCI. Passes every filter except one. Q4 reported 08-11 after close, gapped 31.60 → 37.61 on 08-12 = +19.02%; volume 164.0m vs a ~35m base = 4.7x; prior 20 sessions 27.66 (07-13) → 31.60 = +14.2%; ADV well over $1bn; non-GAAP EPS $1.70 vs $0.62-0.96 consensus, gross margin 17.6% vs 8.2-8.4% guided, FY27 revenue guide $65-72bn. The disqualifier is entry lag: my earliest fill is Monday 08-17, which is three sessions after the gap, outside the 1-2 session window where the n=658 rule measures its edge. I rejected SHOP and PLTR last week on exactly this test and will not reverse a written rule one week later for a more exciting name. The tape confirms the cost of the lag anyway — SMCI has already added a further 5.9% to $39.84, so the drift I would be buying has largely been paid to someone with a faster fill.
(2) NU. Q2 08-13 after close, record $1.1bn net income, gapped 13.93 → 15.23 on 08-14 = +9.33% on 156.2m shares vs a ~50m base = ~2.8x. Correct 1-session lag, huge ADV. FAILS the trend filter outright: 07-20 close was 13.99 and the pre-gap 08-13 close was 13.93, so the prior 20 sessions are flat-to-down, not the >+10% uptrend that is the entire source of the edge in my sample. This is a bounce off a downtrend, not a drift setup.
(3) GLOB. Gapped 40.99 → 37.38 on 08-14 = -8.81% on 6.2m shares vs ~1.5m base = 4x, correct lag. FAILS the capitulation trend filter in the same way but inverted: prior 20 sessions ran 32.29 (07-20) up to 40.99, i.e. +27%, so this is an uptrending name gapping down on a genuine guidance cut (FY26 revenue cut to $2.428-2.462bn, EPS to $5.75-6.15 from $6.10-6.50, Wedbush downgrade, PT $54→$37), not the indiscriminate liquidation of an already-beaten name that my n=463 rule measures.
Also examined and passed on WDAY (+18% 08-13 on a Reuters report that Silver Lake is in talks to take it private, stock closed $206.45, ~$51bn market cap). My mandate's merger-arb leg specifies a signed situation whose realised vol has collapsed into a tight band; this is the exact opposite — a rumour with no agreement, no defined spread, and 18% of downside if talks break. Passed on RDDT (+10.4% on S&P 500 inclusion effective 08-18) because post-announcement index-add drift is historically negative into the inclusion date.

POSITION NEWS CHECK: LMT — NGI Stage 2 static-fire success 08-10, new Missile Technology Solutions product centre; nothing that touches the $58.6bn PAC-3 multiyear thesis, which remains contractual. RTX — Raytheon UUV demo 08-10, $0.73 dividend ex-date 08-14, stock +14.1% over the past month, so the trimmed leg is drifting as intended. No de-escalation reversal, no new escalation. Nothing material on TMO, SLB, THC, TSLA. No new standing orders fired (only the 07-30 META stop, already in the packet).

PRE-ANNOUNCEMENT LEG: NVDA reports Q2 FY27 on 08-26 after close, guided to ~$91bn revenue, consensus EPS $2.08, 61 analysts at Strong Buy with a $302.83 average target. Stock $206.64 (08-03) → $225.16 (08-14). My mandate carries a pre-announcement-premium leg and the book currently has none, and the calendar argues for it: every leg except TEAM expires by 08-21, so an 08-17 to 08-26 window fills a hole rather than stacking on existing exposure.

decisions.reason: Two things expired and one thing was proved out; nothing else changed, so I moved exactly those. The ISRG and NFLX capitulation legs reached the end of the 20-session horizon their edge is measured over on 08-14, and both delivered inside it (ISRG 378.81 to 394.51, NFLX 74.14 to 78.16 in the final week alone). Holding them past 08-14 would convert a tested edge into an untested directional bet on two high-multiple names at a record index, which is precisely the thing my process exists to avoid, so both come out at expiry rather than on a view. That frees 12%. I redeploy it in two places. First, TEAM from 9% to 13%: I explicitly sized that leg small because a 35% single-day gap was the most extreme in this book's history and I expected severe post-gap volatility, and one full week of tape has partially retired that concern — 149.07 to 162.22 with the range never breaking below 151 and no reversal day — while it is now the only position whose window (to ~09-04) survives past 08-21. That is a haircut being removed for an observed reason, not a conviction upsize. Second, a 6% NVDA pre-announcement leg into the 08-26 print, the one mandate leg the book has been missing, sized small precisely because the announcement premium is a published effect rather than one of my own measured statistics. I add nothing from this week's gap tape despite a clean-looking SMCI setup, because it can only be filled at a three-session lag and I disqualified SHOP and PLTR on that identical test seven days ago. Cash rises to 14%, which is deliberate: almost the entire book rolls off its measured window by 08-21 and dry powder into that rebuild is worth more than a forced trade at 4% on the balance.
decisions.novelty: I run no Round-2 book, so no overlap constraint binds; the novelty this week is directional rather than positional — the book stops being a pure post-gap drift portfolio and adds its first forward-dated leg, a pre-announcement-premium long whose catalyst is a scheduled date I am positioning ahead of rather than a gap I am positioning behind.

positions.thesis: PEAD whose catalyst hardened into contract, unchanged and untouched. The signal is intact and still inside its window, which closes ~08-20: +10.54% gap 2026-07-23 on 3.3x volume, prior 20d +12.9%, ADV $511m, every filter of the n=658 rule met (mean +2.81% raw, t=+4.74; +2.06% market-hedged, t=+3.69). The reason this carries the largest weight is unchanged: the 07-30/08-03 Army award of $58.6bn for PAC-3 MSE — the largest Patriot contract ever — converts April's $4.7bn one-year deal into an FY2026-2032 multiyear running to March 2035 that triples interceptor output by 2030, and it is exactly the segment whose +20% revenue print caused the gap I bought. This week added only confirmation of the same production story (successful Next Generation Interceptor Stage 2 static fire on 08-10, a new missile-technology product centre), which is not a new catalyst and does not justify adding. The structural point still holds: with the US-Iran MOU intact, every other defence thesis is hostage to peace headlines while this one is signed procurement that gets funded whether or not anyone is shooting. Stop 10%, no take-profit, because my own test showed a take-profit cuts the mean from +2.81% to +1.37%.

PEAD, held at the trimmed size with the trim vindicated. Signal: +7.33% gap 2026-07-23 on 2.4x volume, prior 20d +12.2%, ADV $790m; window closes ~08-20. The drift continues to work — the stock is up 14.1% over the past month and has kept making highs — which is why I hold a full-sized leg rather than cutting further. The reason I do not restore the 3% I moved to LMT is that the escalation overlay I originally sized on has not come back: the MOU is holding, Hormuz is open, and this week's RTX news was an unmanned-undersea-vehicle demonstration and a $0.73 dividend going ex on 08-14, i.e. ordinary course rather than expenditure of interceptors. Restock orders remain visible ($745.9m MDA, $535.98m Army modification announced 08-07) but restock is the slowest-moving and first-to-soften piece of the defence trade when the shooting stops, and RTX is the more escalation-sensitive of the two names I hold. 10% stop, no take-profit.

PEAD, raised from 9% because the specific risk I discounted for has been observed and largely retired. The signal: reported after the close 2026-08-06, gapped +35.31% on 08-07 from $110.16 to $149.07 on 20m+ shares against a ~4m base (over 4x), prior 20 sessions roughly +20% into the print, filled 08-10 at a one-session lag dead centre of the rule's strongest window. I cut the size to 9% on one stated ground only — that a 35% single-day gap was the most extreme in this book's history and post-gap realised volatility would be severe. The subsequent tape does not support that discount: 151.87, 154.08, 155.24, 165.98, 162.22, an orderly upward grind that never traded back through the gap-day close and is +6.8% from my fill. The fundamentals that should make the move persist are unchanged — revenue +28% to $1.8bn with cloud ACCELERATING to +31%, RPO +44% to $4.8bn, ARR $6.6bn, GAAP EPS +$0.55 from -$0.09, Q1 guide $1.705-1.715bn against $1.665bn consensus, targets lifted to $160-180 — and the stock is now trading into that target band rather than short of it. It is also the only leg in the book whose 20-session window (to ~09-04) survives past 08-21, so it carries the portfolio's event exposure through the roll. Stop stays wide at 14% rather than 10% for the original volatility reason. No take-profit.

PEAD, held unchanged into the last week of its window. +8.71% gap 2026-07-23 on 2.8x volume, prior 20d +21.9% — the strongest pre-gap trend in the book, which is the filter that carries the edge — ADV $1.09bn, window closing ~08-20. The sector read-across I flagged (Bio-Rad -15.7% on soft academic and biotech research demand) still has not propagated, and TMO's own Q2 remains the direct evidence against it: adjusted EPS $6.03 against $5.71 consensus with full-year revenue and earnings guidance raised across all segments. Nothing company-specific happened this week, which for a rule trade five sessions from expiry is the correct reason to leave it alone rather than to trade it. 10% stop, no take-profit.

New pre-announcement-premium long into a dated catalyst — the one leg my mandate specifies that the book has been missing. NVIDIA reports Q2 FY27 on 2026-08-26 after the close, having guided to roughly $91bn of revenue against consensus EPS of $2.08, with 61 analysts at Strong Buy and a $302.83 average target versus Friday's $225.16 close. The edge here is the earnings-announcement premium — the documented tendency of stocks to earn excess returns in the sessions immediately preceding a scheduled report, concentrated in high-attention names — and I am explicit that this is a published effect rather than one of my own measured samples, which is exactly why it is sized at 6% and not larger. The structural reason to take it now is calendar: every other leg except TEAM reaches the end of its measured 20-session window by 08-21, so an 08-17 to 08-26 position fills a hole in the book's event coverage instead of stacking correlated exposure on top of what I already own. Critically, this is a run-up trade, not an event trade: my next reassessment is 08-22, four sessions before the print, and the intended action there is to take the premium off and stand aside for the announcement itself rather than hold a 6% leg through the single most consequential earnings release of the season. 10% stop, no take-profit.

PEAD held at base size, unchanged, running out its window to ~08-21. The event stands: +11.01% gap 2026-07-24 on 2.5x volume, prior 20d +12.5%, ADV $536m, entered at a one-session lag where the rule measures +2.34% raw (t=+3.93), with Q2 revenue $8.97bn and adjusted EPS $0.55 both beating on broad-based sequential international growth led by Latin American offshore, and thirty analysts at a $62.03 average target. What I removed last week was the energy-security premium I could no longer observe once Brent fell back to the low 80s with the strait reopened, and nothing this week restored it — crude stayed quiet and there was no Gulf headline. That is the correct reason to hold the statistical leg at 6% rather than either rebuilding it or exiting: the overlay is dead, the tested event is not. 10% stop, no take-profit.

PEAD, unchanged, window to ~08-21. +17.17% gap 2026-07-24 on 4.0x volume, prior 20d +27.5%, ADV $228m — the most extended and thinnest-ADV name in the book, which is why the weight is deliberately small and the stop deliberately wide at 12% rather than 10%, to give it room for normal post-gap chop near its highs. The sector headwind I bought through still is not showing in the numbers: Q2 adjusted EBITDA +16.3% year over year, EPS +52%, and full-year revenue, EBITDA and free cash flow guidance all raised, against roughly a 10x multiple. No company news this week, so no reason to touch it in its final sessions. No take-profit.

Capitulation long, held unchanged at the minimum size at which I still respect my own rule, with about four sessions left to its 08-20 window. The signal qualifies cleanly — -14.52% gap 2026-07-23 on 3.4x median volume, prior 20d -16.2%, the largest volume ratio in the cohort — and the n=463 statistic is stable by year (2024 +1.19%, 2025 +1.53%, 2026 +1.49% hedged at 15d). It stays small for the reason I gave when I cut it and which has not changed: the gap was genuine fundamental deterioration (EPS $0.33 versus $0.54, gross margin 16.8%, negative free cash flow, target cuts from JPMorgan, Cantor and Mizuho) rather than the indiscriminate liquidation the rule is measured on, and it remains the highest-beta name I own. The Terafab and Megapack headlines are narrative for 2028, not cash flow for this window, and I will not upsize a rule trade on a story. Wide 18% stop per the rule's specification, no take-profit.

Partial beta offset, held at the structural core size with no tactical increment. The reason this exists is unchanged and is purely mechanical: my measured edge is materially larger market-hedged than raw (PEAD +2.06% hedged versus +2.81% raw; capitulation +1.23% hedged versus +2.44% raw), so an index short shifts the book's return toward the event component I actually have evidence for. With ISRG and NFLX retired the book's long-duration growth exposure falls, but TEAM rises to 13% and NVDA enters at 6%, so the high-multiple share of the book is roughly flat and the hedge does not need resizing. I am deliberately not adding to it despite the S&P setting a record on 08-13, July retail sales falling the most in over a year, and U. Michigan sentiment printing 51 against 55 expected — that is a macro view, my own backtests showed the index short was a drag in all three windows, and I retired the last increment precisely because I had justified it on conditions that then reversed. Small enough that 3% borrow is immaterial; shorts pay no funding. 9% stop.

decisions.name: Opus 5 mean reversion
decisions.research_notes:
Checked every leg's mark through the 2026-08-14 close plus the macro tape.

MACRO: S&P 500 set a record above 7,800 midweek and closed the week -0.2% but with a third straight weekly gain. July CPI +0.1% m/m, headline 3.4%, core 2.5% — in line; PPI headline flat, core +0.2%, below expectations. The dovish repricing I bought PEG for did in fact arrive. UMich preliminary August sentiment softened, which capped Friday.

XLE SHORT — PREMISE BROKEN. Energy went from the week's worst sector to the week's best, +7.8%, now +38% YTD, on the US resuming/extending the Strait of Hormuz naval blockade. Brent rose from ~$82.15 (8/7) to close $88.52 on 8/14 (+1.7% Friday alone) after Treasury Secretary Bessent said the blockade of Iranian ports could run "indefinitely." An Iran-Oman reopening deal was reported near and then collapsed as ship attacks persisted. Hormuz traffic is still ~5% of pre-conflict levels and OPEC spare capacity is down to ~2.5M bpd. My entire stated edge was "XLE is discounting a crude price that no longer exists" — crude closed that gap by rising to XLE rather than XLE falling to crude. XLE ~$61.06 on 8/13 vs $57.50 on 8/7. The Hormuz tail I explicitly named as the reason for the tight -15% stop is now the base case, not a tail.

APP. $312.67 on 8/14, down ~9.8% from $346.80, a fresh 52-week low of $303.17 and now -58% from the $745.61 high, >50% down in 2026. Bank of China cut to Hold on 8/11. Fundamentals unchanged and still good: Q2 revenue $1.923B (-0.94% vs consensus), net income $1.27B +54.5%, adj EBITDA margin 84%, Q3 guided $2.055-2.085B = +46-48% y/y, CEO Foroughi attributing the shortfall to the next model step-up landing just after quarter end. No reversion trigger — it made new lows, it did not reclaim them.

HONA. $166.36 on 8/14 vs $168.51 on 8/7, but the 52-week range low has reset to $150.03, ~11% below Friday's close — the washout low was made and reclaimed inside my holding period. BMO cut to $209, Wells Fargo to $195, Jefferies to $175 on 8/10; all still well above spot. Cause unchanged: precision-casting shortage deferring aftermarket revenue, not demand loss.

WMT. $116.17, +3.9% on the week. Q2 confirmed for 8/20 before the open, consensus $0.73 EPS on $186.3B.

AXP $342.48, unchanged. TSLA $342.27, +0.7% Friday on a TD Cowen buy reiteration at $460; the higher-low sequence off $298.32 is intact. SNPS ~$412, flat on the week; Q3 FY26 confirmed for 8/26 after the close. PEG $76.04 — sitting on its 52-week low despite CPI/PPI both cooperating, i.e. my catalyst fired and the stock did not respond.

NEW CANDIDATE — CSCO. Reported FY26 Q4 on 8/12: revenue $17.25B vs $16.82B expected, adj EPS $1.22 vs $1.17, Q1 guided $18.0-18.2B against $16.8B consensus, FY27 guided $72.2-73.4B (+15% at the midpoint). Stock fell 8.4% on 8/13 to ~$111.55 on gross-margin mix, from near a 52-week high. This is structurally the same setup as my AXP thesis — a beat-and-raise sold on a secondary line item — in a ~$440B mega cap with a dividend. Screened but rejected: TTD (plunged on an earnings miss but is ad-tech, duplicating APP's factor), INTU (already bounced +7.0% on 8/13 to $358.29, trigger spent).

decisions.reason: One leg's stated premise was falsified and one leg's stated entry discipline was violated by my own hand, so both get resized. The XLE short existed on a single measurable claim — that the sector was pricing $90 crude while Brent had fallen to $82 — and that gap closed the wrong way: Brent rose to $88.52 on the US declaring the Hormuz blockade indefinite, so XLE and crude are now aligned and my edge is simply gone. I keep a 6% stub because energy is still the crowded top-decile winner cluster my mandate is built to be short, but I will not carry 13% of an unbounded geopolitical supply shock against a mean-reversion rule; the tail I named in my own thesis fired, and when your named risk fires you cut, you do not argue with it. On APP I wrote that I add to a turn already in progress rather than catching the knife, then let a 16% weight ride into fresh 52-week lows with no turn — cutting to 12% applies my own rule to the name it currently indicts rather than only to the names where it was convenient. The proceeds go to two things that did give me a trigger: HONA, which printed and reclaimed a $150.03 washout low inside the holding period on a cause that is deferred revenue rather than lost share, and a new CSCO leg where a beat-and-raise with FY27 guided +15% was sold 8.4% on margin mix from near a 52-week high. Net long rises from 61% to 75% as a direct consequence of shrinking the short, which I accept as the price of not being short a physical supply disruption.
decisions.novelty: I run no Round-2 book, so there is no overlap to manage; the only new name here is CSCO, a mega-cap beat-and-raise dislocation that shares no factor with any existing leg.

positions.thesis: Held at 14% and now the top weight by default rather than by decision. It is +3.9% to $116.17 on the week, doing exactly the ballast job I bought it for while the high-beta legs chopped, and at $116 it is still roughly 13% below the May high near $134, so the reversion is only partly paid. Q2 lands 8/20 before the open against $0.73 EPS on $186.3B, a two-sided catalyst I underwrote at entry and will not dodge now that the position is green — dodging it would be selling the setup and keeping none of the payoff. It remains the only low-beta long against four gap-down names and needs no multiple expansion to work.

Cut from 16% to 12% because it made a fresh 52-week low at $303.17 and closed $312.67, down another 9.8%, with no reclaim of the gap and a Bank of China downgrade to Hold on 8/11. I wrote in the TSLA thesis that I add to turns in progress and not to knives; APP is currently the knife and consistency costs me four points of weight here. I keep a substantial position rather than exiting because nothing fundamental broke: Q2 net income grew 54.5% to $1.27B on an 84% adjusted EBITDA margin, Q3 is guided to $2.055-2.085B or +46-48% year over year, and management attributes the one-percent revenue shortfall to the next model step-up landing just after quarter end. At roughly $102B of market cap that is about 20x annualized earnings for a business compounding near 50%, and it is still the worst-ranked name on both my lookbacks, which is the exact bucket this mandate exists to own. The bear case I flagged at entry — that this is a crowded-momentum unwind that runs past fair value — is winning so far, which is precisely why the weight comes down instead of up.

Held at 12% with no trade for a second week: $342.48 versus $340.91, unchanged in a week the index set a record, which keeps it a laggard on both lookbacks and roughly 12% below the $387 high. The setup is unchanged and unresolved — a beat-and-raise sold on a $50mn revenue shortfall and 12% expense growth, while the actual bear case of consumer credit deterioration is contradicted by provisions improving to $1.1B from $1.4B. Its zero AI-capex exposure is why it does not participate in melt-up weeks and is exactly what I want it to do when the capex complex unwinds. Now that the XLE short is a stub, AXP is my main non-correlated ballast alongside WMT.

Held at 10%. It closed $342.27, up 0.68% Friday on a TD Cowen buy reiteration at $460, and the higher-low sequence off the $298.32 print on 7/29 that triggered my add is intact — nothing has broken it and nothing has completed it. It is still one of the deepest one-month mega-cap drawdowns in the universe against the $419.77 starting price. I keep it at 10% rather than adding because I already sized up on the turn last week and the underlying causes of the decline were fundamental and regulatory rather than a single dislocating flow shock, which historically makes the recovery slower and shallower than the gap-down names alongside it.

Raised from 8% to 10% because the capitulation I was waiting for actually happened inside the week. The 52-week range low reset to $150.03 — roughly 11% below Friday's $166.36 close — so the stock washed out hard and reclaimed the entire move without any new negative news, which is the forced-seller structure exhausting rather than a fundamental leg down. The cause remains what distinguishes this from the guide-downs that cost me money: a precision-casting shortage steering scarce components toward Boeing and Airbus production and away from higher-margin aftermarket, which is revenue deferred against unquestioned end demand. The 8/10 target cuts from BMO to $209, Wells Fargo to $195 and Jefferies to $175 all still sit well above spot even after the reductions. It stops at 10% and not higher because a casting shortage can plausibly persist several quarters and the freshly spun-off holder base can still produce more supply.

New. It fell 8.4% on 8/13 to about $111.55 after a straightforward beat-and-raise: FY26 Q4 revenue $17.25B against $16.82B expected, adjusted EPS $1.22 against $1.17, next-quarter revenue guided $18.0-18.2B versus $16.8B consensus, and FY27 guided to $72.2-73.4B, up 15% at the midpoint. The stock fell on gross-margin mix from hyperscaler AI orders, which is a lower-margin revenue problem inside a revenue guide that is 7% above where the Street was — the market repriced the mix and ignored the volume. That is the same structure as my AXP thesis, a beat-and-raise sold on a secondary line item, in a roughly $440B mega cap with a dividend. I am explicit that this enters on the one-week leg of my ranking and not the one-month leg, since it fell from near a 52-week high; it is a dislocation buy, not a deep-drawdown buy. That is exactly why it carries a tighter -15% stop and a smaller +18% target than the mandate-standard 30/30 — an 8% single-day move in a name this large is already a multi-sigma event, so both the recovery and the tolerable loss are proportionally smaller. It also adds a low-beta, cash-generative leg to a book that had grown concentrated in high-beta gap-downs.

Held at 7% with no trade. It closed around $412, essentially flat on the week, which means it stopped screening as a one-week top-decile winner — the reason I trimmed it last week — without giving back the gain. It remains roughly 36% below the $651.73 high with full-year guidance raised to $9.625-9.705B revenue and $14.72-14.80 EPS on 42% revenue growth, so the divergence is still open. Q3 FY26 lands 8/26 after the close, which is the event that resolves the Design IP softness and Ansys integration questions in either direction; a 7% stub is the size at which I am willing to hold that print without needing to be right about it.

Held at 7%, and I am recording that the catalyst worked while the stock did not. July CPI printed +0.1% monthly with core at 2.5%, PPI came in flat headline and +0.2% core, and rate-hike pricing eased further — precisely the dovish repricing I said was the entire reason to own a bond proxy now rather than a month ago. PEG closed $76.04, still pinned to the bottom of its $76.05-$91.26 range. A non-response to a favorable catalyst is a warning, and it is why I am not adding despite the deeper laggard screen. I am not cutting either: a regulated New Jersey T&D utility with 3,758 MW of carbon-free baseload nuclear, a 3.5% yield and 56 consecutive years of dividends, trading at its low against a $87.88 mean target, is the only leg in the book with no AI or tech beta and no correlation to the four gap-down names, and rising power prices help the merchant nuclear fleet. It stays capped at 7% because the earnings trend is genuinely negative rather than optically so, which is the opposite of what I want in a reversion name.

Cut from 13% to 6%. The specific claim I underwrote — that XLE was discounting roughly $90 crude while Brent had already fallen to $82.15 — has been resolved against me by crude rising rather than XLE falling: Brent closed $88.52 on 8/14 after the US said its naval blockade of Iranian ports could continue indefinitely, and XLE rose 7.8% on the week to about $61 as the Iran-Oman reopening talks collapsed and ship attacks continued. With Hormuz traffic near 5% of pre-conflict levels and OPEC spare capacity down to roughly 2.5M bpd, the sector and the commodity are now priced consistently and my measurable edge is gone. I keep a 6% stub rather than covering entirely because energy at +38% YTD is still unambiguously the crowded top-decile winner cluster this mandate is built to lean against, and because a Hormuz reopening deal was close enough to be reported once and would deflate the entire risk premium in days. But 13% of a short against a live physical supply disruption with non-linear upside is not a mean-reversion position, it is a bet on a war ending, and the -15% stop stays tight precisely because I no longer have a reason to give this leg room.

decisions.name: Opus 5 pairs
decisions.research_notes:
Packet first: Round 3 only (I run no Round-2 book), NAV $1,003.82, +0.38%, max DD -0.71%, gross 90.5%, cash 9.45%, book entered 2026-08-10. No standing orders were attached, so nothing fired; every leg is still at its entry weight.

Marked all ten legs through the 2026-08-14 close and, more importantly, re-checked the evidence each spread was underwritten on.

WFC/BAC — WFC ~$87.5 (consensus $100.02, +14.28%); BAC $64.2 area, closed 08-14 in a $63.81-$64.52 range with a fresh 52-week high of $65.20 and a consensus target of $68.77 (+7.1%). Price moved against me (BAC +1.6% vs WFC +0.3%) but the analyst-implied convergence gap WIDENED from 5.7 points to 7.2. BAC's Q2 was genuinely good (EPS $1.21 vs $1.12, markets revenue +34%, IB fees +50%) — I am short the price of that quality, not the franchise, and the price got dearer. WFC news was confirmatory: stress test passed with a 2.5% SCB, dividend to $0.50, tokenized-deposit consortium. Both reported 07-14, calendar clear.

TSM/KLAC — TSM $430.49 (+2.5% on the week), 52w high $479, target $547.09 (+27%), 18 buys/0 sells. KLAC closed $203.72, -2.70% on 08-14, 55.7x trailing, target $231.78 (+13.8%). Evidence is genuinely two-sided this week: Lam's CEO raised CY2026 WFE to the low-$150bn range from ~$140bn, which makes the cycle peak higher than my short assumed — that is a point against me. Against that, AMAT fell 6% premarket on 08-14 despite record revenue and a 51% growth guide, and KLAC sold off with it. The group is being told that good news is already in the multiple. Mixed evidence, so I do not resize.

LOW/HD — the biggest change in the book. LOW $218.47, sitting near its 52w low of $199.40 after a week's selloff, target $261.06 = +19.5%. HD $338.86, target $374.06 = +10.4%, with BofA ($412) and TD Cowen ($410) actually RAISING targets, so the gap is not a stale-estimate artifact. The consensus-upside gap I trimmed on last week — LOW ~14% vs HD ~15%, i.e. roughly nothing — has re-opened to 9.1 points in favour of my long. Separately, HD disclosed that CEO Ted Decker is on temporary medical leave with CFO McPhail and an EVP covering — an execution question that lands on the short leg. Setups into the prints: HD 08-18 pre-open, consensus ~$47.5bn and EPS $4.71 vs $4.68 (up yoy); LOW 08-19 pre-open, ~$26.2bn and adj EPS ~$4.24 vs $4.33 (down yoy on acquisition costs), comps guided ~+1%, FY26 reaffirmed at $92-94bn and $12.25-12.75. LOW carries the lower bar and the cheaper entry.

MA/V — the pair converged violently and is done. MA $569.29 vs $493.98 a week ago (+15%) on a Q2 beat: net revenue +14% to $9.3bn, adj EPS $5.04 vs $4.77 est, net income $4.4bn (+19%), guidance to the high end, plus Ackman's agentic-commerce position. V $364.15, only 2.7% below its 52w high. The target-implied gap I entered on has collapsed from 9 points (MA +31% vs V +22%) to 2.6 points (MA +16.9% vs V +14.3%). The z-score has reverted; that is the exit condition, not a reason to press.

Factor triangle — MTUM $317.21 (+2.55%), IWF $125.29 (+0.55%). The spread went against me a third straight week. MTUM's top three are still MU 6.18%, AMD 4.93%, AVGO 4.80% — the earnings inflection I admitted last week had falsified my crowding thesis.

Replacement candidates screened and rejected: XLU/D, named in my own mandate, is now uninvestable as a spread — Dominion is inside a proposed $66.8bn NextEra merger with the Virginia governor pledging to intervene, so D trades on deal odds, and both D and NEE (13% of XLU) sit inside the ETF. CVX $200.00 (+8.5% upside, 13.25x fwd) vs XOM $160.10 (+5.3%, 13.18x fwd) — forward multiples are effectively identical, no dislocation. GS $1,039.42 (16.1x, +10%) vs MS $217.36 (17.6x, +8.9%) — a one-point gap is not a stretched z-score. Nothing else cleared the screen, so freed gross goes to cash at 4% rather than into a pair I have not screened.

Resulting net SPY beta: WFC/BAC -0.06%, TSM/KLAC -0.08%, LOW/HD +0.01% — about -0.13% of NAV, i.e. flat, versus the +3.2% residual the prior configuration carried.

decisions.reason: Two of my five spreads stopped qualifying this week for opposite reasons, and the reason I trimmed a third was erased by new information. MA/V hit its exit condition: MA rose 15% on a clean Q2 (net revenue +14%, adj EPS $5.04 vs $4.77, guidance raised) and the target-implied gap that got me in collapsed from 9 points to 2.6. A mandate built on stationary spreads takes the convergence when it arrives; holding on hoping a mean-reverting spread overshoots is not the trade I described, and MA's move was earnings, not noise, so I will not flip the sign either. The factor triangle goes to zero because I already conceded its thesis was falsified — I underwrote momentum's excess as crowding and MU/AMD/AVGO delivered earnings instead — and a residual short of a thesis I no longer believe is just a slow leak, which it proved again this week (MTUM +2.55% vs IWF +0.55%). The November reconstitution will also drag MTUM's beta toward Micron's ~2.2 against the ~1.5 my triangle is matched to, and I cannot re-hedge drift from inside a fund; better to own no beta mismatch than a small one I cannot fix. Against that I add to the two spreads whose evidence improved. WFC/BAC widened against me on price while widening in my favour on substance: BAC printed a fresh 52-week high at $65.20 and its consensus upside fell to 7.1% while WFC's held at 14.3%, so the convergence gap went from 5.7 to 7.2 points on the book's best stationarity evidence (17 mean-crossings, ~zero two-year drift, 0.80 correlation). LOW/HD is the honest reversal: last week I cut it from 21.5% of gross precisely because consensus upside had converged to ~14% vs ~15% and I refused to pay for a two-day earnings window with no edge in it. That gap is now 9.1 points (LOW +19.5% with the stock near its 52-week low, HD +10.4% on freshly RAISED targets), LOW's bar into the print is lower (EPS guided down yoy on deal costs), and HD's CEO is on medical leave. The condition that justified the trim is gone, so I restore the size rather than pretend consistency means never changing back. TSM/KLAC stays exactly where it is because the week cut both ways — Lam lifting CY2026 WFE to the low $150bns says the cycle peak is higher than my short assumed, while AMAT dropping 6% on record revenue and a 51% growth guide says the multiple, not the fundamentals, is the binding constraint. Mixed evidence is a reason to hold a position, not to resize it. Gross falls from 90.5% to 77.7% and cash rises to 22.3%: I cut two sub-books and found no replacement that passed my screen — XLU/D is now a merger-arb instrument because of the NextEra deal, CVX/XOM trade at identical forward multiples, GS/MS is a one-point gap — so the unused gross earns 4% instead of buying a spread I have not measured. I attach no stops or take-profits anywhere: on a beta-matched pair a per-leg percentage stop is triggered by the market's direction rather than the spread's, and firing one leg converts a hedged relative-value position into an outright directional bet, which is a worse outcome than the loss it was meant to cap. Everything fills at the next open — I want the MA/V convergence banked before it can give back, and the LOW/HD size on before the 08-18 print.
decisions.novelty: Not applicable in substance since I run no Round-2 book, but for the record this Round 3 book is now three intra-industry single-stock pairs — WFC/BAC, TSM/KLAC, LOW/HD — with zero ETF, index or factor exposure after retiring the IWF/QUAL/MTUM triangle and the MA/V payments spread, so it shares no same-direction gross weight with any factor- or index-based construction.

positions.thesis: Long leg vs BAC, raised from 18.5 because the spread got more stretched on the measure I actually underwrote. WFC at roughly $87.5 still sits ~10% below its $97.76 52-week high with a $100.02 consensus target implying 14.3% upside, while BAC just printed a fresh high; the convergence gap is now 7.2 points versus 5.7 a week ago. This remains the best stationarity evidence anywhere in my universe — 17 mean-crossings in a year, near-zero two-year drift, 0.80 daily-return correlation, betas 0.76 vs 0.77 — and 12.7x trailing against BAC's ~14.6x is what carries the reversion. The week's news was confirmatory rather than new: stress test passed with the stress capital buffer held at 2.5%, dividend going to $0.50, and membership in the Clearing House tokenized-deposit consortium. Both banks reported 07-14 so there is no calendar event inside my horizon. I accept that at 41.8% of gross this pair is over half the book's risk, which is why I stopped at 21.0 rather than pushing further.

Short leg vs WFC, sized 20.8 against 21.0 so the 0.77 and 0.76 betas cancel to within 0.06% of NAV. Nothing has gone wrong with BAC and that continues to be the entire point: Q2 EPS of $1.21 beat $1.12 by 8%, Global Markets revenue rose 34% to $8.02bn, investment banking fees rose 50%, and Moynihan says pipelines are strong. The stock has responded by taking out a 52-week high at $65.20 and compressing its own consensus upside to 7.1% against a $68.77 target. I am short the price of an excellent franchise at the point where the sell side has almost no room left, not the franchise itself. The risk I own here is that a genuinely accelerating capital-markets cycle keeps re-rating BAC past the sell side, which is exactly why this is a beta-cancelled spread and not an outright short.

Long leg vs KLAC, held unchanged. TSM closed 08-14 at $430.49, still ~10% below its $479 52-week high, with 18 buys and no sells and a $547.09 average target implying 27% upside — it continues to lag the sector it physically manufactures for. The screen showed the largest convergence in my universe, ~19% back to the 250-day mean with a 34-day half-life, 15 mean-crossings and only -12% two-year drift, so last year's relative fall reads as oscillation rather than decay. I do not add despite the week's gain because the evidence on the short leg moved both ways, and resizing one side of a beta-matched pair on ambiguous information is how a spread quietly becomes a directional semis bet.

Short leg vs TSM, held at 6.4 against an 8.0 long because KLAC's 2.70 beta exceeds TSM's 2.15 — beta-matched, not dollar-matched. KLAC closed $203.72, down 2.70% on 08-14, at 55.7x trailing with a $231.78 target leaving 13.8% upside against TSM's 27%. I state the evidence against myself plainly: Lam guided calendar-2026 wafer-fab equipment to the low $150bn range versus a prior ~$140bn, which means the cycle peak I claimed KLAC was pricing is higher than I assumed. What keeps the leg on is the market's own answer — Applied Materials fell 6% premarket on 08-14 despite record revenue and a 51% growth guide. When a group cannot rally on its best possible news, the multiple is the binding constraint. This stays my smallest and most violent spread on purpose; shorting semi-cap into an AI capex boom remains the position most likely to be wrong for the longest.

Long leg vs HD, restored from 9.0 to 11.0 because the specific condition I trimmed on last week has been removed. I cut this pair when consensus upside had converged to roughly 14% for LOW against 15% for HD — no edge worth paying an earnings window for. After this week's selloff LOW sits at $218.47, near its $199.40 52-week low, with a $261.06 target implying 19.5% upside against HD's 10.4%: a 9.1-point gap where there was effectively none. The hedge quality is unchanged and second only to WFC/BAC — 0.88 daily-return correlation, betas 0.65 vs 0.68, 16 mean-crossings, only -6% two-year drift. LOW reports 08-19 pre-open with consensus at ~$26.2bn revenue and adj EPS ~$4.24 versus $4.33 a year ago, i.e. guided down on acquisition costs, comps around +1%, and FY26 reaffirmed at $92-94bn with $12.25-12.75 EPS. That is a low bar on a de-rated price, which is the asymmetry I want on the long side of a two-day print window.

Short leg vs LOW, sized 10.5 against 11.0 so the 0.68 and 0.65 betas cancel to within 0.01% of NAV. HD closed $338.86 and reports 08-18 pre-open, one day before LOW — which is precisely what makes this pair worth carrying through rather than flattening: two near-identical retailers reporting 24 hours apart means the common housing shock, mortgage rates near 6.5% and turnover at multi-year lows, lands on both sets of numbers and leaves the execution difference I am actually betting on. HD's setup is the harder one: consensus wants revenue ~$47.5bn and EPS $4.71 versus $4.68, i.e. growth, against freshly raised targets from BofA at $412 and TD Cowen at $410 that still leave only 10.4% upside. New this week and specific to this leg, CEO Ted Decker is on temporary medical leave with the CFO and an EVP covering — a governance and execution question at exactly the wrong moment in a duopoly where execution is the bet. I carry no stop on this leg: stopping out one side of a beta-matched pair would leave me naked long LOW into its own print.

decisions.name: Opus 5 seasonality
decisions.research_notes:
Week of Aug 10-14 2026, prices through 8/14 close.

TAPE: S&P 500 made a record 7,800 Thursday, closed 7,786 Friday (-0.17%); third straight weekly gain. Nasdaq 26,729 (-0.28% Fri), tiny weekly gain. Russell 2000 notched a fresh record and leads all benchmarks in 2026 at +22%.

MACRO — the two data prints that matter:
- July CPI +0.1% m/m, 3.4% y/y; core +0.2%, 2.5% y/y — all in line, both annual rates down 0.1pp from June. PPI also below expectations. September hike odds fell to ~35% from ~55% a week earlier.
- But the consumer cracked: July retail sales -0.6% vs +0.1% expected (ex-autos -0.3% vs +0.2% expected), and UMich preliminary August sentiment 51 vs 55 expected. This stalled Friday's rally.

RATES: Notably, weak retail sales did NOT produce a bond rally. 10Y finished 4.68% (up from 4.60% last week); 30Y +6bp to 5.267%. Inflation risk premium beat the growth-scare bid. Deloitte/consensus still forecast curve steepening — long end held up by inflation expectations and debt supply, short end falling on easing.

GEOPOLITICS — the biggest single change: my "Hormuz reopening" read from last week inverted. Reopening talks are stalled, the naval blockade of Iranian ports may continue "indefinitely," and Bessent said the administration will unveil "measures like have never been seen in the history of economic isolation on a country" NEXT WEEK. Brent +5% on the week to ~$87 (+1.8% Friday); WTI ~$82.9.

GOLD: $4,400+, ~+10% on the month, on softening inflation plus the Iran escalation. My entry mark was $4,066. UBS sees $5,000 H1-27, JPM $6,000 by year-end. The GLD leg has already earned roughly 2.5x its entire measured Jul-27-to-Oct-27 window average (+3.54%) in the first third of the window.

SECTOR RANKS: XLF #3 (breakout above prior high holding, RRG pointing up, 19% of the top-5 model portfolio). XLI #6. XLU #7 (improved from #9). Technology still #1 but its share of the top-five portfolio has fallen from ~70% to ~50% as breadth widens.

KRE-SPECIFIC: This is the week's cleanest new fact. The Russell 2000 hit a record high WITHOUT regional banks — KRE is still stuck well below its 2022 peak while AI-linked small caps (fuel cells, optical components) drove the index. Small-cap IT is +43% in 2026 and supplied ~6.5pp of the index's return. Combined with retail sales -0.6% and UMich 51, the consumer-credit input for spread lenders is deteriorating exactly as the group refuses to participate in its own index's record.

TECH RISK: Broadcom -6% Friday on a BofA note estimating its AI chip-financing vehicle could carry $370B of senior debt by mid-2029 with AVGO backstopping customer lease obligations. Underlying demand is fine (fiscal Q2 revenue $22.19B, +47.9% y/y; AI chip revenue +143%) — this is a financing-structure/leverage concern, a new and different vector of AI-trade risk than the capex de-rating I got wrong in July.

XLU: up only ~3.5% YTD, trailing PE ~23x vs a ~17x historical norm, badly lagging the narrower electrification/equipment funds. Checked against my own numbers: XLU Jul-27 to Sep-30 is +1.14% absolute but MINUS 0.55% versus SPY — it is an absolute-positive, relative-negative leg until Sep-30, with the real edge in the Sep-30 to Oct-31 window (+1.24%, 19/26, 8/10 last decade). So I declined to add to it now despite the defensive rotation logic; that add belongs to the Oct-1 rotation cash.

EFA: EAFE continues to outperform US equity in 2026 in USD terms on European fundamentals, which is a headwind to the short, but the position is a 3% token.

decisions.reason: Last week I wrote that my error was re-sizing this book on a macro overlay that then inverted inside five sessions. That overlay has now inverted a second time — Hormuz talks stalled, the blockade may run indefinitely, unprecedented Iran sanctions land next week, Brent +5% to $87, and the 30Y rose 6bp even as retail sales missed by 70bp. If I chased that back into the book I would be committing the identical error in the opposite direction, so I am deliberately not touching the macro-sensitive legs: IEF stays at its seasonal 6% and QQQ stays at 17%. I am making exactly one substantive trade, and it is driven by a fact about a specific sleeve rather than by a macro regime call. The Russell 2000 printed a record high this week WITHOUT regional banks — KRE remains below its 2022 peak while AI-linked small caps carried the index — and that stall arrived in the same week retail sales fell 0.6% and UMich sentiment hit 51, which is the consumer-credit input that hits spread lenders hardest and the very risk I flagged when I declined to add KRE last week. My own conclusion then was that the incremental dollar of financials exposure belongs in XLF, and this week's tape made that argument for me: XLF is ranked 3rd, its breakout above the prior high is holding, its RRG lines point up, and a steepening curve with the long end pinned by oil-driven inflation premium is precisely its setup. So I move 2 points from the high-beta expression to the confirmed one, staying inside the same mandate sleeve rather than changing my sector allocation. Second, I am harvesting the gold windfall through the exit rather than the notional: GLD has earned roughly 2.5x its entire measured Jul-27-to-Oct-27 window average in the first third of that window, which by my own calendar logic is exhaustion, but selling the week before an announced escalation is fighting a dated catalyst — so I hold 18% and cut the take-profit from +25% to +18%, which sits near $4,800 and converts an unrealized seasonal win into a committed one before the window closes. Everything else holds because nothing sleeve-specific changed: XLI keeps its 16% through the soft patch because the statistical mass is the Nov-Dec leg at t=+3.78 and one weak consumer month is not a reason to abandon it, XLU stays at 9% because my own numbers say it is relative-negative to SPY until Sep-30 and the add belongs to the Oct-1 rotation, and the 7% cash stays untouched as the pre-committed Oct-1 and Nov-1 dry powder my mandate specifies — which is also where the KRE weight goes back on, into its actual Oct-31-to-Dec-31 window.

positions.thesis: Raised from 17% and now my largest equity-sector leg, funded entirely out of KRE — I am not adding financials exposure, I am upgrading its expression. The seasonal is unchanged and strong: Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +5.04%, positive 20/26 years (77%), 9/10 in the last decade at +8.94%, with the Oct-31 to Dec-31 leg alone at +3.64% in 19/26 years. What improved is confirmation on every axis. Tape: XLF ranks 3rd of eleven, has broken above its prior high and is holding it, RRG lines point up, and it carries a 19% weight in the top-five sector model. Curve: the thing I originally owned this for is coming back — the 30Y rose 6bp to 5.267% and the 10Y to 4.68% this week on oil-driven inflation premium, even against a 0.6% retail-sales miss, while September hike odds fell to 35%, which is short-end-down/long-end-up, the steepener that widens net interest margin. Credit: Q2 charge-offs and provisioning fell at 10 of 11 super-regionals. And the money-centres' investment-banking and wealth fee streams are exactly the buffer that a 51-print consumer-sentiment reading argues you need to own inside financials right now. This leg no longer needs the macro to do the work, but for the first time in a month the macro is doing it anyway.

Held flat at 18% with the take-profit tightened from +25% to +18%. Gold is above $4,400 and up over 10% on the month against my $4,066 entry mark, which means this leg has already delivered roughly 2.5 times the entire average return of my measured Jul-27-to-Oct-27 window (+3.54%, 14/21 years, t=+1.69; +3.13% vs SPY at t=+1.80) with two thirds of that window still to run. By strict calendar logic that is an exhausted edge and I should be cutting notional. I am not, for one reason: the driver is stacking rather than fading. Last week's read that the war premium was deflating on Hormuz-reopening talks has inverted — those talks are stalled, the US says the naval blockade can run indefinitely, and Bessent has pre-announced unprecedented economic-isolation measures for NEXT WEEK. That war bid is now sitting on top of the falling-real-rate bid that in-line CPI at 3.4%/2.5% core and a collapse in September hike odds to 35% already created. Selling into a dated, pre-announced catalyst is bad execution. So I take the gain through the exit instead: +18% from entry prints near $4,800, comfortably above anything my seasonal study justifies and short of the crowded $5,000-$6,000 sell-side targets, which is the right place to be a seller rather than a holder. No stop — this is the leg that pays if the consumer rollover in retail sales and sentiment turns into a genuine growth scare and my cyclical longs break, so protecting it against a drawdown would defeat its purpose in the book.

Held flat at 17% with the -15% stop unchanged.
