I restored this leg last week after wrongly gutting it, and the restoration is working — the Nasdaq set a record Thursday at 26,803 before easing to 26,729. My study's absolute case is what justifies the position: Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +3.97%, positive 20/26 years (77%). The relative case was always thin (QQQ minus SPY +1.05%, t=+1.35) and I have already learned not to let the weak relative number override the solid absolute one on a sleeve my mandate names as a core overweight. The new risk is genuinely new and worth naming rather than dismissing: Broadcom fell 6% Friday on a BofA estimate that its AI chip-financing vehicle could carry $370B of senior debt by mid-2029 with AVGO backstopping customer lease obligations. That is an AI-leverage concern, structurally different from the capex de-rating I misread in July, and it is not refuted by strong demand — AVGO's own AI chip revenue is up 143%. I hold rather than add because technology's share of the top-five sector model has fallen from roughly 70% to 50% as breadth widens, meaning leadership is rotating away from this leg even as the index makes highs. The -15% stop is the right instrument for a financing-driven de-rating: it caps the damage without forcing me to pre-judge a debt story that will take quarters to resolve.

Held flat at 16%, unstopped, deliberately through a weak stretch. This remains the strongest statistic in my entire window set: Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +5.39% at a 21/26-year (81%) hit rate, t=+2.49, 9/10 in the last decade, and crucially the Nov-Dec leg alone is +4.68% at 81% with t=+3.78 and +1.59% versus SPY at t=+3.04. The near-term tape is against me — industrials sit 6th of eleven, and July retail sales at -0.6% with sentiment at 51 is a direct cyclical headwind that says the consumer end of the industrial economy is softening now. But almost all of the measured statistical mass sits in November and December, not in August and September, so a soft late-summer is the price of admission for this window rather than evidence against it, and abandoning a t=+3.78 signal on one bad month is exactly the overreaction I am trying to stop making. One input also re-improved: the defence-spend leg of the case, which I had marked down on Hormuz-reopening progress, is back on with the blockade indefinite and unprecedented sanctions imminent. I add no stop because a stop here would mechanically eject me during precisely the soft patch I have decided to sit through.

Held flat at 9%, and holding is a decision I made against my own instinct. Everything about this week argues for a bigger defensive bond-proxy position: retail sales -0.6%, sentiment at 51, September hike odds down to 35%, and XLU's sector rank improving from 9th to 7th. But I went back to my own numbers rather than the narrative, and they say XLU Jul-27 to Sep-30 is +1.14% absolute while running MINUS 0.55% versus SPY — an absolute-positive, relative-negative leg for the next six weeks. The window where this sleeve actually earns is Sep-30 to Oct-31 at +1.24%, positive 19/26 years (73%) and 8/10 in the last decade. Valuation agrees with waiting: XLU is up only about 3.5% YTD yet trades near 23x trailing against a ~17x sector norm, with the growth premium from merchant-power names like Constellation and Vistra now bid across the whole basket. So the add belongs to the Oct-1 rotation cash I have already earmarked, not to today. What I keep at 9% is the mandate's measured Aug-Sep defensive leg plus the structural AI power-demand bid and sector-leading breadth, sized to be paid by calendar and flow rather than by momentum.

Held flat at 6% with the -8% stop unchanged, and this is the position where holding still is the entire point. The seasonal case is the most extreme statistic in my study and is unchanged: intermediate Treasuries beat SPY in only 5/23 years (22%) over Jul-27 to Dec-31 and in just 1 of the last 10, averaging -6.00%. Six percent is what that seasonal alone justifies; the 17% I carried two weeks ago was a macro bet on a September hike, and I cut it when that bet died. This week the macro tried to pull me back the other way — the long end rose despite a 0.6% retail-sales miss, with the 30Y up 6bp to 5.267% and the 10Y to 4.68%, because oil at $87 and imminent Iran sanctions put an inflation premium back into the curve, and consensus still forecasts steepening on debt supply and inflation expectations. That is a real tailwind for a duration short and I am declining to size for it, because the same overlay inverted on me twice in three weeks and the belly is simultaneously anchored by hike odds collapsing to 35%. I would rather collect a small, well-measured seasonal edge than rebuild a conviction bet on a macro signal with a demonstrated two-week half-life. The -8% stop stays: a bond rally that large would mean recession is being priced, and I want out before that correlates with my cyclical longs.

Cut from 7% to 5%, the funding source for XLF, on the single clearest new fact of the week. The Russell 2000 printed a fresh record high and leads all benchmarks in 2026 at +22% — and regional banks did not participate, with KRE still stuck well below its 2022 peak while AI-linked small caps (fuel-cell and optical-component names) supplied the move, small-cap IT alone contributing roughly 6.5pp of index return. A group that cannot rally when its own index makes an all-time high is telling you something the seasonal cannot see. That refusal landed in the same week retail sales fell 0.6% and sentiment hit 51, which is the consumer-credit input that bites spread lenders hardest — and regionals lack the investment-banking and wealth fee streams that cushion the money-centres, with CRE nonperforming loans still rising at select names and credit costs only 'manageable barring a recession.' I keep 5% rather than exiting because the sleeve is named in my mandate and its window is the highest-return one I measured: Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +7.24%, 15/20 years (75%), t=+2.28, 8/10 in the last decade at +10.14%. But that return is overwhelmingly back-loaded — Oct-31 to Dec-31 alone is +5.91% — so KRE earns nothing in August or September, and the cheapest way to own its Q4 window is to be small now and rebuild with the Nov-1 rotation cash. I note the counterargument honestly: a steepening curve should favour spread-dependent regionals most. The tape is simply refusing to pay it yet. Stop held at -18% because labor- and consumer-driven credit stress arrives faster than a beta drawdown.

Held flat at 3% as a residual mandate sleeve, with the -10% stop unchanged. The seasonal remains one of my better relative measures — EFA minus SPY was positive in only 9/24 years (38%) over Jul-27 to Dec-31 and just 2/10 in the last decade at -2.65% average — and developed non-US equity is a short my mandate names explicitly, so I keep a token rather than vacate the sleeve entirely. I am candid that the trade is fighting its trend: EAFE has outperformed US equity through 2026 in USD terms on European fundamentals, overcoming what should have been a currency headwind, and a Fed that is no longer hiking while foreign central banks hold is the wrong rate differential for the dollar leg of the thesis. Both halves of the original mechanism are impaired. That is precisely why it is 3% and not 5%: at this weight the roughly 3% annual borrow costs about 0.04% of NAV over the remaining window, so being wrong is an irrelevance and being right is a modest carry, and the -10% stop caps the tail if European outperformance accelerates.

decisions.name: Opus 5 trend following
decisions.research_notes:
Re-scored every leg on my two filters (price vs 50/200dma + 3m time-series momentum) using data through the 2026-08-14 close, and screened the sleeves I exited last week for re-entry.

EQUITY INDEX — SPY closed 776.01 (S&P 7,785). The index printed a record 7,800 Thursday, gave back 0.2% Friday, and still booked a third consecutive weekly gain. Both filters positive, unchanged; lowest vol in the book.

HEALTHCARE — XLV traded 168.01 with a fresh 52wk high of 169.66 this week, up from 165.68 and the $168.53 old high. Trend strengthened, not just held.

FINANCIALS — XLF ~57.00-57.60, essentially flat to slightly lower on the week off its 57.60 record. Still above both MAs so the signal survives, but the slope is gone. Backdrop deteriorated on the consumer side: July retail sales fell the most in over a year and preliminary August UMich sentiment printed 51 vs 55 expected. July CPI +0.1% m/m, 3.4% y/y, core 0.2%/2.5%; PPI final demand unchanged m/m but +4.7% y/y. FedWatch now 64% for a September hold (from 52%), i.e. hike odds fading.

ENERGY — the big change and a direct falsification of last week's cut. I trimmed XLE from 19 to 11 because Iran-Oman talks made the driver "diplomatic rather than physical." The US-Iran ceasefire has since broken down, Hormuz remains shut, and the IEA cut its 2026 supply forecast: global supply -4.3 mb/d (~4%) this year, running ~1.27 mb/d below demand, aggravated by the US blockade of Iranian exports, Bab el-Mandeb attacks and reduced CPC Blend flows. COPPER — CPER ~$40.12, just off the $40.97 area high; COMEX copper $6.59/lb after an all-time intraday $6.77 on 7 Aug, +4.76% on the month, +47.46% y/y. Trend unambiguously intact. AGRICULTURE — DBA $27.59 vs $27.62, unchanged. Above both MAs, beta ~0.12, cheapest diversifying risk I own.

RE-ENTRY SCREENS ON WHAT I EXITED — Gold $4,364.96, up over 10% on the month to a two-month high, and it has reclaimed the ~$4,243 level that stopped my short. But it fell through its 200dma in June for the first time since October 2023 and traded near $4,040 in July, against a January all-time high of $5,589; the 200dma sits far above spot. Above the 50dma and below the 200dma is a no-signal, not a long, so I stay flat rather than reverse a position I covered seven days ago. Silver $64.21 same problem. URA $45.25, back at its ~$44.5 50dma — a coin flip, not a trend, and it just whipsawed me. EUR/USD strength argues a long-EUR trade; I refuse to flip a short I was just stopped out of into a long one week later.

CRYPTO — the one clean new signal. BTC $62,875, below its 20d, 50d, 100d ($66,735) and 200d ($72,097) EMAs after a failed 50-EMA breakout lasted two sessions; 14d RSI 46.3, back under its midline. Three-month momentum is decisively negative: BTC closed May near $73,469, fell 20.5% in June (worst month in four years), and is roughly 50% off the $126,000 cycle high. Both filters negative in the same direction, which is a short by my rules, and it is the only non-equity, non-commodity sleeve available to me. Caveat I am sizing for: price has been range-bound $60-64k for about seven weeks, so this is a chop risk, and perp shorts pay no funding (10% APR applies to longs only) so the carry cost of being early is near zero.

decisions.reason: One leg's exit thesis was falsified by price and one asset class re-entered my universe, so I resize rather than rebuild. Last week I cut XLE from 19 to 11 on the explicit view that the driver had become diplomatic (Iran-Oman talks on reopening Hormuz) rather than physical; that view is now wrong on the facts and, more importantly, wrong on the tape — the ceasefire broke down, Hormuz stayed shut, the IEA cut 2026 supply by 4.3 mb/d into a 1.27 mb/d deficit, Brent went from ~$82 back to $88.38, and energy was the best S&P sector on the week at roughly +6%. A trend follower who trims into an accelerating trend because of a narrative he has since had to abandon has to put the weight back, so XLE goes to 17 and its stop widens back to -25% to match a physical rather than negotiated driver. Against that I take weight from the two legs whose risk is no longer being paid for: XLF is flat on the week off its record with the slope gone while July retail sales fell the most in over a year and August UMich sentiment printed 51, and CPER's trend is intact but the pending Section 232 refined-copper decision is a binary that would unwind the COMEX premium the fund actually holds — a gap risk inverse-vol sizing cannot see. XLV earns a point for making a new 52wk high at 169.66. SPY and DBA are untouched because nothing in their signal changed. I also add a small short BTC perp: it is the only candidate where both of my filters point the same way in an asset class I have zero exposure to. I do NOT re-enter gold, silver, uranium or EUR despite all four having moved my way after stopping me out last week — gold is above its 50dma but still below a 200dma it broke in June, which is a no-signal, and reversing a covered short seven days later is exactly the whipsaw that cost me last week. Net gross 78% to 87%, cash 22% to 13%, because the surviving signals are broadly positive and 22% cash at 4% was pure drag on a book already down 1.42%.
decisions.novelty: This book is not a variant of any other book I run — it is a pure systematic time-series trend sleeve whose only inputs are moving-average position and 3-month momentum, and this week that rule set produced a directional short (BTC perp) alongside a commodity-driven energy overweight and an explicit refusal to re-enter four sleeves whose narratives improved but whose 200-day filters have not, which is a different exposure profile from any discretionary long-equity construction.

New leg and the only candidate in my screen where both filters point the same way in a direction I can act on, in an asset class where I currently hold nothing. decisions.name: Opus 5 unrestricted
decisions.research_notes:
Checked the five live drivers of this book against the 8/11-8/14 tape.

OIL / HORMUZ (the binary I sized down for last week): the de-escalation path has visibly receded. Iran and Oman have NOT reached agreement; Iran now says the strait "will remain closed unless the United States ends the war and meets Tehran's conditions," Trump counters that the US has "total control," and the Treasury Secretary committed to unprecedented economic measures plus an indefinite naval blockade of Iranian ports. Ship attacks persisted through 8/12. Hormuz vessel traffic actually FELL this week, with tankers running transponders dark, contradicting official claims that flows have normalised. Brent +5%+ on the week to $88.52 (touched $89.60), WTI $82.40.

THE PHYSICAL NUMBER THAT MATTERS: IEA's August Oil Market Report doubled its Q3-2026 deficit estimate to 1.8 mb/d from ~0.8 mb/d — the deepest quarterly deficit since Q4 2021. 2026 supply now seen -4.3 mb/d; 3Q26 supply revised down 1.7 mb/d on the closure and renewed hostilities. Demand was also cut (-1.6 mb/d for 2026) on high fuel prices, so this is a deficit with demand destruction, not a demand boom — but it is still a deficit, and it draws inventories now without needing any diplomatic outcome.

PRICE CONTEXT I HAD UNDERWEIGHTED: Brent printed above $120 earlier this year on this same closure and is now $88.52. The market has faded the risk premium while the physical balance deteriorated. XLE rose over 6% on the week to ~$61.06 (52wk high $63.46); ERX ~$99 against a 52wk high of $110.78 — the levered fund has not made the move the underlying has.

MACRO: July CPI +0.1% m/m, 3.4% y/y — a second consecutive cooling print. S&P 500 closed at a record Thursday. Sector week: Energy +6%, with Healthcare, Tech and Financials each up more than 1%.

METALS: gold held above $4,400 intraweek, +10% on the month, easing to ~$4,371 spot Friday on profit-taking off a two-month high. Silver $64.21, gold/silver ratio 67.22 (down from 67.50). Both theses intact, both extended near-term.

HEALTHCARE: XLV led all sectors in August on a 12-month basis (+16.0%), ~18x forward P/E, beta 0.65-0.75, broad Q2 beats and continued GLP-1 expansion. Doing exactly the job I bought it for.

AIRLINES: JETS fell 4% in a single session mid-week, extending a two-day decline after challenging all-time highs. Jet fuel is spiking again — US carriers' May fuel bill was $6.66bn, +85% y/y — and coverage now explicitly frames record summer volumes as masking a fragile margin story, with discretionary leisure first to flinch as fares climb.

DEFENSE (considered, rejected): ITA is -12% since early March despite five months of war and is up only 8% YTD. A war-driven sector that has floundered through the war itself is telling me the trade does not work; I am not adding it back merely to satisfy the letter of my mandate.

CRYPTO: DOGE ~$0.0699, flat on the week, still stuck below $0.08. Nothing changed.

decisions.reason: I cut energy from 26% to 20% last week for one stated reason: an Iran-Oman draft accord sitting in the Iranian parliament made the de-escalation binary too live to run a 52% effective single-sector bet into. That reason weakened this week rather than strengthened. The accord is deadlocked, Iran has re-anchored on ending the war and sanctions relief as preconditions, the US has committed to an indefinite blockade, ship attacks continued, and Hormuz vessel traffic fell rather than normalised. At the same time the physical case got materially better: the IEA doubled its Q3 deficit to 1.8 mb/d, the deepest since Q4 2021, which draws barrels regardless of what any parliament does. And the reason I thought I had spent my cushion — XLE +6% on the week — does not survive the wider frame: Brent printed above $120 earlier this year on this same closure and sits at $88.52 today. The premium has been faded, not extended. So energy goes back up. The second change follows from the same fact: JETS is the only leg where both drivers turned my way in the same week, cost and demand, and it is simultaneously my only hedge against an S&P sitting at a record. I am funding both out of a 19% cash pile that was insurance against a resolution the week made less likely. The rest of the book is untouched in size — I am tightening stops on three legs that have run, because on a 2x fund and on metals up 10% in a month, size is the real protection and the stop only bounds what is left.
decisions.novelty: The overlap constraint does not bind me — I run no Round-2 book, so there is no same-direction gross weight to test against; this is my only book and it remains a single concentrated oil-supply-shock expression carried by low-beta ballast.

positions.thesis: Unchanged at 25% because it is doing precisely what I bought it to do and I have no reason to touch it. It led all sectors in August on a 12-month basis at +16.0%, added over 1% in a week when the index made a record, and it does that at ~18x forward earnings with a 0.65-0.75 beta — the combination of leadership and low beta is rare and is exactly what makes a 48%-effective energy position carryable. The support is not just rotation: Q2 earnings beat broadly and the GLP-1 obesity franchise keeps compounding, so this is a sector with its own earnings engine rather than a defensive hiding place. Two cooling CPI prints and a Fed heading toward cuts is the regime where low-beta quality compounds. Still deliberately unlevered rather than 3x CURE: the whole point of making this the largest equity leg in a book that also runs a 2x energy fund is that it does not add variance. Still no stop, for the same reason as last week — this is the position I want to still own if everything else here is wrong, and a stop on my lowest-beta leg would only ever fire in a market-wide flush, which is the exact moment I would want to be holding it.

Raised from 20% back above where I trimmed it, because the specific risk that drove the trim receded while the physical case got stronger. Last week I wrote that a written Iran-Oman proposal was a different order of risk than a rumour and that I would not run 52% effective XLE into it. That proposal has stalled: Iran conditions reopening on the US ending the war and meeting its terms, Trump claims total control of the strait, the Treasury Secretary has committed to an indefinite naval blockade plus unprecedented economic measures, attacks on shipping continued through 8/12, and — the detail that matters most — Hormuz vessel traffic FELL this week with tankers going dark, directly contradicting the official line that flows have normalised. Against that, the IEA doubled its Q3-2026 deficit estimate to 1.8 mb/d, the deepest quarterly deficit since Q4 2021, revising 3Q supply down 1.7 mb/d. A deficit that size draws inventories whether or not anyone signs anything. My convergence worry does not survive the longer frame either: XLE ran over 6% to $61.06 this week, but Brent traded above $120 earlier this year on this same closure and is $88.52 now — the market has faded the war premium into a worsening balance, which is the mispricing, and ERX at ~$99 against a 52-week high of $110.78 has not made the move the underlying has. This is 48% effective XLE and remains by far my largest directional risk. The honest bear case is unchanged and is one headline wide: a deal lands, crude gaps down, and a 2x fund halves the move twice over. That is why this is 24 and not 30, and it is why the true protection here is size rather than the stop, which would gap through on that headline. Stop tightened from -28% to -22%, capping the leg at ~5.3% of NAV — roughly an 11% XLE break, wide enough to survive the daily noise of a levered fund, tight enough to end the trade if the supply story genuinely breaks.

Held flat at 20% because it is still the only asset I own that wins in both tails of my own book, and nothing this week changed that. If the stalemate persists, gold keeps the geopolitical bid alongside ERX. If Iran and the US suddenly settle and crude collapses, taking ERX with it, that resolution lands on a labor market that shed 23,000 jobs against a +80k consensus with roughly 100k of prior downward revisions, and on a second consecutive cooling CPI at +0.1% m/m and 3.4% y/y — a Fed cutting into a softening economy is what gold is built for. Every other long leg here needs one of those two worlds; this one is indifferent to which arrives. The bid stays layered rather than single-source: rate-cut repricing, central-bank buying, a soft dollar, and the Hormuz premium. Still bullion rather than GDX — stacking mining operating leverage on top of a 2x levered energy fund would concentrate variance in exactly the thing I am trying to reduce. What I am respecting is that a 10% month above $4,400 and a Friday fade to ~$4,371 on profit-taking off a two-month high means this is extended near-term, so the stop comes in from -18% to -13%, capping the leg at 2.6% of NAV. That is still far outside any headline-driven shakeout but close enough that a genuine break of the record-high structure — which would mean the rate-cut thesis died — takes me out of a hedge that has stopped hedging.

Raised from 6% to 10% — the first week since I put this on where both drivers cut the same way at the same time. The cost half, which was actively working against me last week when crude fell 5%, has flipped hard: Brent is back up over 5% to $88.52, jet fuel is spiking again, US carriers' fuel bill ran $6.66bn in May at +85% year over year, and the coverage has turned to how quickly fuel costs outpace revenue gains — carriers are rewriting earnings expectations, and record summer passenger volumes are now being described as masking a fragile margin story rather than as a bull case. The demand half is intact and independent of that: a contracting labor market with leisure and hospitality specifically called out soft is a direct read on discretionary air travel, and discretionary leisure is the first cohort to flinch as fares climb to cover fuel. Crucially the tape finally confirmed — JETS fell 4% in a single session and extended a two-day decline after challenging all-time highs, so this is no longer a short fighting its own chart. The third reason is portfolio-level: with the S&P at a record close this is my only equity hedge and the only thing here that pays if the indices break. I accept that this doubles down on the same oil call as ERX and that a Hormuz deal costs me on both legs at once — that is the concentrated failure mode of this book and I am naming it rather than pretending it away. Squeeze risk stays specific and live: the $2.5bn Frontier/Avelo federal liquidity ask with a government equity stake, even with Transportation Secretary Duffy publicly preferring private funding. It is an ETF, so no single-name earnings gap. Borrow at 3% APR on 10% is about 30bps a year. Stop -18% caps the leg at 1.8% of NAV; take-profit held at +25% for a smaller, faster exit.

Unchanged at 7%. Silver sits at $64.21 with the gold/silver ratio at 67.22, ticking down from 67.50 — the catch-up is grinding rather than accelerating, which is fine at this size. The thesis is the same dovish repricing that drives GLD, expressed with more beta: two cooling CPI prints and a Fed path toward cuts, on a metal up 67% over the past year. The ambivalence I flagged when I sized it is still the reason it is 7% and not 20%: silver carries an industrial demand component gold lacks, and a weakening labor market cuts against that component even as the monetary case strengthens. I keep respecting the instrument's own history — it traded to the mid-$80s in February and is $64 now, a drawdown that would have taken out any tight stop — so the stop stays wide in absolute terms. Tightened from -22% to -18% only because the leg has run with the metal; that caps it at 1.3% of NAV while still leaving room for ordinary silver noise, which is violent.

Held completely untouched for a second week, because literally nothing changed and resizing a 3% leg would cost more in fees and attention than it could earn. DOGE closed the week around $0.0699, flat over 24 hours, still pinned below $0.08 and still the weakest thing in its asset class. The edge remains structural rather than a market view: short perps pay zero funding while long perps pay leverage times 10% APR, so this 3x is genuinely free carry — I am being paid to hold a short on the worst horse in the race. The honest risk is unchanged: the same rate-cut repricing that makes my gold leg work lifts high-beta risk assets, and DOGE amplifies the tape in both directions, which is exactly why this stays 3% at 3x rather than anything larger. Loss is hard-capped at the 3% margin, the -50% stop caps it at 1.5% of NAV, and the +90% take-profit corresponds to DOGE down roughly 30% for about 1.8:1.

decisions.name: Opus 5 vol regime
decisions.research_notes:
WEB SEARCH BUDGET WAS EXHAUSTED BEFORE I COULD USE IT (200/200 consumed at session start), so this week's work is built entirely on price/vol data I pulled and computed myself from the Yahoo chart API through the 2026-08-14 close, plus one FedWatch fetch that returned no probabilities. Stooq and Cboe's delayed-quote CDN both blocked me. All numbers below are my own calculations.

VOL STATE. VIX closed 14.25, down from 15.15 at my 08-10 entry and a new low for this experiment, 2nd percentile of the trailing year (1y range 13.47-31.05). SPY realized: 10d 11.64%, 20d 13.33%, 60d 13.93% - realized is DECELERATING, not reverting. This matters for my thesis: I underwrote long vol on "1.7 points of premium vs a 3-4 point norm" using 20d realized. Against 10d realized the premium is now 2.6 points, i.e. approaching normal. My edge did not close because VIX rose; it closed because realized fell faster than VIX did. VVIX 87.48 (cheap vol-of-vol) and SKEW 138.36, up +4.4% in a week VIX fell -4.4% - tail demand rising while ATM cheapens.

CARRY DETERIORATED, MEASURED. VIXM/VIXY rose from 0.7336 to 0.7622 in five sessions, +3.9% in a week against a ~1.1%/week average over the prior three months. Decomposing: VIX -4.4%, VIXY -4.8% (beta ~0.87 implies ~3.8% expected), VIXM -1.0% (beta ~0.45 implies ~2.0% expected). That is roughly 1 point per week of EXCESS front-month decay, ~50%/yr annualised. On 08-08 I wrote that compressed contango meant I was paying "a third to a half of the 43.8%/yr I underwrote at entry." That is no longer true - the roll cost is back at or above where I started. My single largest stated objection to this leg has re-armed.

DISPERSION IS STILL EXTREME AND I WAS EXPRESSING IT WRONG. SPY 20d rv 13.33 vs QQQ 23.64, XLK 32.73, SMH 46.39 - the gap is intact. But RSP (equal-weight S&P) realizes 9.79% at 20d and 10.92% at 60d against SPY's 13.33/13.93. The equal-weighted index realizes ~27% LESS vol than the cap-weighted one. That falsifies the specific mechanism I used to justify a 40% SPY core: I invoked "index variance = average constituent variance x correlation" to argue the wrapper is safer than its contents at record-low correlation. That identity assumes equal weighting. In a cap-weighted index with ~40% in megacaps realizing 25-45%, concentration eats most of the correlation benefit - and RSP is the empirical proof, same tape, same window.

I STRESS-TESTED IT RATHER THAN TRUSTING 20 DAYS. Over SPY's 8 worst days of the trailing year, RSP's average downside capture is ~68%. Trailing 1y: RSP +21.8% vs SPY +22.0% - identical return - with max drawdown -7.9% vs -8.9%. RSP dominates SPY on every risk-adjusted measure I can compute, at 20d, 60d and 1y horizons.

ENERGY SHOCK, IGNORED BY EQUITIES. The single largest move in the tape: BNO (Brent) +7.9% on the week, USO +7.3%, XLE +7.7%, DBC +3.8% - the stalled Hormuz transit-fee negotiation I flagged on 08-08 evidently did not resolve. Meanwhile SPY +0.4% and VIX FELL. OVX dropped -11.3% on an +8% oil rally, so oil options read this as physical tightness rather than crisis. Rates confirm the inflation channel: ^IRX 3.70, unchanged on the month (front end pricing NO extra Fed), while ^TNX rose to 4.70, +2.8% on the month. A steepening driven by the long end with an anchored front end is a term-premium/inflation-expectations move, not a policy move.

HEDGE-QUALITY COMPARISON THAT DECIDED THE BOOK. On SPY's 8 worst days: XLE printed POSITIVE on 5 of 8; SPLV positive on 4 of 8; USMV ~60% capture on all 8; VIXY +5.8% to +12.4% on all 8. Trailing 1y return for that protection: XLE +49.2%, USMV +9.8%, SPLV +6.2%, VIXY -50.9%. XLE buys me drawdown protection at least as good as SPLV's while having returned eight times as much, and it is long the live macro shock instead of short it. SPLV, by contrast, is -0.57% over the month, is ~25% utilities against a 10y at 4.70 and rising, and its whole defensive premise is a rate call that the energy impulse is actively arguing against. XLU -2.55% on the month says the same thing.

SYNTHESIS. My vol sleeve is expensive insurance against a shock whose most likely proximate cause is sitting in plain sight in the oil tape. Owning the beneficiary of that shock is cheaper insurance than paying ~50%/yr to own the volatility it would create - so I fund most of the VIXY cut with XLE and keep VIXY only at genuine tail-hedge size into the dated 15-16 Sep FOMC.

decisions.reason:
Two pieces of my own evidence turned against last week's construction and one turned against last week's arithmetic, so this is a correction rather than a view change - the regime call (calm index, violent components) is unchanged and this book expresses it better.

First, the arithmetic. I built a 40% SPY core on 'index variance equals average constituent variance times correlation', arguing the cap-weighted wrapper is safer than its contents at a 23-year correlation low. That identity is an equal-weight identity. RSP realizes 9.79% at 20d and 10.92% at 60d against SPY's 13.33% and 13.93%, on the same tape in the same window - the equal-weighted index captures the diversification benefit I was describing while SPY's megacap concentration consumes most of it. I checked this was not a 20-day artefact before acting on it: over the trailing year RSP returned +21.8% against SPY's +22.0% with a smaller max drawdown (-7.9% vs -8.9%) and roughly 68% average downside capture across SPY's eight worst days. Identical return, a quarter less volatility, at all three horizons. If my mandate is return per unit of realized vol, RSP is simply the better vehicle for the exact thesis I already hold, so 30% moves to RSP and SPY keeps 20% because I am correcting an expression, not abandoning cap-weighted beta entirely.

Second, the carry. VIXM/VIXY moved +3.9% in five sessions against a ~1.1%/week three-month average; netting each ETF's beta to spot leaves roughly a point a week of excess front-month decay, about 50% annualised. On 08-08 I explicitly justified upsizing VIXY to 11% on the claim that compressed contango had cut my roll cost to a third-to-a-half of the 43.8%/yr underwritten at entry. That claim is now false by my own measurement. Separately, the value case has thinned: VIX 14.25 against 10d realized 11.64% is 2.6 points of premium, near normal, and realized is falling faster than implied. I am not abandoning the hedge - VVIX at 87 is cheap convexity, SKEW rose to 138 in a week VIX fell, and the 15-16 Sep FOMC is a dated live binary inside my horizon - but a leg whose price of carry has doubled while its value case thinned should shrink to true insurance size, so 11% goes to 7% with the take-profit untouched.

Third, SPLV. I kept it for tech-free diversification, but its protection is a rates bet and rates went the wrong way: ^TNX to 4.70 with ^IRX pinned at 3.70, a long-end-led steepening, which is precisely the inflation-expectations move an +7.9% Brent week produces. XLU -2.55% and SPLV -0.57% on the month confirm it. Once RSP is in the book, SPLV's broad-diversification role is redundant and only its concentrated utilities bet remains, so I exit it.

What replaces it is the reason I am comfortable cutting the vol sleeve. XLE printed positive on five of SPY's eight worst days of the trailing year - better crash behaviour than SPLV's four of eight - while returning +49.2% over that year against SPLV's +6.2%. It is long the one macro shock actually running (Brent +7.9%, XLE +7.7%, USO +7.3% in a week the S&P gained 0.4% and VIX fell), and an energy-led inflation impulse is the single state where SPY, USMV and cash all lose together and only my hedges help. Sized at just 7% because it realizes 24.5% vol and because a leg that ran 7.7% in five sessions deserves respect, not enthusiasm. The net effect is a book with the same equity beta, materially less realized volatility, a hedge that earns rather than bleeds, and 18% cash at 4% into a live September Fed.
decisions.novelty: I run no Round-2 book, so there is no overlap to manage; the novelty against my own prior book is that I have replaced a paid-for-defensiveness structure (min-vol and low-vol funds that buy calm with surrendered return, plus a front-month vol ETF paying ~50%/yr to carry) with an earned-defensiveness structure - equal-weight index beta that gets its low volatility free from record dispersion, and an energy leg that has historically been positive on the days the index falls hardest - cutting the bleeding hedge to true tail size rather than treating insurance as a position.

positions.thesis: The corrected core, and the honest version of the trade I thought I already had on. Last week I argued that at a 23-year implied-correlation low the S&P wrapper is safer than its contents, because index variance is average constituent variance scaled by correlation - and then bought SPY, which is not what that identity describes. The identity is an equal-weight statement. RSP realizes 9.79% at 20d and 10.92% at 60d against SPY's 13.33% and 13.93%: the equal-weighted index collects roughly a quarter less volatility from exactly the dispersion I identified, because SPY's ~40% megacap concentration in names realizing 25-45% (QQQ 23.64, XLK 32.73, SMH 46.39) claws most of the correlation benefit back. I refused to act on 20 days of realized vol alone, so I checked the full year: RSP returned +21.8% against SPY's +22.0% - the return is not being surrendered, which is the whole point and the thing USMV and SPLV cannot say - with a shallower max drawdown (-7.9% vs -8.9%) and roughly 68% average downside capture on SPY's eight worst sessions. Same return, less volatility, less drawdown, better crash behaviour, at 20d, 60d and 1y. This is what a high-dispersion regime is supposed to pay a long-only book, and I was leaving it on the table. The -14% stop is a regime brake rather than a trading stop, set to the same ~1.4 annual sigma as SPY's -18% given RSP's lower realized vol, so the two core legs are stopped at equivalent severity rather than at equivalent-looking numbers.

Halved from 40% rather than eliminated, because the case against it is relative, not absolute. RSP beats it on every risk-adjusted measure I computed, but SPY still returned +22.0% over the year and the megacap complex is where the earnings growth that has driven this tape actually sits - a book with zero cap-weighted exposure is a full-conviction bet that equal-weight leadership begins now, and I have twenty days plus one year of volatility data, not a leadership forecast. Keeping 20% means the concentration question costs me a fraction of the book rather than all of it if I am wrong about which wrapper wins from here. The residual worry from last week is unchanged and unresolved: the melt-up ran on a jobs contraction, so the rate channel rather than earnings is doing the work, and the 15-16 September FOMC under Warsh remains live - now with an energy impulse (Brent +7.9% on the week) feeding the inflation side of that decision while the front end at ^IRX 3.70 has not moved to price it. The -18% stop stays wide and stays deliberately loose, because VIXY and XLE are the actual hedges here and stacking a tight stop on top of convex protection double-pays for the same insurance and invites a whipsaw exit at precisely the wrong moment.

Trimmed 22% to 18% to make room, but this is the leg I am least inclined to argue with, because it is the only defensive sleeve in the old book that actually delivered on both sides of its promise. It realizes 7.94% at 20d - the lowest of anything I own - and still returned +4.12% over the past month, ahead of SPY's +3.41%, so for once the calm was not bought with foregone return. The composition logic holds: MSCI's min-vol optimizer excludes high-volatility constituents, so its ~32% technology label sits in low-beta software, services and payments rather than semiconductors, which is why it captured roughly 60% of SPY's move across the eight worst days of the year while SMH realizes 46%. Its role is unchanged from last week and its role is why it survives the cut: it is the sleeve that keeps working in a soft-landing rotation that punishes beta without producing a volatility event - the single state where neither my equity core nor VIXY nor XLE helps me. What it is not is a hedge against the inflation shock now running, which is exactly the gap XLE is being added to fill. Stop unchanged at -14%, capping this leg near -2.5% of NAV.

New, and it is a hedge rather than a momentum chase - I want to be judged on that distinction. The test I applied was not the +7.7% week; it was behaviour on the days my book actually hurts. Across SPY's eight worst sessions of the trailing year, XLE printed positive on five, better than SPLV's four, the leg it replaces. The difference is what that protection costs: XLE returned +49.2% over the year against SPLV's +6.2%, so I am buying comparable crash behaviour without paying for it in surrendered return, which is the same principle that moved my core from SPY to RSP. The macro fit is why I chose energy rather than another decorrelated sleeve. The stalled Hormuz transit-fee negotiation I flagged on 08-08 evidently did not resolve - Brent +7.9%, WTI +7.3%, DBC +3.8% in a week the S&P added 0.4% and VIX fell to a two-year low. The rates tape confirms the transmission channel: ^IRX unchanged at 3.70 while ^TNX rose to 4.70, a long-end-led steepening that is an inflation-expectations move, not a policy move. An energy-led inflation impulse into a live 15-16 September FOMC is the one scenario where my equity core, my ballast and my cash all lose together, and it is also the most plausible mechanism by which the record-low implied correlation underpinning this entire book normalises upward - a common macro factor re-correlating everything is precisely what my VIXY leg is paying 50%/yr to bet on, and this leg bets on it while collecting dividends instead. Sized at only 7% because it realizes 24.5% and because a position that has already run 7.7% in five sessions deserves respect rather than enthusiasm; OVX falling 11.3% on that rally says options markets read this as physical tightness, which is a slower and more persistent thing than a crisis spike but also a less explosive one. The -22% stop is wide by design so ordinary crude noise cannot knock me out of a position held for its behaviour in stress, while still capping the leg near -1.5% of NAV.

Cut from 11% to 7% because I made a specific, checkable claim last week and the check came back against me. I upsized this leg on the argument that compressed contango had reduced the roll cost to a third-to-a-half of the 43.8%/yr I underwrote at entry. Measuring it now: VIXM/VIXY rose +3.9% over five sessions against a ~1.1%/week average across the prior three months, and after netting each fund's beta to spot (VIXY ~0.87, VIXM ~0.45) that leaves roughly a point a week of excess front-month decay, about 50% annualised. The carry advantage I paid up for has not merely faded, it has inverted, and the leg is -9.4% on the month as a result. The value case thinned in parallel and not in the way I expected: VIX at 14.25 against 10d realized of 11.64% is 2.6 points of premium - near a normal risk premium, not a cheap one - and it got there because realized vol fell faster than implied, with 10d 11.64 below 20d 13.33 below 60d 13.93. I am cutting rather than exiting because the reasons to hold insurance are still genuinely present and cheap on the axes that matter for convexity: VVIX at 87.48 means options on VIX itself are near the low end of their range, SKEW rose 4.4% to 138.36 during a week ATM vol fell 4.4% so someone is quietly bidding tails, VIX sits at the 2nd percentile of its trailing year, and the 15-16 September FOMC is a dated binary inside my horizon now carrying an active energy-inflation impulse. This leg was positive by +5.8% to +12.4% on every one of SPY's eight worst days of the year; nothing else I own is convex like that. So it stays, at a size that is honestly a tail hedge rather than a position, funded partly into XLE which expresses the same shock at positive carry. Take-profit held at +60% so a moderate scare leaves the hedge intact and only a genuine dislocation converts it to cash. No stop, for the reason that has never changed: stopping out of insurance while it is losing money is the one thing insurance must never be allowed to do.

decisions.name: Opus Broadening
decisions.research_notes:
Web search budget for the session was exhausted before I could use it, so I worked from point-in-time price and momentum data pulled directly (Yahoo chart API) for my whole universe through the 2026-08-14 close: 1w/1m/3m/6m/12m returns, 12-month-minus-1-month momentum, 52-week range position, 10/50/200-day MA status, and realized vol at 10/20/60 days.

MACRO. 30-year yield closed 5.26%, UP from 5.21% a week ago and now ABOVE the 5.22% level I explicitly cited last week as the reason to cut duration; 10-year 4.70% from 4.66%. The rate-relief argument I used to restore IWM/XBI/KRE has fully unwound inside one week. Crude went the other way: WTI $78.18 -> $82.40 (+5.4%), Brent $83.55 -> $88.52 (+6.0%) as a grind rather than a headline spike.

RSP +1.22% w/w vs SPY +0.40% and QQQ +1.11%; on 3 months RSP +9.81% vs QQQ +1.68%, so the anti-concentration spread is paying on the horizon that matters even though it lost last week. XLU is the only sector below its 50- and 200-day. ETH at $1,876 is flat on the week and the month with 10-day realized vol of just 11% - a speculative tail currently speculating on nothing.

MOMENTUM (Round 3 mandate). The screen has moved against two of my legs. SMH sits at 78.8% of range, 12% below its 52-week high, BELOW its 50-day, and +1.64% over three months - dragged by AVGO (-8.13% w/w, below its 10-day) - while the memory names that carry the thesis I actually wrote ripped: MU +10.72% w/w, 12-1 momentum +607% (top of my entire universe), above all MAs. PLTR fails my mandate's own construction outright: 12-1 momentum -24.12%, 66.8% of range, 12m -1.77%, and flat since I bought it four sessions ago at $175.23 despite a +29% month - the post-earnings drift has stalled. Best unowned leaders on 12-1: CRWD +90.5% at 93.8% of range above all MAs; NET +35.6% at 91.2% of range, +5.17% w/w; MDB +50.6% but duplicates SNOW's data theme. On the short side HOOD is a weak laggard that is now bouncing (+2.43% w/w, back above its 10-day, 12-1 only -7.1%), whereas COIN is at 3.0% of its 52-week range, below its 10-, 50- AND 200-day, -3.34% w/w and -7.49% 1m with 12-1 of -49.5%. ORCL remains the best-qualified laggard on the screen (16.9% of range, 12-1 -49.4%) but is squeezing, +21% on the month. Vol check for stop sizing: MU rv20 104% / rv60 110% (one weekly sigma is ~15%, so it must be sized small with a wide stop), COIN rv20 73%, CRWD rv20 46%, NET rv20 51%, XLE rv20 25%.

decisions.reason: The week falsified two of my calls in opposite directions and only one of them needs money moved. I cut energy 17->8 on the argument that a war premium had left the tape; crude then ground from $78.18 to $82.40 with no fresh headline and XLE put in +7.67% to 99% of its 52-week range, with XOP +8.47% and OIH +8.51% alongside it. That is no longer a geopolitical premium I would be paying for - it is a cyclical sector making highs on price, which is precisely the breadth signal this mandate exists to own, so I am buying it back on a different reason than the one I abandoned rather than re-buying my old mistake. The funding comes from the leg where my stated rationale actually died: I restored IWM, XBI and KRE last week because the 30-year had fallen from 5.22%, and it closed Friday at 5.26%, higher than when I cut. IWM and KRE made record closes anyway so price overrides the vanished rate story there, but XBI is the one long that did nothing (+0.03% while the whole book made highs) and it is the longest-duration asset I own facing a 30-year that went back up - lost rationale and missing price confirmation in the same position is what a funding source looks like. I am not touching RSP, IWM, XLI, KRE, TNA, ETH or the QQQ short, because a book that just beat SPY by 125bps with every breadth index at 100% of range is not a book to redesign.

positions.thesis: Untraded at 19 for a third week and the anchor of the book. Closed at a 52-week high, 100% of range, +9.81% over three months against QQQ's +1.68% - the anti-concentration view is being expressed here by the long leg, which is why the size sits here and not in the short. Held rather than pressed because it is already my joint-largest and adding at a record close is how a breadth basket turns into a momentum basket.

Held at 19 despite the reason I gave for restoring it having reversed - I put it back to 19 because the 30-year fell from 5.22%, and it is now 5.26%. I am keeping the position and discarding the argument: IWM closed at a 52-week high with 12-1 momentum of +31.5%, so small caps are making records with long yields against them, which means the driver is domestic cyclical earnings breadth rather than the rate call I talked myself into. No trade, so this costs nothing to hold while I watch which explanation the tape prefers.

Rebuilt 8->13 after cutting it 17->8 exactly one week too early. The distinction that makes this a re-entry and not a round trip: last week's case was a supply-shock premium from strikes near Hormuz that had visibly drained out of the price, and I was right that it drained. This week's case is that crude ground $78.18->$82.40 without a headline, XLE closed at 99% of its 52-week range with 12-1 momentum of +37%, and XOP and OIH both added over 8% - a whole cyclical sector confirming on price is the breadth signal my mandate names, not a war trade. Sized 13 rather than back to 17 because I have now been whipsawed on this sector twice and the second mistake should be smaller than the first, with a -18% stop (roughly 2.5 monthly sigma at 25 vol) so the third one is capped at 2.3% of NAV.

Untraded at 11. Industrials closed at 100% of their 52-week range with 12-1 momentum of +21% and no crude beta and no semiconductor supply-chain exposure, so it is the cleanest domestic cyclical breadth I hold and does not double-count the energy add I just made. Left alone because nothing about it changed and a position doing its job does not need my attention.

Untraded at 10 and the best-performing non-energy leg this week at +2.26%, closing at a 52-week high. Notable because it did that with the 30-year rising to 5.26%, which is the opposite of the securities-portfolio argument I used to justify the weight - regional banks are levered small-cap breadth first and a rates trade second. Capped at 10 because payrolls at -23,000 with heavy negative revisions is a credit-quality signal and banks are where a labour-market crack shows up first.

Cut 12->8, reversing last week's restoration honestly. I took it from 7 back to 12 because the 30-year had fallen from 5.22% and the reason for the earlier trim was gone; the 30-year closed at 5.26% on Friday, so the reason is back and my restoration was wrong. It is also the only long in the book that failed to participate in a week when RSP, IWM, XLI, KRE and TNA all closed at 52-week highs - +0.03%. Kept at 8 rather than cut to zero because 12-1 momentum of +68% is still among the best in my universe and it satisfies the equal-weight construction leg of the mandate by design; I am removing the size I added on a bad argument, not exiting a good asset.

Untraded at 6 and up 8.28% on the month - the mandate-named amplifier finally earning its slot. Not pressed despite working, because 3x daily compounding is a bet on trend without chop and the reason to hold it small is unchanged: a sideways month costs decay whether or not the direction is eventually right. Stop stays -25%, which caps this leg at 1.5% of NAV.

Untraded at 3% so I pay no crossing cost. Being explicit that this is now dead weight rather than a tail: flat on the week, flat on the month, and 10-day realized vol of 11% on an asset whose entire purpose in this book is convexity. It is a mandate-required speculative sleeve and at 35bps a side it is not worth paying to express indifference, so it stays at 3 with a -30% stop until it either wakes up or costs me the stop.

Untraded at 6 and vindicated on the horizon that counts. I halved this after it caused my worst single-leg drag; since then QQQ returned +1.11% against RSP's +1.22%, and over three months QQQ is +1.68% against RSP's +9.81%, so the concentration spread is paying and last week was the exception rather than the trend. Deliberately not upsized back toward 12 - upsizing this leg into strength is the exact mistake I made a fortnight ago, and the mandate calls for a small anti-concentration short, which at 6% against 89% of longs is what this is.

decisions.reason: Three legs stopped satisfying the screen this mandate is defined by, and momentum is the one style where you cannot keep a position on the story after the ranking has moved. First, SMH: I own it as my largest position on a memory-shortage thesis I wrote out in detail - SK Hynix guiding supply 20% below demand to 2030, Micron HBM sold out through 2027 - yet SMH is 12% below its high, below its 50-day, and up 1.64% over three months because AVGO (-8.13% this week) and the non-memory half are dragging it, while MU alone did +10.72% on the week with the highest 12-1 momentum in my universe at +607%. I have been holding a diluted proxy for my own view; I am cutting SMH and taking a small, wide-stopped position in the thing the thesis is actually about, small because 104% realized vol means one weekly sigma is 15%. Second, PLTR fails my own construction outright - 12-1 momentum of -24% and 67% of range make it a laggard on the signal I trade, I bought it for post-earnings drift, and it has gone nowhere in four sessions despite a +29% month, so the drift has stopped paying and I am left holding a 139-vol name on a lapsed reason. Third, HOOD is the weaker of my two shorts and is now bouncing - above its 10-day, +2.43% on the week, 12-1 of only -7% - while COIN sits at 3.0% of its 52-week range, below its 10-, 50- and 200-day, down on the week and the month with 12-1 of -49%. If the mandate says short persistent losers, I should be short the one confirming, not the one squeezing. The freed capital plus some of the 23% cash goes to the two cleanest unowned leaders on 12-1 momentum, CRWD and NET, because carrying that much cash in a trend book while every index closes at 100% of its range is a bet against my own mandate. SNOW, PANW and the ORCL short are untraded - all three still pass the screen and there is no reason to pay to touch them.
decisions.novelty: The two books share no symbol at all - zero same-direction gross-weight overlap - and are built on opposite selection rules: Round 2 owns broad equal-weight, small-cap and cyclical-sector index exposure hedged with an index short, while Round 3 owns single-name cross-sectional momentum leaders in software and semis hedged with single-name laggard shorts, so this week's Round 3 changes (adding MU, CRWD and NET, shorting COIN) move it further into idiosyncratic single-name risk that the index book cannot express.

positions.thesis: Untraded at 18 and now the largest position by default. At 96% of its 52-week range with +118% over three months it remains the strongest relative-strength reading among my longs, and the earnings date sitting at Sept 2 keeps the print outside my holding window. Held rather than pressed because -0.48% in a week when PANW did +5.61% and MDB did +15.43% is the first sign of relative fade, and because 156x forward after a +118% quarter has no valuation floor to land on - the -22% stop is the whole risk control here.

Cut 24->15. Not a change of view on semis, a change in the vehicle: SMH is at 78.8% of range, 12% below its 52-week high, below its 50-day and up only 1.64% over three months, because the memory names carrying my thesis are being netted against AVGO at -8.13% on the week and the rest of the non-memory complex. I originally chose the diversified ETF explicitly to avoid single-name gap risk, and that was the right instinct - so I keep 15% of it for broad NVDA/TSM exposure I do not want to pick individually, and stop paying for the half that is diluting the specific supply-shortage argument I actually hold. Stop stays wide at -18% because the complex still swings 15-20% in a week.

Untraded at 15 and the best long in the book this week at +5.61%, closing at 95% of its 52-week range with 12-1 momentum of +99.9%. It is doing exactly what I sized it for and earnings remain out at Sept 1, so there is nothing to fix and no reason to pay to touch it. China's security review is still the live negative and still the reason this is 15 rather than 20.

New at 11. On the single measure my mandate is built from - 12-month-minus-1-month momentum - CRWD at +90.5% is the strongest name in my universe that I did not already own, and it backs that with 93.8% of range and closes above its 10-, 50- and 200-day. I am aware this puts 26% of the book in security alongside PANW, and I am accepting that concentration deliberately: security is the leading theme inside software right now and a cross-sectional momentum mandate is supposed to concentrate in whatever is leading, not spread evenly for its own sake. Sized 11 rather than higher precisely because of that correlation, with a -20% stop at 46 realized vol.

New at 9, funded from SMH, and it is the undiluted version of the thesis I have been writing for three weeks - SK Hynix guiding memory supply roughly 20% below demand through 2030, HBM sold out through 2027, Kioxia's 2026 NAND fully committed. 12-1 momentum of +607% is the top reading in my entire universe by a factor of three, it added 10.72% this week and trades above every moving average. Small at 9 and stopped wide at -30% for one arithmetic reason: 104% realized vol means one weekly sigma is about 15%, so a conventional -20% stop would be noise-triggered and a conventional weight would make this leg the book's whole vol budget. This is sized so a total stop-out costs 2.7% of NAV, which is the price of expressing the view directly instead of through a proxy that keeps netting it away.

New at 7. Passes every leg of the screen - 91.2% of range, +5.17% on the week, +15.9% on the month, 12-1 momentum of +35.6%, above all three moving averages - and it is the one addition that does not double an existing theme, adding edge and network infrastructure rather than more security or more data platform. Sized smallest of the longs because +35.6% on 12-1 is a middling reading next to CRWD and PANW, so it earns a slot on breadth within the mandate rather than on conviction.

New at 6, replacing the HOOD short at the same size and keeping the same crypto-retail factor on a strictly better-qualified name. COIN sits at 3.0% of its 52-week range, below its 10-, 50- and 200-day averages, -3.34% on the week and -7.49% on the month with 12-1 momentum of -49.5%. In a week when every index I track closed at or near 100% of its range, a name at 3% of its own range is not cheap, it is a laggard confirming itself - and that non-participation is the entire signal. HOOD by contrast rallied 2.43% back above its 10-day with 12-1 of only -7%, which is a bounce I do not want to be short into. Kept small with a wide -25% stop because it is the highest-beta squeeze candidate in the market in exactly the melt-up my longs need.

Untraded at 4 and roughly flat since I re-entered at this size on 08-10. It is still the best-qualified laggard on my screen - 16.9% of its 52-week range and 12-1 momentum of -49.4%, the worst pair of readings in my universe - against -$23.7B free cash flow, $97.6B net debt and a BBB- rating one notch off junk with ~$40B of FY27 financing needed. The +21% month is real and is exactly the recent-month reversal that 12-minus-1 construction deliberately excludes, so it is not evidence against the position, it is the reason the position is 4% and not 8%. At this size a full stop-out costs 0.8% of NAV, which is the correct price for a view I believe on fundamentals and cannot time.

decisions.name: Opus Picks-and-Shovels
decisions.research_notes:
WEB SEARCH BUDGET WAS EXHAUSTED (200/200) BEFORE I STARTED — all research this week was done via direct WebFetch of quote/news pages (stockanalysis.com), so my coverage is thinner than usual on primary sources. Reuters was unreachable. Flagging that as a limitation on this week's confidence.

MARKS vs my 2026-08-07 thesis prices (book filled 2026-08-10, so realized P&L is worse than these deltas imply — semis gapped up Mon/Tue then were sold hard Thu/Fri):
R2: GEV $1,063.25 (+7.4%, PE 30.4, tgt $1,238 = +16.5%, raised 2026 revenue guide, $176B backlog). ANET $198.82 (+5.4%, fwd PE 42.8, tgt $241.82 = +21.6%). VRT $293.84 (+7.4%, fwd PE 37.7, tgt $338 = +15.1%). MU $971.66 (+10.7%, fwd PE 6.76, tgt $1,502 = +54.6%, now back ABOVE the $970.95 50-dma I cited as my reason to cut it). AMAT $507.18 (-5.9%; fell 5.12% on Aug 14 on its OWN Q3 print — 25% y/y revenue growth, margin expansion, raised guide, yet sold on "intensifying competition"; fwd PE 28.8, tgt $638). AVGO $392.99 (-8.1%; fell 5.94% Aug 14 on sector beta despite Apple multi-year deal ">$30B" and the Samsung ~$200B collaboration; fwd PE 24.94, tgt $527.88 = +34.3%; reports Sept 2).
R3: GDX $89.97 (+1.93% Fri but roughly FLAT on the week). GLD $401.48, gold pressing ~$4,450 resistance, "Wall Street goes full-bull on gold as rate-hike bets recede." XLE $61.91 (+1.39% Fri, only 2.4% below its $63.46 52w high). COPX $85.70 (-2.6% from my add). EWZ $33.93 (PE 9.68, 4.31% yield; BCB cut to 14%; 25% US tariff intact). UUP $28.11 (essentially unchanged).

MACRO — the week's real content, and it cuts two ways:
1) A genuine consumer/growth scare arrived with disinflation: July retail sales -0.6% (first decline in 9 months, vs +0.1% expected), UMich sentiment 51.0 from 55.2, PPI flat vs +0.2% expected. September hike odds fell. Cleveland's Hammack publicly dissented calling for immediate hikes, which is why the dollar has NOT broken.
2) NEW AND SPECIFIC TO MY R2 MANDATE: Nvidia scaled back its ~$250B data-center guarantee for the OpenAI project while advancing a $500B AI-infrastructure funding vehicle with investment firms; coverage now openly discusses "the increasingly leveraged foundations of the AI boom" with buildout financing needs framed at up to $2 trillion. That is the first crack I have seen in the input my entire Round 2 book depends on — the $720-745B capex number is now visibly financing-dependent rather than cash-flow-funded.

WHAT I CONCLUDED: the AI-infrastructure trade bifurcated this week along exactly the axis my mandate cares about. Legs whose demand is physically constrained and already in backlog (GEV turbines, VRT power/cooling, MU memory, ANET fabric) rose; legs whose demand is an order book that a financing squeeze can defer (AMAT wafer-fab equipment) were sold on good numbers. Equipment orders are the first line item cut when capex financing tightens, and AMAT additionally now carries a competition overhang the market chose to price on a beat-and-raise day. That is a structural downgrade, not a timing one. Meanwhile my MU cut last week was simply wrong — the falsifying evidence (price reclaimed the 50-dma, YMTC's share gain is in NAND and does not touch the HBM/DRAM profit pool) arrived within five sessions, and MU is the only thing in either book at a single-digit forward multiple.

On the mandate's "15% 3x-semis leverage kicker": I am deliberately not running it. Max drawdown is already -14.61%, at the ~-14% tolerance the mandate sets, and adding 3x semis beta into a tape that just started questioning AI capex financing would be the exact mistake the cap exists to prevent.

decisions.reason: Two facts changed the ranking inside my own theme, and neither is a market call. First, AMAT fell 5.12% on its own beat-and-raise print (25% y/y growth, margins up, guide raised) on competition fears, in the same week GEV, VRT, MU and ANET all rose — that is idiosyncratic rejection, and it lands on the one leg whose revenue is an order book rather than a backlog, which is also the first thing deferred if the newly-visible AI capex financing strain (Nvidia trimming its $250B OpenAI guarantee, $2T of buildout financing needs, a $500B funding vehicle) actually bites. AMAT stops being my number-two position. Second, my MU cut last week was falsified within five sessions: the stock reclaimed the $970.95 50-dma I cited as my reason to leave, YMTC's share gain is NAND and does not touch the HBM/DRAM profit pool, and at a 6.76 forward multiple it is the cheapest physical bottleneck available to me — I am rebuilding it rather than defending a bad call. GEV funds part of this: it worked, but at 16.5% to consensus it now has the least room of anything I own. Gross comes down 85 to 82 because a new systemic risk to the capex number appeared while my drawdown is already at the mandate's -14% tolerance; I am not adding the 3x-semis kicker for the same reason.

positions.thesis: Still the only leg whose constraint is physical rather than cyclical — $176B backlog, raised 2026 revenue guidance, turbines sold to hyperscalers off their own balance sheets rather than through SPV financing, which is exactly the resilience the week's AI-leverage story tests for. Trimmed 20.8 to 17 purely on relative discount: at $1,063.25 versus a $1,238 consensus it has 16.5% of room, the least in the book, and PE 30.4 is no longer the bargain it was. It funds MU rather than being sold on any doubt.

Held through an 8% mark-to-market loss and now co-largest, because the drawdown is sector beta and the news flow is the opposite: an Apple multi-year agreement expected to exceed $30B on top of the ~$200B Samsung manufacturing collaboration. The distinction that matters after this week is who pays — Broadcom's custom-silicon customers are Apple, Google and Samsung, the strongest balance sheets on earth, not the debt-financed neocloud buildouts whose leverage the market just started pricing. Fwd PE 24.94 is the cheapest growth multiple I own against a $527.88 target. Sept 2 earnings is a known event I am carrying deliberately.

Held. The only leg that has now confirmed twice: Q2 revenue $3.036B versus $2.83B consensus, EPS $1.02 versus $0.89, full-year guide raised to $12.6B implying ~40% growth, and it has since repriced from $188.67 to $198.82 as the market caught up to what I bought. Fwd PE 42.8 against a $241.82 target is the risk; compute-fabric growth at 40% with no dependence on either turbine lead times or wafer-fab order timing is why it stays, and it diversifies a book otherwise made of semis and power.

Cut 19.8 to 13. The fundamentals delivered — 25% revenue growth, margin expansion, raised outlook — and the market sold it 5.12% anyway on competition, which tells me the multiple, not the quarter, is the problem. Layered on top is that wafer-fab equipment is the most financing-elastic link in the chain: if AI buildout capex is genuinely leaning on $2T of external funding, tool orders are what gets pushed a quarter. Fwd PE 28.8 against a $638 target is why I keep a real position rather than exit; it is no longer entitled to be my number two. Stop tightened to -18% from -22% now that the earnings gap risk I widened for has passed — if the competition threat is structural I want to be taken out early, not proved right slowly.

Rebuilt 4.9 to 11, correcting last week's cut. I sold it because it sat below its 50-day average and because SK Hynix capex looked like the supply response that ends memory shortages; it has since reclaimed that average at $971.66 and rallied 10.7% while I was underweight. The supply response is 2027 capacity against a 2026 shortage, and YMTC's rise to third-largest NAND supplier is in the commodity tier, not the HBM/DRAM pool that carries the margin. At a 6.76 forward multiple against a $1,502 consensus this is the cheapest physical bottleneck in AI infrastructure. Wide -22% stop: it has run ~200% this year and cyclical peak risk is genuine, so it needs room without being a catastrophe bet. Earnings Sept 22, outside the window.

Raised 7.9 to 9. Bought a week ago at a 28% discount to its high on a Q2 revenue miss management attributed to project timing and supply-chain slippage; it is up 7.4% since, which is the market beginning to agree that deferred revenue in a capex cycle this size is not lost revenue. Power distribution and liquid cooling sit on the same physical-bottleneck side of this week's bifurcation as GEV. Fwd PE 37.7 against $338 and 28 analysts at Strong Buy. Stop tightened -25% to -20% because the position is now in profit and no longer needs the extra width I gave a broken-and-unproven name.

decisions.reason: The macro moved further toward this book — July PPI flat, retail sales -0.6%, sentiment at 51.0, September hike odds receding, and gold pressing ~$4,450 with Wall Street turning outright bullish on it — so the book itself is right and I am only correcting two weights the data specifically calls out. GDX went up 3 points because the miners did NOT follow bullion this week: GDX finished roughly flat while gold made new ground, leaving the equity 23% below its $117.18 high while producers earn record margins at this gold price. That widening gap is the opposite of chasing; it is the entry a crowded-short squeeze last week denied me. UUP short comes down 7 to 4 because it failed a live test: a week of soft retail sales, soft PPI and collapsing consumer sentiment is precisely the news that should have broken the dollar, and it did not budge, with Hammack publicly agitating for hikes putting a floor under it. Short UUP also costs roughly 6% a year all-in once its 3.30% distribution and 3% borrow are paid, and I already own a weaker dollar four other ways through GDX, COPX, EWJ and EWZ, so I am paying carry for redundant beta. I am not re-adding to XLE despite it rallying to within 2.4% of its high after I trimmed it — reversing a trim on one week of price action is how a thesis becomes a coin flip.
decisions.novelty: Zero symbol overlap and zero same-direction gross-weight overlap with my Round 2 book: Round 3 owns gold miners, copper miners, energy, Brazil, Eurozone and Japan and is short the dollar, with no exposure whatsoever to the hyperscaler capex assumption that every Round 2 leg depends on — indeed it is the hedge against the AI-financing strain that surfaced this week.

positions.thesis: Raised 22 to 25 and clearly the anchor. Gold pushed toward $4,450 on receding hike bets, flat PPI and a consumer sentiment print at 51.0, yet GDX ended the week roughly unchanged at $89.97 — the miners did not participate, which is exactly the divergence I want to buy rather than the squeeze fuel I refused to pay up for last week. Still -23% below its $117.18 high at PE 13.6 while producers earn record margins at this metal price. No take-profit, because a monetary-credibility thesis should not be closed by a price target; stop stays -18% from the new level.

Held at 20 rather than restored. I demoted it last week on the read that a dovish tape was pricing energy as a demand cyclical, and it promptly rallied to $61.91, within 2.4% of its $63.46 high, on Middle East supply risk and refiner margins. That says my read was wrong on the week, but retail sales just fell 0.6% and sentiment collapsed to 51.0, so demand risk is now a real and growing input — which is precisely why this should be a strong second position and not the anchor it used to be. 2.45% yield, PE 20.0, +49% over the year.

Held at 15 through a 2.6% pullback to $85.70. Copper miners remain the one leg levered simultaneously to a softening dollar, a Fed drifting from hikes toward cuts, and physical tightness meeting grid electrification and datacenter buildout — and unlike my Round 2 names, copper demand from the AI buildout is realized in physical construction rather than in financed equipment orders. PE 20.1, 2.25% yield, +86% YTD and still 14% below its $99.99 high. This is the industrial counterpart to the monetary bet in GDX.

Held at 10. PE 9.68 with a 4.31% dividend yield is still the cheapest carry available to me, and Brazil's central bank cutting to 14% into moderating inflation gives it a domestic easing cycle running ahead of the Fed's. The 25% US tariff, with further penalties floated on sugar and ethanol, is the reason this is 10 and not 15 — but Vale and Nu Holdings at a third of the fund give it commodity and financial leverage to the same weakening dollar the rest of the book is positioned for.

Held at 10 and untouched for a second week. Eurozone value near its 52-week high on broadening earnings growth, PE 17.6, 2.57% yield — a non-US, non-AI earnings stream with zero exposure to the hyperscaler capex argument my Round 2 book makes, which is exactly the diversification I want in the week that argument first showed strain. A leg making new highs on improving fundamentals does not need managing.

Held at 9. Japan's governance-reform and buyback cycle keeps compounding at PE 18.6 with a 3.68% yield and +33% total return over the past year, near its 52-week high. Its second job is currency: any Fed easing that firms the yen adds to dollar-based returns here, so this leg now carries part of the weak-dollar expression I just took out of the UUP short, at a positive yield instead of a negative carry.

Cut 7 to 4, reduced to a tail expression. The structural fiscal-credibility case is unchanged, but the leg just failed a clean live test: soft retail sales, flat PPI and sentiment at 51.0 is the exact news set that should have broken the dollar, and UUP finished the week unchanged at $28.11 in the upper half of its $26.40-$28.60 range, with Hammack openly campaigning for hikes keeping a bid under it. It also carries roughly 6% annualized cost once its 3.30% distribution and the 3% borrow are counted, for beta I already own through GDX, COPX, EWJ and EWZ. Kept rather than closed because the fiscal thesis has a fat tail; sized so it costs me almost nothing to wait. Tight -8% stop.

decisions.name: Opus Momentum
decisions.research_notes:
WebSearch budget was exhausted at session start (200/200), so I verified everything from direct daily-close history fetches rather than headlines. Week measured Aug 7 close -> Aug 14 close.

SEMIS ARE ROTATING, NOT ROLLING OVER. On Aug 14 AVGO fell -5.94% while AMD rose +6.50% and MU rose +2.30% in the same session. Over the week: MU +10.7%, AMD +6.4%, SMH +0.9%, AVGO -8.1%. This is dispersion inside the complex, not a sector break - QQQ was +1.1% and printed a new closing high at $732.07 on Aug 13.

MY LARGEST CALL LAST WEEK WAS WRONG AND THE TAPE SAID SO IN FOUR SESSIONS. I cut MU from 13% to 6% on Citi's DRAM/NAND deceleration note and moved the capital into AVGO (7% -> 9%). Since my 08-10 entry MU went $861.00 -> $971.66 (+12.9%) and AVGO went $422.40 -> $393.06 (-6.9%). Confirming detail: New Street upgraded MU to Buy on a $2-3T AI-memory framing, consensus PT is $1,501.98 (+54.6%), stock +200% YTD, next catalyst earnings 2026-09-22. Live bear case still exists (YMTC now #3 in NAND), which is why I restore MU to 12% rather than to 13%+ and split the rotation into AMD. AVGO's own news was mixed-to-good (Samsung $200B MOU, Apple >$30B) - the negative was Goldman removing it from the US Conviction List (Buy kept). Good news plus an -8% week is a momentum book's exit signal.

AMZN's DRIFT IS DEAD. $278.09 -> $262.65, five consecutive down sessions. A post-earnings drift thesis that declines five days running is falsified by construction regardless of cause. Exited.

ENERGY: I trimmed XLE to 5% arguing a -23k payroll print was a demand-side negative for crude. XLE then ran +7.7% on the week and is +49% over one year. Supply premium is dominating demand softness; I raise it in both books.

CRYPTO - THE MANDATE'S PREMISE IS CURRENTLY FALSE. My Round-2 mandate funds itself partly by shorting BTC/ETH/SOL perps "riding the persistent downtrend." I checked: BTC $62,891, 7d -3.1%, 14d 0.0%, 30d +1.9%, 1y +47.1%. IBIT confirms a range, not a trend: Jul 1 $34.00 -> Aug 14 $35.63 (+4.8%). There are bearish near-term headlines (ETF outflows, break below $63k) but a 14-day-flat, 1-year +47% asset is not a persistent downtrend. Putting perp leverage against a rising asset to satisfy a structural template is exactly the unforced error that cost me on AVGO. Declining the short, deliberately.

RATES - THE BELLY IS BEATING THE BACK END, AS I ARGUED IT WOULD. IEF -0.14% vs TLT -0.87% on the week; the payroll-driven rally did not extend. One week does not falsify a Fed-reaction-function thesis, so IEF stays at 15%. But my own stated reason for capping TLT at 6% was that the long end carries fiscal supply risk no amount of Fed dovishness fixes, and the belly/back-end spread just confirmed it. Cutting TLT is my framework applied, not reversed.

REAL ASSETS OVER NOMINAL DURATION. GLD ran $374.16 (Aug 4) -> $401.48 (+7.3%) and XLE +7.7%, while both bond sleeves were flat-to-down and HYG was flat with spreads not widening. Cuts to the front plus live inflation risk is a coherent bullish-real-asset, ambiguous-long-bond regime. Round 3 shifts along exactly that axis.

Round 3 is the better book (+2.20%, max DD -0.75%) and gets a surgical trim, not a rebuild. Round 2 (+0.30%, max DD -3.86%) gets the real work.

decisions.reason: Two of my largest sizing calls from last week were contradicted by price within four sessions, and the contradiction is the same trade in both directions. I cut MU 13%->6% on a sell-side DRAM-deceleration note and moved that capital into AVGO 7%->9%; MU then returned +12.9% from my entry and AVGO -6.9%, with AVGO -5.94% on Aug 14 in the very session AMD rose +6.50% and MU +2.30%. That divergence proves the complex is rotating from custom-ASIC/networking into compute and memory, not breaking - QQQ printed a new closing high on Aug 13 and SMH was up on the week. A momentum mandate that lets a model note override the tape is not running its mandate, so I restore MU, buy the mandate-named AMD I did not own, and cut the laggard. I also exit AMZN, whose entire thesis was post-earnings drift and which has now fallen five consecutive sessions, and I raise XLE after trimming it on a demand argument the tape overruled with a +7.7% week. Separately, I am declining the crypto perp short my mandate names: I checked and the 'persistent downtrend' it assumes does not exist right now (BTC 14d flat, 30d +1.9%, 1y +47.1%), and shorting a rising asset with leverage to satisfy a template is the same unforced risk that just cost me on AVGO.

positions.thesis: Still the core and still the cleanest expression of the mandate, and this week is precisely why it is sized first: it returned +0.9% while its own constituents ranged from AVGO -8.1% to MU +10.7%. When single-name dispersion inside a sector is that violent, the index is how I stay long the confirmed uptrend without having to pick which sub-sector's pricing curve breaks next - which is the exact mistake I made on memory. Trimmed one point only to fund the single-name rotation.

Restored from the 6% residual I cut it to. I sized it down on Citi's call that DRAM and NAND decelerate for four straight quarters, and the tape answered in four sessions: $861.00 -> $971.66, +12.9% from my entry and +10.7% on the week, with New Street upgrading to Buy on a $2-3T AI-memory framing and consensus PT at $1,501.98. Deliberately 12% and not back to 13%+ because the bear case is live rather than dead - YMTC is now the third-largest NAND player - so I take the trend back at size while splitting the memory/compute rotation across two names. Stop kept at -15%, which is roughly one week of this name's realised range and sits below the Aug 10 low.

New leg, explicitly named in my mandate, and the position I should have owned instead of the AVGO add. It rose +6.50% on Aug 14 in the same session AVGO fell -5.94%, and +6.4% on the week. That is the leading edge of the rotation into merchant compute, and buying it alongside MU rather than doubling MU means the thesis I am expressing is 'capital is moving into compute and memory' rather than 'I am right about DRAM pricing' - the narrower claim is the one that already burned me.

Raised from 7% and now the larger half of the defence sleeve because it is the half that is actually trending: +3.5% on the week to $608.68 against RTX flat. Backlog visibility plus live geopolitical reinforcement, and near-zero correlation to the AI capex debate that every other position here depends on. In a book carrying 46% single-name-and-index semis plus two 3x instruments, this is the leg that keeps working if the AI trade stops.

Raised from 5% because the reason I cut it was overruled. I trimmed on the argument that a -23,000 payroll print is a demand-side negative for crude leaving only a supply premium; the sector then returned +7.7% on the week and is +49% over one year. Supply is clearly the binding factor, and this remains the only sleeve that pays if inflation rather than employment turns out to be the problem - which matters more now that I hold no crypto short to offset the book's single long-beta factor.
