The mandate's named leveraged semis instrument, held flat at 7% and pointed the right way into an uptrend that survived a week of severe internal dispersion. Not raised despite the trend being confirmed, because a daily-rebalanced 3x fund decays hard in exactly the choppy, rotational tape I just documented - SMH traded 569 to 589 and back to 588. Both brackets kept so the convexity stays defined on the downside.

Cut from 9% to 7% and now the smaller half of the defence pair. Nothing deteriorated - it closed the week at $222.97 against $223.03, essentially unchanged - but flat is the argument: in a momentum book, capital sitting in a name going sideways for a week while LMT moves +3.5% on the identical catalyst belongs in the one that is moving. Retained rather than exited because the sleeve's purpose is zero AI-cycle correlation and I want it expressed across two names.

Raised from 4% because the broad Nasdaq leg is the part of my thesis that got cleanly confirmed this week - QQQ +1.1% to a new closing high of $732.07 on Aug 13 - while the chips leg was messy and rotational. This is the instrument that captures the index-level move without taking a view on which chip sub-sector wins. Still capped at 6% with a wide -18% stop: 3x index beta stacked on an already-long book is where a growth-scare reinterpretation of the labour data would hurt fastest.

Trimmed from 8% to 5%. The Azure print that broke the capex-fear narrative is now three weeks old and the drift has stopped paying - $499.99 to $495.40 on the week, and it has closed lower in three of the last four sessions from the Aug 10 high of $506.06. Kept as a residual because the AI-to-revenue conversion story is intact and it is my only large-cap software exposure, but momentum capital does not fund a fading drift at full size.

Cut from 9% to 5% and reduced to a genuine minimum anchor. It did its job quietly at +1.0% on the week, but with the uptrend confirmed at the index level and the book's real opportunity sitting in the semis rotation, paying leveraged-momentum capital for defensive breadth at 9% is not defensible. Five percent still gives the book something that holds up if the AI complex de-rates, which matters more than usual now that I carry no crypto short as an offset.

Cut from 9% to a residual - the direct reversal of last week's worst decision, which was funding this add out of MU. Down 8.1% on the week and -5.94% on Aug 14 alone, and the diagnostic is that its own news flow was good (Samsung $200B MOU, Apple agreement above $30B) while Goldman pulled it from the US Conviction List. A name that falls 8% into positive company news is being de-rated on valuation, and it fell on the exact session AMD rose 6.5%, so this is idiosyncratic underperformance rather than sector beta. Not zero because the custom-AI-silicon thesis against $400bn+ hyperscaler capex is unbroken and 48 analysts still carry a $527.88 target; 4% keeps the option without paying for a laggard.

decisions.reason: The book is working as designed (+2.20% with a -0.75% max drawdown), so this is a surgical weekly rebalance along one axis the market moved, not a rebuild. The axis is that real assets paid and nominal duration did not: GLD ran +7.3% from Aug 4 and XLE +7.7% on the week, while IEF was -0.14% and TLT -0.87% and HYG was flat with spreads still not widening. I reinstated TLT one week ago on a Fed-reaction-function call, and the specific structure I flagged when I capped it at 6% - that the back end carries fiscal supply risk no amount of Fed dovishness fixes - is exactly what showed up, with the long end lagging the belly by 73bp in five sessions. So I cut the long end by more than half, add a point each to the two real-asset sleeves the tape rewarded, and move a point to cash, which yields 4% risk-free and is the cheapest carry available when nothing else is signalling. IEF stays at 15% untouched because one flat week is not a falsification of a multi-week reaction-function thesis and it remains the only sleeve that rallies in a genuine growth scare. Gross drops 92 to 91, which lowers portfolio variance - the direction an inverse-vol mandate should move when its highest-vol bond sleeve stops paying.
decisions.novelty: This book shares exactly one symbol with my Round-2 momentum book - a 6% energy sleeve, held here for inflation-linked dividend and FCF carry and its low correlation to the rest of the basket rather than for price momentum - representing under 7% of either book's gross, while its entire core of belly duration, min-vol equity, gold, REITs, high-yield credit and staples dividend carry has no counterpart in Round 2 at all.

positions.thesis: Held at 15% and still the top weight. It returned -0.14% on the week, so the payroll-driven repricing did not extend - but a Fed reaction-function thesis is measured in months, not five sessions, and the belly outperformed the long end by 73bp over exactly that window, which is the relationship I underwrote. This remains the only asset in the basket that rallies outright if the labour-market crack resolves as a genuine growth scare rather than a dovish gift, and it takes rate-cut exposure without the fiscal term-premium risk sitting at the back of the curve.

The core equity-risk-premium sleeve and the lowest-volatility asset in the basket, so inverse-vol weighting keeps it near the top. Untouched: nothing about a min-vol equity book deteriorated this week, and it is exactly the vehicle I want owning the equity premium into a tape where the index made new highs on rotation rather than on broad conviction.

Raised one point, deliberately only one. Gold has run $374.16 to $401.48 since Aug 4 (+7.3%) and finished the week +0.8%, and the regime argument behind it is coherent rather than momentum-chasing: a Fed pushed toward cuts with inflation risk still live is unambiguously bullish real assets and only ambiguously bullish the long bond. That is the same observation driving the TLT cut, so the two moves are one trade. Sized up modestly rather than aggressively because adding hard after a 7% eight-session run is how a low-vol book imports volatility it was built to avoid. Stop stays at -12% to survive post-squeeze mean reversion.

Held. Up 0.6% on the week and quietly compounding, it supplies a rent-yield cash-flow stream that is distinct from both equity beta and credit spread - the definitional job of a sleeve in a cross-asset carry book. It is levered to the same long-rate path as my duration sleeves but gets paid a contractual yield while it waits, which is why I would rather carry rate sensitivity here than at the back of the Treasury curve.

Held at 8%, not restored. The thing I feared when I cut it from 11% - that employment cracking would be the trigger for the first spread widening - has not happened, with the ETF flat at $79.71 and spreads still tight. But one quiet week is not evidence of safety either, and the structural worry is unchanged: this is credit carry standing in front of a debt-funded AI complex and a contracting labour market. Collecting roughly 7% at a reduced size with the tight -6% stop is the right shape for that asymmetry.

Held. Low-volatility equity selected on a pure realised-vol screen rather than USMV's optimisation, so the two hold materially different names and genuinely diversify each other rather than duplicating a factor. Keeping both is what lets the equity-premium allocation stay large in a book whose mandate is portfolio variance minimisation.

Raised from 5% because the reason I trimmed it was overruled by the tape: I cut on the view that a contracting labour market is a demand-side negative for crude, and the sector then returned +7.7% on the week against a +49% one-year trend. Supply premium is the binding factor. Held to 6% rather than higher because this is the highest-volatility sleeve in the basket and inverse-vol weighting caps how much of it a low-beta book should own regardless of how well it is performing. It remains the only inflation-linked leg and the only position that does not need rates to keep falling.

Held. Consumer staples as defensive dividend carry, taking the bond-proxy income role at similar yield and beta to utilities with none of the AI-datacenter-power exposure that has made utilities a levered bet on the same capex cycle everything else here is trying to avoid. This is precisely the equity that holds up if the next payroll print is read as recessionary rather than dovish.

Held. The single-name expression of defensive dividend carry with the strongest trend of any staple, on a stable and growing dividend. It benefits from the same falling discount rate as every other bond proxy here while carrying essentially no exposure to the AI capex debate, and it is where low-beta money has actually been going rather than where it theoretically should.

Held. Telecom yield carry on regulated domestic cash flows with near-zero correlation to the AI capex cycle. A high-dividend, rate-sensitive payer expresses the same duration view as my Treasury sleeves but through equity and with a coupon attached, which is the diversification a cross-asset carry mandate is supposed to buy.

Cut from 6% to 3%, applying my own stated framework rather than reversing it. When I reinstated this last week I wrote that it was capped precisely because the long end carries fiscal supply risk that Fed dovishness cannot fix - and in the five sessions since, TLT returned -0.87% against IEF -0.14%, the exact underperformance that argument predicts. It is also the highest-volatility bond sleeve in an inverse-vol book, so halving it lowers portfolio variance in the same stroke. Kept at a 3% satellite rather than cut to zero because my mandate names term premium as a target and the back end is where a hard growth scare would pay the most.

decisions.name: Opus Value
decisions.research_notes:
Checked every line in both books against 2026-08-14 closes plus the macro drivers I named last week.

MACRO — the week's one genuinely new fact: the Hormuz de-escalation trade broke. WTI is back to $82.40, up ~5% on the week from $78.18, with Iran/Oman negotiations reported STALLED, the US Treasury announcing "unprecedented economic measures" plus port blockades, and the IEA warning of the most severe global supply shortage in five years for 2026 (Q3 consensus $86, 12-month $100). That is the exact opposite of the ceasefire narrative I cut energy on seven days ago. TLT closed $82.04 against a fresh 52-week low of $81.82, -2.14% on the year, with commentary on bond vigilantes and ~$40T debt — so the inflation/fiscal channel is open at the same time.

ROUND 2 MARKS: UNH $401.73 (-1.3% w/w) vs 27-analyst target $475.23 (+18.3%), forward PE 18.9, dividend raised, banks still lifting targets post-Q2. GLD $401.48 (+0.63%), spot gold a seven-week high near $4,300 on a sliding dollar and receding rate-hike bets, but GLD still 21% below its $509.70 52-week high. CRM $196.21 (+1.8%), forward PE 14.08, 52 analysts at $242.29 (+23.5%), print 2026-08-26. NOW $124.00 (-0.7%), forward PE 27.4, target $140.25 (+13.1%), hundreds of job cuts announced alongside the strong Q2. XLV $167.37 (+1.0%), 1-yr +27.8%, within 1.4% of its 52-week high, described as a haven for money leaving tech. ADBE $264.02 against a consensus target of $269.72 — 2.16% upside, rating now Hold, Morgan Stanley Underweight. ETH $1,878 (-2.2% w/w, +0.5% on 30 days) but still taking ETF inflows against a weak tape. BTC $62,891 (-3.1% w/w) with ETF outflows extending and institutional selling described as mounting.

NEW NAME SCREENED: CVS $97.16, forward PE 11.92, 27 analysts Strong Buy at $116.08 (+19.5%), Q2 revenue $106.1bn (+7.3%) with net income nearly tripling to $2.9bn on Aetna improvement and guidance raised. Also screened PFE ($26.79, forward PE 9.67, 6.4% yield) and rejected it: only 6.9% consensus upside on declining revenue is a yield trap, not a dislocation.

ROUND 3 MARKS: XLE $61.91 (+1.39%), 1-yr +49.09%, within 2.5% of its 52-week high. GDX $89.97 (+1.70% on the day), 1-yr +56.02% — still the strongest relative strength I can verify. SPMO $153.31 (+0.39%), 1-yr +31.17%; SOXX flat on the week (-0.06%) but 1-yr +117.8%, so the semiconductor re-rating is intact rather than extending. SCHD $34.52, 1-yr +30.33%, sitting at an all-time high — my supposed ballast is quietly one of my best trends. QUAL $225.84 (-0.59%), 1-yr +20.8%, near its high. JEPQ $60.53, 1-yr +21.4%, 10.78% yield, near its high. GOOGL $345.90, PE 17.36, 64 analysts Strong Buy at $428.04 (+23.8%), and Berkshire raised its stake 83% in Q2 to a $37.9bn third-largest holding. AMZN $262.65, down 4.3% from the $274.48 I added at — the post-gap fill I explicitly said I was watching for. SPLV $76.36, 1-yr +5.45% — by a wide margin the worst thing in the book.

decisions.reason: Two theses reached their stated endpoints and one macro hedge got its confirmation, so the book pays out and redeploys rather than holding green positions out of inertia. Adobe was bought as the most extreme valuation dislocation in profitable quality software; at $264.02 against a $269.72 consensus target the gap is 2.16% with the rating now Hold and Morgan Stanley at Underweight, which means the mispricing I was paid to identify no longer exists and what is left is a bet on multiple simultaneous strategic transitions rather than a value argument. Bitcoin exits on the rule I wrote for myself last week — weight belongs where reversion is observable, not merely available — and a week of -3.1% with ETF outflows extending and institutional selling mounting is that rule scoring against the position rather than an opinion I am revising. Gold goes up because the single macro assumption underpinning the rest of the market broke: Iran/Oman Hormuz talks are stalled, the US is adding blockades and unprecedented economic measures, the IEA is forecasting the worst supply shortage in five years, crude is back to $82.40, and TLT printed a fresh 52-week low — GLD is the only line here that pays if that compounds, and at 21% below its own 52-week high I am adding to a discounted hedge, not chasing one. CVS enters because the managed-care recovery I own through UNH now has independent corroboration from a second, cheaper issuer.

positions.thesis: Held at 18% and still the anchor. The stock fell another 1.3% to $401.73 this week while XLV rose 1.0% to within 1.4% of its 52-week high, which extends the divergence I have been paid to own: a company whose Q2 adjusted EPS beat by 30% and whose targets were raised by JPMorgan, Wells Fargo and Goldman is being left behind by the sector re-rating around it. 27 analysts average $475.23 for 18.3% upside on an 18.9x forward multiple with the dividend just raised. I do not add because at 18% it is already the largest single-name risk a prudently sized contrarian book should carry, and the second managed-care line I am opening expresses the same recovery more cheaply.

Raised 15->18. Last week I called gold advancing into rising long yields the confirmation I wanted; this week the reason arrived. Hormuz negotiations between Iran and Oman are stalled rather than near a deal, the US is layering port blockades and unprecedented economic measures on Iran, the IEA is warning of the worst supply shortage in five years, and crude is back to $82.40 — while TLT printed a fresh 52-week low of $81.82 on debt and inflation concerns. That is a simultaneous geopolitical and fiscal impulse and this is the only position in the book that profits from it. It stays a contrarian add rather than a momentum chase because at $401.48 GLD is still 21% below its $509.70 52-week high, so I am buying a hedge in its own drawdown, not at its peak.

Held at 13%. Up another 1.8% to $196.21 with a 14.08x forward multiple and 52 analysts averaging $242.29 for 23.5% upside on net income +29.3% against revenue +11.0% — the widest remaining gap between fundamentals and price in this book. I hold rather than add for exactly the reason I gave last week: the 2026-08-26 print is nine days out, and increasing size into a binary event would convert a valuation thesis into an earnings bet. The Agentforce adoption debate cuts both ways in the coverage and I have no edge on which way it resolves in one quarter.

Held at 9%. Essentially unchanged at $124.00, still 36% below its $194.73 high on 22.2% revenue growth with AI ACV past $1bn, and the restructuring announced alongside Q2 is management acting on the cost base rather than denying the pressure. I do not raise it for the reason I named when I sized it: at a 27.4x forward multiple this is the most rate-sensitive duration I own, and with TLT at a fresh 52-week low and oil re-accelerating, the discount rate is moving against it even as the business does not.

Held at 9% and now the entire crypto expression. Down 2.2% on the week to $1,878 and roughly flat over 30 days, so the bounce has stalled rather than reversed — but the coverage this week was specifically Ethereum rallying on strong ETF inflows amid broader crypto weakness, which is the opposite of the outflow story that pushed me out of Bitcoin. Relative strength inside a weak complex is the distinction the mandate is built on. I neither add nor cut: the institutional catalyst is intact and the price is 62% below its all-time high, but a stalled month is not the moment to press. Stop stays at -25% because oversold assets can still trend down.

Held at 8%. The rotation I bought this for is now visible rather than hoped for — $167.37 within 1.4% of the 52-week high, +27.8% over a year, with healthcare explicitly described as the haven absorbing money rotating out of technology, and a 0.56 beta. It stays a stub rather than a core weight because I am now running two managed-care single names and the sector fund exists to keep that concentration from being the whole healthcare bet, not to be the bet itself.

New 7%. This is the same managed-care recovery I own through UNH, bought at a much steeper discount and with the fundamental inflection already reported: Q2 revenue of $106.1bn up 7.3%, net income nearly tripled to $2.9bn on Aetna margin repair, and full-year guidance raised. At $97.16 it trades on an 11.9x forward multiple with 27 analysts at Strong Buy and a $116.08 target for 19.5% upside, plus a 2.7% dividend. Two independent issuers reporting the same cost-trend improvement is corroboration of my largest thesis rather than a doubling of it, and I sized it below UNH because the leverage and integration overhang is real — this is the cheaper, lower-conviction leg of the pair, funded by the Adobe and Bitcoin exits.

decisions.reason: A trend-follower's job is to follow the driver it named, in both directions, and the driver I cut energy on last week has reversed on me. I halved XLE at $78.18 crude on reports that Iran and Oman were near a landmark Hormuz deal and that traders were bearish through the disruptions; this week the talks are stalled, the US has added port blockades and unprecedented economic measures, the IEA is forecasting the worst global supply shortage in five years, WTI is $82.40 after a 5% week, and XLE closed +1.39% at $61.91 within 2.5% of its 52-week high on a 49.1% one-year return. Taking the round-trip cost of roughly 2bps a side to re-establish is the price of actually obeying my own rule rather than defending last week's decision, and the alternative — refusing to re-enter because I would look inconsistent — is how trend books die. The funding comes from the two positions the tape is arguing against: SPLV exits entirely because a momentum mandate cannot carry a 7% weight in a sleeve returning 5.45% over a year while everything around it compounds at 20-56%, and AMZN comes down because the post-gap retrace I explicitly said I was watching for has begun, with the stock 4.3% below where I added into a flat market. GDX takes a point because it remains the single strongest verified relative-strength line I hold and gold just made a seven-week high on the same Hormuz escalation that is bidding crude.
decisions.novelty: This book shares no symbol with my Round 2 contrarian book — zero same-direction gross-weight overlap — and it is built on the opposite selection rule: Round 2 buys UNH, CVS, CRM, NOW and ETH precisely because they are depressed relative to their own histories, while this book owns XLE, GDX, SPMO, SCHD, QUAL and JEPQ precisely because they are at or near 52-week highs with demonstrated one-year relative strength, and it enforces that with hard stops on every line where Round 2 carries almost none.

positions.thesis: Restored 8->14 and the stop widened back to 12%. I halved this seven days ago on a named, falsifiable driver — crude at $78.18 with a Hormuz deal reportedly close — and said explicitly that the commodity leads the equity. The commodity has now led the other way: WTI $82.40 after a 5% week, negotiations stalled, US blockades and unprecedented sanctions announced, and the IEA forecasting the most severe supply shortage in five years for 2026 with a $86 Q3 and $100 twelve-month consensus. The equity is confirming rather than diverging this time, closing +1.39% within 2.5% of its 52-week high on a 49.09% one-year return, with a 20.9x PE and 2.45% yield underneath. I take it above the original weight because the supply story is now structural forecast rather than a single headline premium, and because this is the only sleeve that profits if the inflation re-acceleration that has TLT at a 52-week low keeps going.

Raised 10->12. Still the strongest relative-strength reading I can verify anywhere in my universe at +56.02% over twelve months, up another 1.70% into the close, with spot gold extending a seven-week streak near $4,300 on a sliding dollar, receding rate-hike expectations and the same Middle East escalation that is bidding crude. At $89.97 against a $117.18 high this is a resumed trend rather than a terminal blow-off, which is the distinction that decides whether adding is trend-following or top-ticking. The add is two points rather than five because miners run roughly three times bullion's volatility and I am simultaneously raising energy, which correlates with gold through the same geopolitical channel. Stop stays wide at 15% because a tighter one on this volatility is a noise generator, not risk control.

Held at 12%. This is the literal instrument of the mandate and it did nothing wrong this week: +0.39% to $153.31, 5.5% below its 52-week high, +31.17% over a year, with Micron 10.0%, NVIDIA 8.9% and Broadcom 7.0% at the top. SOXX was flat at -0.06% while still up 117.8% over twelve months, which reads as a re-rating consolidating rather than rolling over — and consolidation after a vertical move is the condition under which a trend follower holds rather than adds. Its quarterly reconstitution also rotates me out of fading leaders mechanically, which is the cheapest way to run trend without forecasting.

Held at 12%, and I am reclassifying rather than resizing it. I have been calling this drawdown ballast, but it closed at $34.52 — its all-time high — with a 30.33% one-year total return that beats my dedicated momentum sleeve, on an 18.1x multiple, a 3.04% yield and a 0.69 beta. A dividend fund making new highs while long yields make new lows is not a defensive concession, it is a trend I already own, and its Abbott, Amgen and Merck top weights give the book healthcare exposure that pairs with nothing else in it. It stays at 12% because the low beta is genuinely load-bearing now that I am carrying 26% in energy and miners.

Held at 12%. Down 0.59% to $225.84 and still within 1% of its 52-week high on a 20.8% one-year return. The rate argument for it strengthened rather than weakened: TLT printed a fresh 52-week low of $81.82 with commentary on bond vigilantes and $40T of federal debt, and high-return-on-equity businesses carrying little leverage are the part of the equity complex least damaged by a permanently higher cost of capital because they never need to visit that market. Nothing about the position or the regime changed this week, so neither does the weight.

Held at 11% after last week's trim. I cut this because Demis Hassabis and Jeff Dean left in the same week and I judged the quality half of the case damaged; the counter-evidence this week is unusually hard to dismiss — Berkshire raised its stake 83% in Q2 to $37.9bn and a third-largest holding, which is a quality verdict from the most quality-obsessed buyer in the market, delivered after the departures. Against that, price is soft at $345.90 with the cap down to $4.23T from $4.33T, so the tape has not yet ratified it. A 17.4x multiple with 64 analysts at Strong Buy and a $428.04 target is cheap enough that I will not cut further, and Gemini 3.7 Flash shipping says the lab is still delivering. Holding rather than restoring the trim is the honest position when my own evidence is split.

Held at 10%. Near its 52-week high at $60.53 with a 21.4% one-year total return and a 10.78% distribution yield paid monthly, most recently $0.705 on 2026-08-03. Written-call income is the counter-cyclical property I hold this for: it improves precisely when the dispersion in my directional sleeves rises, and I am raising directional risk this week by taking energy to 14% and miners to 12%. Its NVIDIA, Apple, Microsoft and Micron top weights also keep me in the megacap complex with a capped upside, which is the right shape for exposure I want but do not want to add beta to.

Cut 10->8. I raised this a week ago at $274.48 on the specific reasoning that the post-earnings gap had held rather than filled; at $262.65 it is 4.3% lower against a broadly flat tape, which is the retrace I named as the thing that would invalidate the add. Reversing the add rather than waiting for the 12% stop is what a stated invalidation condition is for. I keep 8% because nothing in the business deteriorated — EPS $12.44 up 89.7%, revenue +12.4%, AWS momentum intact, 60 analysts at Strong Buy with a $326.07 target — and because expressing AI through cloud monetization complements rather than duplicates the semiconductor weight in SPMO. Stop and take-profit unchanged.

decisions.name: Opus Quality Defensive
decisions.research_notes:
Checked both books against 8/14 closes plus this week's macro tape.

MACRO (new since I set these books on 8/10): July CPI cooled and PPI was flat, but July retail sales fell -0.6% — the first decline in 14 months, as tax-refund stimulus rolled off — and NY Fed data shows credit-card and auto delinquencies still elevated. Treasury yields fell on the retail print. Jackson Hole is next up with the September cut no longer priced as certain. Net: disinflation plus a visibly cracking consumer, layered on the -23,000 payroll print that drove my last reassessment. That is a confirming regime for a low-beta quality book and a warning for anything consumer-credit-sensitive.

ROUND 2 TAPE (all figures 8/14): every long is above both moving averages. XLV $167.37, +1.02% wk, +3.44% mo, +14.14% qtr, +24.94% 1yr, 4.7% above 50d, 9.0% above 200d, beta 0.57, RSI 62 — leading the defensive set without being extended. SCHD $34.52, +1.83% wk, +8.55% qtr, +25.85% YTD, 5.2%/13.1% above 50d/200d, but RSI 71.9. USMV $101.13, +0.51% wk, +6.25% qtr, 4.0%/6.2% above 50d/200d, RSI 72.2 — min-vol at RSI 72 is a stretched configuration. XLP $86.09 still the laggard: +1.14% wk but +1.31% qtr and -3.50% half-year. GLD $401.48, +0.76% wk, +10.01% mo, and now only -2.64% below its 200-day after being 3.2% below it a week ago — the turn I bought is progressing and it stalled precisely at 200-day resistance (~$4,450-4,500 spot), which is normal, not a failure. SMH $587.82 is the single most important read: it is the ONLY instrument on my entire board still below its 50-day (-0.62%), RSI 54, +1.64% over three months against XLV +14.14% and XLF +13.39%, and -12.5% from its 52-week high. My 4% short cost 3.5bp this week and the relative thesis is quietly intact. No stop or take-profit fired.

ROUND 3 TAPE: DBMF $31.35, +1.36% wk, +1.52% mo, above both MAs, beta -0.18 — the cross-asset core is doing its job. EFA $108.64 stalled at +0.08% on the week but sits at its 52-week high with +4.65% mo, +5.01% qtr, 3.9%/8.0% above 50d/200d. JEPI $58.02 +0.76% wk, +3.63% qtr, above both MAs, RSI 68.5 — for a written-call fund with capped upside that is as good as the sleeve gets. IWM $305.09 printed a new 52-week high, +17.55% half-year, 13.6% above its 200-day — trend perfect, but it is my highest-beta (1.12) and most consumer-credit-sensitive leg on the exact week retail sales turned negative and delinquencies were flagged. XLF $58.16 +13.39% qtr, above both MAs. PDBC $17.91 was the board's best week at +3.83% (+5.60% mo), driven by USO reclaiming its 50-day (+5.19% above it now) and gold's +10% month — but its quarter is still -7% to -4%, so the oil-demand reason I cut it from 24% has not been refuted.

Two legs failed their own tests. ETH: the ETHA/ETHE proxies now sit BELOW their 20-day (-0.86%), RSI decayed to 51, and they are ~21% below the 200-day and 61% off the high. Crypto was the only asset class that did not participate in a third consecutive up week for the S&P. Non-participation in broad risk-on is exactly how a trend mandate identifies a dead trend.

The genuinely new trend-and-carry signal is copper, not oil: spreads are at their highest since 2021 (backwardation = positive roll yield, literally the commodity carry my mandate names), copper is at record prices on AI/grid demand plus tariff and supply constraints, and CPER $40.01 is +5.12% mo, +12.67% half, +42.94% 1yr, above all three moving averages, only 2.3% from its record — with RSI at just 57. A trend at a record high that is not overbought is the best setup on my board, and it expresses the carry far more cleanly than adding back PDBC, which is ~55% energy.

decisions.reason: The week's data confirmed this book rather than changing it, so trading it would be pure churn. Cooling CPI, a -0.6% retail sales print and elevated consumer delinquencies are precisely the environment a 0.57-beta healthcare-led defensive core is built for, and the book returned +2.00% with no stop or take-profit touched and every long above both its moving averages. Each leg is doing the specific job I assigned it a week ago: XLV leads on the horizon that matters (+14.14% over three months) with broad leadership rather than one drug, SCHD compounds free-cash-flow quality without QUAL's tech weight, USMV is the ballast, XLP is deliberately the small underweight because it is the one defensive not participating, and GLD has advanced its turn from 3.2% below its 200-day to 2.6% below it — stalling at that resistance is what a recovering trend does, not a broken thesis. The token semis short is the one thing I re-examined hardest, because SMH is now the only instrument on my entire board still below its 50-day, with a +1.64% quarter against XLV's +14.14%: the overextension view is working in relative terms at a cost of 3.5bp this week, which is exactly what I wanted from it, but SMH being merely up-less rather than falling is not a reason to press a short with 3% borrow in a defensive book. The single argument for action is that my own defensives are getting hot — USMV at RSI 72.2 and SCHD at 71.9 — and that argues for keeping the 13% cash buffer earning 4% into Jackson Hole, not for spending it. Confirmation is a reason to sit still.

Two things a trend mandate must act on happened this week, and neither is a change of mind about the book's core. First, the crypto leg failed its own confirmation test: ETH went sideways-to-lower and lost its 20-day while every other asset class I track rose in a third straight up week for the S&P, with RSI decaying to 51 and price still roughly 21% below its 200-day. A trend sleeve that cannot participate in broad risk-on is not a trend, and I said last week that a trend mandate cannot justify size in a market whose primary trend is down — so I cut it toward a marker rather than defend it. Second, a genuinely new carry signal appeared where I was not positioned: copper spreads are at their highest since 2021, which is backwardation paying actual positive roll yield, against record prices driven by AI and grid demand into constrained supply. That is the literal 'commodity carry' my mandate names, and CPER expresses it far better than adding back PDBC, which is majority energy and whose three-month return is still negative — the oil-demand reason I cut PDBC from 24% two weeks ago has not been refuted just because crude bounced, so I leave that weight alone rather than whipsaw myself into paying for the same trade twice. I also trimmed IWM two points and tightened its stop, not because its trend broke — it made a new 52-week high — but because it is my highest-beta, most consumer-credit-sensitive holding and the two datapoints that landed this week, retail sales falling for the first time in 14 months and elevated card and auto delinquencies, hit that exposure specifically. Everything that is working is untouched: DBMF, EFA, JEPI and XLF all hold above both moving averages and keep their weights.
decisions.novelty: This book shares no symbol and no direction with my Round-2 defensive book — zero same-direction gross-weight overlap — and expresses an orthogonal idea: Round 2 owns low-beta US quality equity and bullion for capital preservation, while this book stacks negative-beta managed futures, unhedged developed-international currency trend, written-call income, small-cap momentum, financials and now industrial-metal backwardation carry, deriving its return from trend persistence and roll yield rather than from defensive earnings streams.

positions.thesis: The structural core of the mandate and untouched: cross-asset managed futures that re-position themselves when the regime turns, so I capture the next trend rotation without having to be early on every leg by hand. It earned its keep this week at +1.36% while holding above both moving averages (1.5% above the 50-day, 4.2% above the 200-day) and +20.7% over twelve months. Its -0.18 beta is the reason it sits at the top of the book: with the consumer visibly cracking, the one sleeve that can be structurally short equities if the tape rolls over is the most valuable diversifier I own.

Still the most consistent uptrend on my screen and held at full weight despite a flat week (+0.08%), because it is sitting at its 52-week high with every longer horizon positive: +4.65% one month, +5.01% three months, +13.13% year-to-date, 3.9% above its 50-day and 8.0% above its 200-day. A pause at a high is consolidation, not distribution. Unlike the US momentum complex it never had the AI-capex air pocket, so there is no unwind overhanging it, and falling Treasury yields on weak US consumer data keep the dollar soft — which is a direct, mechanical tailwind to unhedged developed-international returns. Trend and currency carry in one line.

The covered-call income sleeve, held at full weight. It clears the same trend filter I apply to everything else — 2.4% above its 50-day, 1.4% above its 200-day, +3.63% over three months — while paying roughly 8% in distributions, which is why its price return understates what it earns. Its RSI of 68.5 does not worry me the way it would elsewhere: written-call upside is capped by construction, so this leg is not something I can get hurt by chasing. If a record-high tape built on softening economic data turns into the choppy, low-drift market that retail sales and delinquency data point toward, harvested call premium is the right carry to own.

Deliberately left at the residual weight I cut it to, even though it was the best performer on my board this week at +3.83%. The bounce came from crude reclaiming its 50-day and from gold's +10% month, not from a repair of the thing that broke: its three-month return is still negative and the fund is majority energy, while a contracting labour market and falling retail sales are straightforwardly demand-negative for oil. I am not going to reverse a two-week-old decision on one strong week and pay the round trip for the privilege. It holds above both moving averages (5.3% above the 50-day, 12.9% above the 200-day) at +35% year-to-date, which is why it is not zero, and it keeps me in the broad commodity basket while I express the specific carry signal in copper instead.

Trimmed two points and the stop tightened from 10% to 8%, as a risk adjustment rather than a change of view. The trend itself is impeccable: a new 52-week high this week, +7.26% over three months, +17.55% over six, 13.6% above its 200-day and 3.4% above its 50-day. But at beta 1.12 this is the highest-beta and by far the most consumer-credit-sensitive thing I own, and the two datapoints that landed this week hit it precisely — retail sales fell 0.6% for the first decline in 14 months, and the New York Fed flagged elevated card and auto delinquencies. Small-cap earnings and small-cap balance sheets are where that shows up first. The rate-cut repricing that powered this leg is also less certain into Jackson Hole, so I keep the momentum exposure the mandate requires but stop paying full size for it.

Held unchanged. It still does two mandate jobs at once — a confirmed uptrend at +13.39% over three months, 4.9% above its 50-day and 9.5% above its 200-day, plus dividend carry — and falling front-end rates with a steepening curve remains the classic setup for wider net interest margin alongside strong capital-markets activity. The elevated consumer delinquencies reported this week are the live risk to this leg, and they are exactly why I chose XLF over KRE in the first place: money-centre banks, insurers and exchanges are far better collateral than regional-bank loan books if consumer credit is genuinely deteriorating. The wider 12% stop reflects that this is a sector I expect to be volatile around Jackson Hole rather than one I want shaken out of.

New, and the cleanest carry-plus-trend setup available to me. Copper calendar spreads are at their highest since 2021, meaning the curve is backwardated and the fund earns positive roll yield simply by holding — this is literally the commodity carry my mandate names, as opposed to a directional bet dressed up as carry. The trend confirms it on every horizon: +5.12% one month, +12.67% six months, +42.94% over twelve, above its 20-, 50- and 200-day, and within 2.3% of a record price. What makes it a better entry than the rest of the commodity complex is that RSI is only 57 — a trend at a record high that is not overbought is rare and is the opposite of the squeezed conditions I refused to buy in gold miners. The demand story is structural rather than cyclical (AI datacentre power, grid buildout, supply constraints and tariffs), which is what I want when the cyclical data is deteriorating.

Cut from 5% to a marker because the trend failed its confirmation. The only reason I held it a week ago was that it was the strongest short-horizon crypto trend on offer, sitting above its 50-day; it has now lost its 20-day, RSI has decayed to 51, and it remains roughly 21% below its 200-day and 61% off its high. Decisive is that it went nowhere in a week when every other asset class I track rallied — non-participation in broad risk-on is how a trend mandate identifies a dead trend. I keep 3% rather than zero because it is still marginally above its 50-day and I am not willing to call it a confirmed downtrend either, and because crypto is a sleeve the mandate names. Held spot rather than as a perp so I am not paying 10% APR funding to be long something whose primary trend is down, with the stop tightened slightly and the take-profit left where a 50-day reclaim would have become a real base.

decisions.name: Opus-fleet dividend growth
decisions.research_notes:
Web search budget was exhausted this session, so I pulled current quotes, consensus targets and news directly from stockanalysis.com fundamentals pages for every held name plus two redeploy candidates. Prices are 2026-08-14 close.

WHAT I HELD, MARKED AGAINST MY OWN 2026-08-10 ENTRY THESES:
- SCHD $34.52, +30.33% trailing 1yr, 3.04% yield, 18.1x P/E, 0.06% fee, $105.7B AUM, 103 holdings, sitting at an all-time high. Top holdings ABT 4.78%, AMGN 4.62%, MRK 4.35%. Thesis fully intact.
- ABBV $249.46 vs my $246.04 entry. Consensus $276.24, 10.74% upside — still the widest gap in my book. NEW AND MATERIAL: FY26 adjusted EPS guidance was CUT to $13.87-$14.07 to absorb a pending Apogee Therapeutics acquisition, even as revenue guidance stayed raised at ~$67.6B. So the "guidance raised" half of my thesis is now half true. Apogee is immunology, adjacent to Skyrizi, so this is dilution for strategic fit rather than a core deceleration — a demerit, not a falsification.
- CVX $200.00, +1.16% Friday, up roughly 7% since I bought it. This is my best leg and it has spent its own thesis: upside to the $216.83 consensus has compressed from 16.3% at entry to 8.48%, and yield has fallen from 3.82% to 3.56%. The specific reversal risk I named at entry is now an actual headline — Trump publicly attacking Big Oil for "making too much money" and demanding pump-price cuts, against a Q2 profit surge that Chevron itself attributes to a Middle East geopolitical premium.
- XOM $160.10. Consensus $168.55, only 5.28% upside; yield 2.57%; some analysts now downgrading on valuation. It has run 4.8% since entry.
- KO $87.71 vs $87.05 entry. Consensus $94.70, 7.97% upside, 26.4x for a 2.42% yield. FY26 guidance raised, World Cup and zero-sugar demand strong. One new negative: the fairlife dairy subsidiary had a July cyber incident that halted four US plants before resuming.
- MDT $91.27, up 4.7% since I bought it at $87.16. UBS upgraded to Buy from Neutral with a $100 target calling "a turnaround underway." 3.16% yield, 0.57 beta, 15.3x forward. Consensus $98.44, 7.86% upside. Earnings still Sep 1.
- ABT $111.25. BOTH of my stated reasons for trimming it have now resolved in my favour: Abbott says the cybersecurity incidents left "no operations affected," and the 2022 formula shareholder suit is settled. Consensus was raised to $119.40 but the price rose faster, so upside is 7.33% at 36x. New Google Health partnership on Lingo biowearable glucose data.
- JNJ $260.35 vs $259.24. Consensus $272.50, 4.67% upside — the thinnest in the book — on the lowest yield in the book at 2.06%. FY26 EPS guidance was lowered again to $10.86-$11.01 on acquisition impacts, and the company keeps spending outside the dividend (Firefly Bio closed, a $2.58B Sail Biomedicines partnership). Talc is settled at $5.5B across ~76,000 suits, OTTAVA approved, Rybrevant Faspro has priority review.

REDEPLOY CANDIDATES I CHECKED AND REJECTED:
- PEP $140.79: a 4.21% yield, the richest in my universe, at 18.5x with 10.09% upside. I rejected it anyway because the pattern is identical to the P&G setup I killed last week — Hold consensus, multiple firms cutting targets after Q2, and a North America snacking business one analyst calls "soft despite price cuts." Buying that pattern seven days after exiting it for that exact pattern would make my process incoherent.
- AMGN $415.21: trades ABOVE its $383.66 consensus, i.e. 7.6% implied downside, plus an FDA proposal to withdraw Tavneos and a killed obesity program. No.

THE ONE CONCLUSION THAT DROVE THE TRADE: the book made +3.36% in four days and not one thesis was falsified, but consensus upside has compressed across every single leg into a 4.7%-10.7% band. When a whole universe compresses like that, the question stops being "which thesis broke" and becomes "which legs no longer pay me enough for the risk they carry."

decisions.reason: Nothing in this book was falsified this week — the problem is the opposite. The book gained 3.36% in four days and in doing so spent most of its own upside: every leg now sits in a 4.7%-10.7% band to consensus. Two legs no longer clear the bar for what they cost me. XOM goes to zero because it is now the worst position on both axes my mandate cares about, 2.57% yield and 5.28% upside, against CVX at 3.56% and 8.48% off the identical crude driver; my entry thesis already said every dollar in a fixed energy budget is better spent next door, and I only paid for a second operator because both had double-digit upside — that premise is gone. JNJ goes to zero because it is a duplicate function, not a bad company: I hold it purely as low-beta ballast, and MDT does that identical job at 0.57 beta with 154bp more yield and 3.2x the upside, so owning both is paying twice for one role — and JNJ specifically has the lowest yield in the book at 2.06%, cut FY26 EPS guidance again, and keeps deploying cash outside the dividend into Firefly Bio and a $2.58B Sail deal. CVX is trimmed rather than exited because it is my best performer and that is precisely the issue: the Middle East geopolitical premium I flagged at entry as one-headline-reversible has now been banked as a 7% gain while the risk turned into an actual headline, with Trump publicly attacking Big Oil profits and demanding pump-price cuts. I bank part of it and keep 7% for the second-highest yield in the book. The freed 13 points go where the evidence is strongest: 4 to SCHD, because when single-name upside compresses everywhere the right home is a 103-name quality-income basket at 3.04% yield and 0.06% fee rather than another idiosyncratic bet; 2 to MDT, which took a UBS upgrade to Buy on an explicit turnaround call and now absorbs JNJ's ballast role; 2 to ABBV, still the widest gap in the book at 10.74% upside, sized up only two points rather than more because the pending Apogee deal did cut FY26 EPS guidance and that is a real demerit against my entry note. The remaining 5 points go to cash at 15%. That is a considered position, not residue: with the median upside in my entire universe now around 8% and a 3.36% gain already in hand, 4% risk-free is a competitive return, and my mandate names harvesting that cash yield explicitly. I also pulled every take-profit down to just above where the sell-side actually is — +18% on CVX, +15% on ABT and MDT and ABBV were set against wider gaps and would now simply never fill, which is the same correction I made to KO last week.
decisions.novelty: I run no Round-2 book, so the 50% cross-round overlap constraint does not bind here; the genuinely new expression this week is the collapse of a two-operator energy sleeve into a single 7% Chevron leg and the retirement of JNJ in favour of MDT as the sole low-beta ballast, which is a different shape from anything I have run.

positions.thesis: Core anchor, raised from 36% to 40% and now 47% of gross. This is the deliberate destination for capital freed by two single-name exits, and the reason is structural rather than a fresh bullish call: when the upside to consensus on every individual name I own has compressed into a 4.7%-10.7% band, the marginal dollar is better spent buying 103 quality-screened dividend growers than concentrating further into one earnings date. The fund still wins on every axis I selected it for — 30.33% trailing 1yr total return, 3.04% yield, 0.06% expense ratio, 18.1x P/E, $105.7B AUM. It is at an all-time high, which I note and do not treat as a sell signal: this is a rules-based basket that rebalances into quality and cash-flow screens, not a momentum trade with a price memory. Useful second-order effect of concentrating here — its top holdings are ABT at 4.78%, AMGN 4.62% and MRK 4.35%, so I retain diversified large-cap pharma ballast through the basket even after retiring JNJ as a direct line. Deep 12% stop is portfolio-level protection only, not a trading stop on a 103-name basket, and no take-profit because you do not take profits on the compounding core.

Upsized from 11% to 13% and still my largest single name, but deliberately only by two points. It remains the widest gap in the book: $249.46 against a $276.24 consensus from 31 analysts, 10.74% upside, versus 4.7%-8.5% everywhere else I own. The Q2 print I waited out landed right — adj EPS $3.65 on $16.99B revenue, Skyrizi immunology momentum, FY26 revenue guidance held at the raised ~$67.6B, plus FDA acceptance of the supplemental Botox Cosmetic filing. A 53-year raise streak at a 2.77% yield with the earnings binary already banked is still the best risk-adjusted setup in my universe. I add only two points rather than five because one thing did change against me: FY26 adjusted EPS guidance was cut to $13.87-$14.07 to absorb the pending Apogee Therapeutics acquisition. I read that as dilution bought for strategic fit — Apogee is inflammation and immunology, directly adjacent to the Skyrizi franchise that is driving the beat — rather than the core-deceleration-plus-outside-spending pattern that made me exit P&G. But it is a demerit against a thesis that said guidance was raised, and it caps how hard I press. Take-profit comes in from +15% to +12%, which lands just above consensus and can actually fill; the 12% stop stays wide because there is no earnings event before the next reassessment.

Upsized from 7% to 9% and promoted to the book's sole low-beta ballast, taking over the role JNJ was holding. The head-to-head is decisive: MDT yields 3.16% against JNJ's 2.06%, offers 7.86% upside to a $98.44 consensus against JNJ's 4.67%, and does it at the same 0.57 beta — so I was paying twice for one function and keeping the worse half. The 48-consecutive-year aristocrat streak and the richest yield among healthcare aristocrats are intact, and the position is already working, up 4.7% from my $87.16 entry to $91.27. New this week and the actual reason I add rather than merely hold: UBS upgraded to Buy from Neutral with a $100 target on an explicit call that a turnaround is underway, which converts my 'cheap defensive in the bottom third of its range' thesis into one with a named catalyst. Forward P/E of 15.3x against a 24.5x trailing says the earnings recovery is already modelled. Pipeline continues to move — expanded CE Mark for Affera in ventricular arrhythmias, SPR Therapeutics and Scientia Vascular closed. I explicitly give up the one property I praised at entry, that it carried no near-term earnings binary: Sep 1 results are now two weeks out, so the 10% stop stays tight rather than widening to match my other core holds.

Held flat at 9%, which is the right answer for a name where nothing moved. It is up 0.8% since I trimmed it, and the reasoning that took it from 13% to 9% last week — 26.4x for a 2.42% yield with upside compressed to single digits — is unchanged, with the $94.70 consensus now 7.97% away. The business continues to execute: FY26 guidance raised on the Q2 print, volume and organic revenue growth intact, World Cup engagement and zero-sugar demand both cited as drivers, a 62-year King's streak, and 2025 earnings up 23.3%. One new blemish that does not change the size: the fairlife dairy subsidiary took a July cybersecurity incident that halted production at four US facilities before operations resumed — contained, quantifiable, and not a franchise issue. This stays my single staples position and my best staple, held at a real but not oversized weight because the staples complex it belongs to is still the dead-money corner of the market relative to healthcare. Take-profit comes down again from +12% to +9% so it sits essentially at the analyst consensus and can realistically fill rather than expiring worthless; 9% stop unchanged.

Held flat at 7%, and the flat hold is itself the decision because the evidence cut both ways this week. Both specific negatives I cited when trimming from 9% to 7% have now resolved in my favour: Abbott has stated the cybersecurity incidents left no operations affected, removing the unquantified operational unknown, and the 2022 infant formula shareholder lawsuit is settled, removing the last legal overhang after the DOJ probe closed. A new commercial angle also opened — a Google Health partnership integrating Lingo biowearable glucose data with AI coaching, on top of the FDA-approved Freenome SimpleScreen blood-based colorectal test Abbott will commercialize. Against all that, the price did the work first: at $111.25, up 3.2% since I trimmed, the raised $119.40 consensus now implies only 7.33% upside at 36x earnings. Cleared risk plus richer valuation is a wash, so I neither add back nor cut. I also still own it indirectly as SCHD's single largest holding at 4.78%, and since SCHD just went to 40%, my effective Abbott exposure rose to roughly 9% without buying a share — which is precisely why the direct line stays at 7%. Take-profit tightens from +15% to +10% to sit near where the sell-side actually is.

Trimmed from 9% to 7% and now my only energy position, taking the whole sleeve from 15% to 7%. This is my best-performing leg, up about 7% to $200.00, and that is exactly why I cut it: the trade largely worked, and the upside that justified the size has halved from 16.3% at entry to 8.48% against a $216.83 consensus, while the yield that justified it in a dividend mandate fell from 3.82% to 3.56%. More importantly, the one risk I named explicitly at entry has stopped being hypothetical. I wrote that this was the single leg whose thesis had a genuine one-headline reversal risk because the earnings were levered to a Middle East geopolitical premium and there was political pressure on pump prices. This week Chevron itself attributed the Q2 profit surge to that geopolitical premium, and Trump publicly attacked the majors for making too much money and demanded consumer price relief against $48B of quarterly Big Oil profits. When the flagged risk materialises as an actual headline and the compensation for carrying it has halved, the disciplined response is to bank part of the gain rather than re-underwrite at a worse price. I keep 7% rather than exiting because at 13.25x forward with the second-highest yield in the book it still earns income-sleeve capital, and because it beats XOM on every axis. The 10% stop stays for the same one-headline reason; take-profit drops from +18% to +10% because a +18% target from here is simply not a fillable order.

decisions.name: Opus-fleet deep value
decisions.research_notes:
Checked every leg against the 2026-08-10 marks and, critically, against the specific facts I cited when I sized each one. Two of the three macro premises behind last week's book have reversed.

OIL: Brent is $88.52, +5% on the week and +4.2% on the month. The Iran-Oman agreement to reopen Hormuz - the single fact I cited when cutting CVX from 16% to 11% - is deadlocked. Bessent announced unprecedented economic measures alongside a continuing naval blockade of Iranian ports; Houthi militants struck Saudi Arabia's Jazan refinery; the IEA now forecasts the widest global supply deficit in five years for 2026. Brent at $88.52 is back ABOVE the $88-90 level I originally sized CVX up on. Some tankers are running with transponders off but ~9m bbl/d still transits Hormuz under expanding US escort.

RATES: TLT is $82.04, a 52-week low and the lowest since 2024, down on the day. The long end is backing up, not rallying. This is the exact opposite of the 30-year-at-5.20%/hike-odds-42% repricing I used to justify raising VZ and MO. Note these two macro facts are the same trade: an $88 crude with a supply deficit is inflationary, which is why the long bond is at its lows. Energy up and bond proxies down are one coherent move, not two.

PRICES (8/10 entry -> 8/14 close): PFE $26.76 -> $26.79 flat; VZ -> $48.48; C $135.00 -> $139.33 (+3.2%); CVX ~$187 -> $200.00 (+7.0%); VLO $314.95 -> $341.67 (+8.5%, and +14.5% off my 7/31 fill); MO $68.35 -> $65.70 (-3.9%); SMH short $569.41 -> $587.82 (3.2% AGAINST me, so the hedge is losing).

NAMES: PFE raised FY26 revenue guidance by $500m at the midpoint on oncology and Eliquis, announced $2.5bn of incremental productivity savings through 2029, got EMA validation on the Lyme vaccine, and the CEO bought $1m of stock personally - every post-entry datapoint is confirming, price unchanged, 6.42% yield, $28.64 target, 28 analysts at Buy. VZ beat on subscribers with 184k postpaid adds, raised revenue and FCF guidance, and the $1bn+ Google data-centre deal is confirmed; it ROSE this week while its rate proxy hit a 52-week low, so the market is paying for the operating story rather than the coupon. C is 11.93x forward against a $154.50 target (+10.9%), still the cheapest large-cap US bank, buying Kard Financial and hiring aggressively from BofA and Morgan Stanley. VLO is 8.45x forward but now trades 8.4% ABOVE its $315.26 consensus target and within 1.3% of its 52-week high of $346.09; the driver (Hormuz cracks, plus the Jazan refinery strike removing capacity) is intensifying but is by nature the most mean-reverting cash flow in the book. MO deteriorated on its own merits too: Q2 revenue virtually flat with lower profit as oral tobacco softened, Barclays cut to $58 Underweight, and $65.70 vs a $70.00 target leaves 6.5%. SMH is 44.89x with NVIDIA at 21.7% of the fund and the top ten over 71%, and the China-catching-up and capex-bloat narrative is finally turning, but it rose 3.2% against me anyway in the same days the long bond made new lows - the market was handed my mechanism and rejected it.

decisions.reason: Last week I made two explicit macro calls and both premises have since reversed, so consistency requires unwinding them rather than defending them. I cut CVX from 16% to 11% naming one fact: Brent had fallen 7% to $83.55 on a potential Iran-Oman deal to reopen Hormuz. That deal is deadlocked, the US is running a naval blockade of Iranian ports, the Houthis hit Saudi's Jazan refinery, the IEA now sees the widest supply deficit in five years, and Brent is $88.52 - back above the $88-90 I originally sized on. So CVX goes back to 16%. Symmetrically, I raised VZ and MO on a dovish duration repricing with the 30-year at 5.20%; TLT is now at a 52-week low and its lowest since 2024, so the long end is backing up and that tailwind is gone. MO comes back to 5% and VZ to 13%. These are one trade, not two: $88 crude with a supply deficit is what is pushing the long bond to its lows. VLO is the funding source, and this is a deep-value rule I have already applied once to Citi - when a name runs past its analyst target the specific dislocation is harvested. VLO is up 8.5% in four sessions, sits 8.4% above its $315.26 consensus target and 1.3% off its 52-week high, and the crack blowout driving it is geopolitical and mean-reverting; I rotate that capital into CVX, which expresses the identical oil thesis at 13.25x forward with a 3.56% yield and 8.5% of upside to consensus instead of negative upside. C goes 13% to 14% because I trimmed it on 42% hike odds and a steeper curve from a rising long end is the bigger NIM lever I said it was, held back from 15% because $88 oil plus a weak labour market is a genuine consumer-credit risk in its cards book. PFE holds at 20% on unchanged price and four confirming post-entry datapoints including a CEO open-market purchase. The SMH short stays at exactly 5%: the China-catching-up and capex-bloat narrative plus a rising discount rate both argue for it, but SMH rose 3.2% against me this week, and I will not add to a losing short on a mechanism the tape has just rejected.
decisions.novelty: I manage no Round-2 book, so there is no same-direction overlap to constrain; what distinguishes this book is that it is sized by reversing my own prior week's stated premises rather than by chasing the tape - CVX restored on a collapsed Hormuz deal, MO and VZ cut on a long bond at 52-week lows, VLO harvested for trading above its analyst target, and a losing hedge deliberately left unaltered.

positions.thesis: Held flat at the top weight because nothing changed in the price and everything changed for the better in the facts. Since my fill Pfizer raised FY26 revenue guidance by $500m at the midpoint on oncology and Eliquis strength, announced $2.5bn of incremental productivity savings through 2029, secured EMA validation of its Lyme vaccine candidate, and - the datapoint I weight most - the CEO bought $1m of stock in the open market after the print. At $26.79 it is 9.6x forward against a ~19x industry, yields 6.42%, and sits 6.9% below the $28.64 consensus with 28 analysts at Buy. It is the only holding in the book with no AI-capex duration, no oil beta and no economic cyclicality, which is precisely why it carries the largest weight while the rest of the book is repositioned around a crude shock. The one honest negative is that a 6.4% yield is a worse relative proposition with the long bond at a 52-week low - the same duration logic that makes me cut MO. I do not cut PFE for it because PFE is a valuation-and-pipeline holding that happens to yield 6.4%, not a bond proxy, and the tape agrees: flat on the week while MO fell 3.9%. Stop stays wide at -18% so a valuation thesis is never converted into a stop-out by one bad session.

Restored to 16% from 11%, reversing last week's cut in full because the single fact I cut on has evaporated. I wrote that I was unwinding the macro add because Brent had fallen more than 7% to $83.55 on reporting of a potential Iran-Oman agreement to restore Hormuz shipping. Those negotiations are deadlocked, the US is maintaining a naval blockade of Iranian ports alongside what Bessent called unprecedented economic measures, Houthi militants struck Saudi Arabia's Jazan refinery, and the IEA is forecasting the widest global supply deficit in five years for 2026. Brent is $88.52, above the $88-90 that justified the original 16%. I am paying $200.00 rather than the ~$187 I sold at, and that whipsaw cost is the honest price of having sized off a headline; but refusing to re-add now would be defending a position rather than a view. The company leg was never in doubt and is why I keep a real weight regardless of crude: record quarterly net income of $20.59bn, up 50% year over year, production up on Hess and the Permian, record US refinery throughput, and a 20-year Microsoft data-centre power agreement. At 13.25x forward, a 3.56% yield, beta 0.49 and a $216.83 consensus 8.5% above spot, this is the book's cheapest expression of the oil thesis and its inflation hedge.

Nudged back up from 13%. I trimmed it explicitly because September hike odds had fallen from two-thirds to 42%, removing a NIM tailwind. The front end is not the whole story and I said so at the time - a steeper curve is the larger NIM driver - and the long end has now backed up hard, with TLT at a 52-week low and its lowest level since 2024. That is curve steepening, the lever I named. The valuation case is intact: $139.33 is 11.93x forward, still the cheapest large-cap US bank, against a $154.50 consensus implying 10.9% upside, on 2025 revenue of $75.7bn up 6.7% and earnings up 13.6%. Management is also using the balance sheet offensively - the Kard Financial acquisition, a $4.6bn Japan-US investment facility, and aggressive senior hiring from BofA and Morgan Stanley. I stop at 14% rather than restoring the full 15% because the other half of my trim reason is not only intact but worse: an $88 crude shock on top of a labour market that printed negative payrolls with 103,000 of downward revisions is a forward credit-cost signal for a bank whose US Personal Banking and cards book is consumer-levered. And my own correction stays on the record - at roughly 1.34x tangible book there is no buyback-accretion kicker here, just an ordinary cheap bank. Stop stays wide at -20% because the rate debate keeps the group volatile in both directions.

Trimmed from 15% to 13%, a partial rather than a full reversal, because the two legs of my add have diverged. I raised it from 12% purely on duration: a 6% yield re-rating as the 30-year fell to 5.20% and hike odds dropped to 42%. TLT is now at a 52-week low, so that leg is not merely gone but inverted, and discipline says I give back what I took on it. What stops me at 13% instead of 12% is that the operating leg strengthened in the same week and, more tellingly, the stock ROSE while its rate proxy made new lows - the market is paying for the company, not the coupon. Q2 beat on subscribers with 184,000 postpaid adds, full-year revenue and free-cash-flow guidance were raised, the buyback target went to $4.5bn, and the $1bn+ Google dark-fiber deal means the AI buildout pays Verizon rent rather than costing it multiple. At $48.48 it is 12.63x trailing and roughly 9.3x forward with a 5.84% dividend covered by free cash flow, beta 0.24, and a $51.56 target. The reason this is not larger is unchanged and real: SpaceX direct-to-cell is a genuine long-run terminal-value question on the network moat that I cannot dismiss.

Cut from 9% to 6% - harvesting into strength, not exiting. This is the same rule I already applied to Citi and I apply it to myself consistently: once a name runs past the analyst target, the specific dislocation is harvested and what remains is an ordinary holding. VLO went $314.95 to $341.67 in four sessions, is up roughly 14.5% from my 7/31 fill, sits 1.3% below its 52-week high of $346.09, and now trades 8.4% ABOVE the $315.26 consensus target - I bought it when consensus saw 3.85% upside, and consensus now sees downside. The driver is a Hormuz-induced crack blowout: prolonged crude supply disruption sent product prices and refining margins surging, and the Houthi strike on Jazan removes refining capacity, widening cracks further. That driver is intensifying right now, which is exactly why I keep a real 6% and an unchanged +20% take-profit rather than selling out - the crack spike is also, by its nature, the most mean-reverting cash flow in the book. At 8.45x forward on $3.7bn of quarterly net income with renewable diesel swinging positive and a 59% payout, the multiple is still cheap; it is the discount to fair value that has closed, not the business. I tighten the stop from -18% to -12% because the position now sits on a large geopolitical gain that a single Hormuz de-escalation headline could take back, and a wide stop on an extended winner protects nothing.

Back to 5% from 7%, unwinding the duration add and taking the company news as confirmation. I stated plainly that I was raising this because near-zero-beta contracted carry is worth more with the 30-year at 5.20%, hike odds at 42% and payrolls negative. TLT is now at a 52-week low and its lowest since 2024; the long end is backing up, a ~6.5% bond proxy is once again the wrong duration, and the position must come back down. The fundamentals also softened rather than held: Q2 showed virtually flat revenue and lower profit as oral tobacco sales weakened enough to offset cigarette-segment gains, Barclays cut its target to $58 with an Underweight, and the stock is down 3.9% since my fill while the rest of the book rose. At $65.70 against a $70.00 consensus there is 6.5% of upside, which confirms what I already wrote - the deep-value discount here is largely closed. This survives at 5% purely as what I called it: ballast and carry, an 11.9x forward multiple with a 6.45% yield and beta 0.50 in a book that is otherwise long oil and long a consumer-levered bank. It is not a discount trade and I will not pretend it is one.

Held at exactly 5% - deliberately not added to, despite an improving argument, because the tape has not confirmed it. The mandate requires a small short in the most stretched growth cohort and at 44.89x with NVIDIA at 21.7% of the fund and the top ten over 71%, SMH is honestly that cohort. Two things moved my way this week: the narrative turned, with reporting on tech giants' ballooning spending and signs that China may be catching up in the AI arms race, and the discount rate turned, with the long end backing up to its lowest since 2024 - the precise mechanism that argued against me last week now argues for me. The reason I still do not add is that SMH went from $569.41 at my entry to $587.82, 3.2% against me, over the same days the long bond made new lows. The market was handed my mechanism and rejected it. Adding to a losing short on a thesis the tape has just tested and refused is how a hedge becomes a bet, and my own rule from last week was that I size this for survival rather than for a view. 5% of NAV with a -22% stop risks about 1.1% of the book, and 3% borrow is negligible carry. This is insurance against a broad de-rating that would hit my long book, nothing more.

decisions.name: Opus-fleet quality compounders
decisions.research_notes:

NVDA $225.16 (-0.06%). Forward P/E 22.59 vs trailing 34.48; TTM revenue $253.49B, +70.7% y/y; consensus $302.83 (+34.5%), Strong Buy from 61 analysts. New this week, cutting both ways: NVDA is scaling back the $250B OpenAI datacenter guarantee to backstopping only about half of the 10GW project (balance-sheet-protective, supports the net-cash premise), it disclosed a $21B SpaceX stake consistent with the SpaceX-exclusive buildout I underwrote, and Goldman is marketing a $500B AI-infrastructure financing initiative amid rising scrutiny of leverage/vendor-financing circularity. GOOGL $345.90, P/E 17.36 against 2025 earnings +32.0% on revenue +15.1%; still ~15.3% below its $408.61 high, the widest own-tape discount in the book; consensus $428.04 (+24%). Material new item: Berkshire raised its Alphabet stake 83% to a top-three holding in the Q2 13F filed this week — a direct, independent answer to the moat-durability doubt (AI-leadership departures, infrastructure bond raise) that made me cap the add at 2 points last week.

MA $569.29, P/E 31.31. Growth accelerated versus what I underwrote: TTM revenue +16.0%, net income +19.7%, EPS +22.6% (I had modeled net income ~+16%). Consensus $665.26 (+16.9%). BVNK closed, Fiserv merchant-cloud integration live, Synchrony/PayPal financing extended network-wide; Ackman disclosed a new position. V $364.15, P/E 31.00, forward 25.20, consensus $416.20 (+14.3%) — the narrowest upside in the book — and now within 2.7% of its $373.97 52-week high. decisions.name: Opus-fleet price momentum

EVERYTHING ELSE IS WORKING AND UNCHANGED. IWM, KRE, TNA and XLI all printed 100% range position (new 52-week highs); XBI 90.9% with 12m +74.4% and 3m +16.8%; XLV 97.0%; QQQ 92.4%; SPY 99.0%; VIX 14.25 and falling; 10y 4.70%, steady. NEW CANDIDATE THAT EARNED A SLOT: XAR (aerospace/defense) — 100% range position, 1w +3.45%, 1m +14.54%, 3m +9.38%, 12m +38.2%, above all MAs, and the strongest of the defense vehicles (vs ITA 12m +30.5%, PPA +27.1%). It is the equity-beta expression of the same Iran risk premium bidding crude, so it adds the geopolitical hedge without adding more commodity beta.

REJECTED AFTER CHECKING: precious metals (GDX +26% 1m, SLV +16% 1m, but range positions of 56.6%, 34.3% and GLD 50.5% with GLD/SLV below their 200-day — recovering from a break, not an intact trend); uranium (URA 37.5%, URNM 28.7% range position); homebuilders (ITB, XHB both negative on 12m); China (KWEB 20.1% range position, 12m -22.9%; FXI -7.3%); EWZ (below all MAs); IGV and ARKK (12-1 momentum negative); XME (18% 1m spike but 3m negative and 72% range position). decisions.reason: Energy's relative rank flipped from falling-on-every-horizon to rising-on-every-horizon in a single week — XLE went from 9.4% below its high to 0.3% below it, +7.67% on the week, on crude reclaiming $82 as the Iran risk premium came back. I kept a 7% residual precisely as an option on that scenario and it is the second-best leg in the book; a rules-based momentum mandate has to follow the signal back in as readily as it followed it out, and refusing to re-enter because I sold lower would be anchoring, not discipline. I fund it by cutting semis, which are now the only leg below their 50-day with 3m +1.6% and AVGO down 8% on the week, and by trimming the two legs with the weakest 12-month trends (XLV, and a nick off XBI after two flat weeks). I add XAR because aerospace/defense just printed a 52-week high on a +14.5% month and is the equity-beta version of the same geopolitical driver, so it hedges the tail that would hit small-caps, biotech and semis together without doubling my commodity exposure. I deliberately rebuild energy to 12%, not the 36% I ran in July: the driver is a headline premium that has already round-tripped 8% in one session once, so I size it to be additive if the trend persists and survivable if the next Hormuz headline reads the other way. Gross goes 89% to 92% because the tape supports it — SPY at 99% of its range, VIX 14.25, four of my legs at new highs.
decisions.novelty: I do not run a Round-2 book, so there is no same-direction overlap to manage; within Round 3 the novelty this week is the deliberate re-entry into the theme I exited a week ago plus a first-time defense sleeve, both driven by the Iran risk premium re-pricing rather than by any change in the equity themes my mandate names.

positions.thesis: Still the strongest intact trend on my board and the core of the mandate: +74.4% over twelve months, +16.8% over three months, 90.9% of its 52-week range and above all three moving averages. Trimmed two points only because it has gone sideways for two weeks (+0.03% on the week) while energy and defense broke out, so the marginal dollar is better used there — not because anything in equal-weight biotech deteriorated. The 12% stop stays wide because an 8% stop on a high-volatility equal-weight index exits on noise rather than on trend damage.

Closed the week at a fresh 52-week high — 100% range position — with +35.7% over twelve months and +1.17% on the week. This is the cleanest unlevered breakout I own and small-caps are a theme the mandate names explicitly. Unchanged weight because there is nothing to fix: holding the unlevered exposure here is what lets me keep the levered small-cap leg small and stopped independently.

Re-added from a 7% residual on a genuine signal reversal, not a bounce: 99% of its 52-week range, +7.67% on the week, +8.58% on the month, +49.2% over twelve months, above every moving average, and confirmed across the complex by XOP +8.5%, OIH +8.5% and IEO at its own 52-week high. Crude at $82.40 is up 5.4% on the week and 42% YTD on a renewed Iran risk premium. Sized at 12% rather than the 36% I once ran because the driver is a geopolitical premium that erased 8% in a single session on a diplomacy headline three weeks ago, so I want this additive if the trend persists and merely annoying if the headline flips again. The stop is tightened to 8% from 9% for the same reason — I am re-entering near the high, so my margin for error on the entry is smaller than it was in July.

Kept as ballast and trimmed two points. It remains the highest-quality trend I own on the distance-from-high test — 97% of its 52-week range, 0.6% below the high, positive on the week — but +25.0% over twelve months is the weakest twelve-month trend in the book, so it is the natural funding source. Large-cap pharma is bid by the same defensive rotation that would break the small-cap and biotech legs, which is exactly why I keep a meaningful slug of it rather than zeroing it.

Cut from 13% because semis are now the only theme in the book failing the intermediate-horizon momentum test: SMH is the sole leg below its 50-day, 12.1% off its high, and up just 1.6% over three months against a +99.4% twelve-month number that is entirely historical. SOXX and XSD confirm it is the basket and not the wrapper, and AVGO falling 8.1% on the week while sitting 18% below its high shows the damage is concentrated in megacap semis rather than in NVDA. I keep a meaningful position because the twelve-month trend is still the strongest of any unlevered theme I can own and the leg was up 3.2% since I entered it, but I stop pretending leadership is recovering and tighten the stop to 10% so a further break exits rather than bleeds.

Unchanged. Large-cap tech, +27.2% over twelve months, 92.4% of its 52-week range and 1.9% below the high after a +1.11% week. This is the low-volatility way to hold the AI complex next to a now-smaller SMH: with megacap semis the specific thing breaking, the megacap index is absorbing the same theme far better than a 26-stock semiconductor basket is, and the relative price action this month says so.

Held unchanged because it strengthened again: a fresh 52-week high at 100% range position, +2.26% on the week, +15.7% over three months and +29.6% over twelve. A steep curve with the 10-year at 4.70% and a small-cap tape printing new highs are the two things regional banks need, so this leg and IWM reinforce each other on the same macro rather than duplicating a single bet.

The mandate's select-leverage clause, and still the only levered vehicle that earns it. TNA closed at a 52-week high, +3.29% on the week and +8.28% on the month, with 12-month momentum of +104% — versus SOXL at 43.5% of its range with three-month performance of -22.2%, which measures exactly how much daily rebalancing decay each underlying trend has absorbed. In small-caps it has absorbed almost none. Held at 6% so effective exposure is 18% and the 15% stop triggers on roughly a 5% move in IWM, which would be a real failure of the breakout rather than a shakeout.

New position. Aerospace and defense closed the week at a 52-week high with a 100% range position, +3.45% on the week, +14.54% on the month and +38.2% over twelve months, above every moving average — the strongest defense vehicle on every horizon versus ITA at +30.5% and PPA at +27.1% on twelve months. decisions.name: Opus-fleet small/mid-cap growth
decisions.research_notes: Checked the 14 Aug close on every line plus macro.
